title: Falcons Hope Nick Folk Can End Frustrating History at Kicker
full_text:
The Atlanta Falcons have spent the better part of the last two seasons searching for stability at kicker, cycling through multiple options while struggling to find a dependable answer in critical moments.
After going through a lot of kickers in recent years, Atlanta believed it had finally found that consistency by bringing in veteran Nick Folk. However, even with his impressive track record, the Falcons are experiencing some familiar problems.
Folk’s recent struggles have brought renewed attention to the position, making special teams coordinator Craig Aukerman’s confidence in the veteran especially important as the season progresses.
Through eight games, Folk has converted 12 of his 16 field goal attempts and missed an extra point, snapping a streak of 67 consecutive successful extra-point attempts. That is a significant departure from his previous three seasons, when he missed just one field goal in each campaign and consistently ranked among the NFL’s most accurate kickers.
The Falcons’ problems at kicker extend beyond Folk’s current season.
Atlanta went through three different kickers in 2025, with Younghoe Koo, John Parker Romo and Zane Gonzalez all getting opportunities. The trio combined to make 32 of 39 field goal attempts, an 82% conversion rate that ranked among the league’s worst.
There were several costly moments along the way, including Koo’s missed potential game-tying field goal against Tampa Bay in Week 1 and Romo’s missed extra point in a one-point loss to New England.
Those struggles ultimately contributed to Atlanta making a change in the offseason, bringing in Folk and Aukerman in hopes of establishing a more reliable special teams unit.
Folk appeared to be the right answer. Before joining Atlanta, he had led the NFL in field goal percentage in each of the previous three seasons, including a 96.6% mark with the New York Jets in 2025.
Now, the Falcons need that same consistency to return.
Despite the recent misses, Aukerman continues to stand behind his veteran kicker. Speaking to reporters in Madrid ahead of Sunday’s international matchup, Aukerman explained that much of his responsibility involves maintaining Folk’s confidence rather than overcorrecting his technique.
“It’s a little bit of the rain, it’s a little bit of distance, it’s the weather — it’s all these different types of things,” Aukerman said when discussing Folk’s missed 53-yard attempt against Tampa Bay. “And Nick will tell you the first thing, it’s no excuse. Same thing with me. But it just went over to the left a little bit and it’s unfortunate the rain started coming down really hard at that time. But it is what it is.”
Aukerman also emphasized the importance of moving forward instead of allowing one missed opportunity to affect the next.
“My biggest thing is I just want to support him, make sure that he knows that I’m there,” Aukerman said during an earlier press conference. “If he does miss a kick, I know the next one, we have all the confidence in the world with him.”
That relationship could become one of Atlanta’s biggest advantages moving forward. Aukerman previously worked with Folk in Tennessee in 2023, when the veteran enjoyed one of the best stretches of his career. Their familiarity gives the Falcons an established working relationship rather than forcing a kicker and coach to build trust from scratch.
Atlanta has already experienced what happens when consistency is missing at the position. The organization made a significant investment in Folk because of his experience and production, and abandoning that approach after a difficult stretch would be premature.
With Aukerman continuing to offer his support, Atlanta hopes its latest kicking solution can finally end a frustrating stretch at one of football’s most important positions.
Darius has a Master's in Communications from Georgia State and has previous experience covering the Atlanta Falcons with 3 Point Conversion and covering the NFL with On SI.

title: The Usual Suspects Are Up To Their Usual Antics Reporting On Lamar Jackson's Latest Injury. Beware
full_text:
Lamar Jackson does an incredible job of not letting people into his private thoughts or inner circle.
Through years of the highest-profile contract negotiations in modern US sports and for nearly a decade in the NFL, he has managed to keep access merchants and national-media types at bay regarding details and timetables and ongoing machinations of all sorts. And it drives them mad and drives them to extremes to the point that whenever he suffers an injury or reaches another inflection point in his contract, the misinformation and guessing or quasi-information that they peddle for others hoping to influence Jackson in some way or another reaches critical mass.
It never takes long for them to come out telling you when Jackson should be back and will be back; and if you are paying attention, the results speak for themselves. History has a way of repeating and I'd expect more of the same here. I doubt he throws a pass this season and might never again in Baltimore without massive capitulation from owner Steve Bisciotti this offseason.
Of course, many of the very same people who told you there was a “realistic chance” he’d play a week after suffering a high-ankle sprain in Week 4, are up to their usual tricks. The same people who said he would be back for the Packers game last year or who said he would be back for Week 17 two years before that – or certainly the playoff game with the Bengals – now want you to believe they have the scoop on what comes next for Jackson before he has even really begun any sort of recovery from the thumb surgery he just underwent.
Of course, this reporting always frames things like Jackson has every chance to swoop in and save the day. Somehow, it always seems to come from a perspective that would sell hope and expectations to fans, and put that all on one individual. In this case, it's made to seem like the QB has given some sort of explicit promise to his teammates to save them from the front office and coaching staff that is under intense scrutiny for the serious miscalculations they continue to make , and rescue them all.
Meantime, Zay Flowers, one of the players closest to him, wouldn't dare make a public projection about where he would ever catch a pass from Jackson again after he suffered the thumb injury in Week 8: "That's not really anything I can comment on, and that's not anything I can really control in my situation. So, that's something I can't really comment on for you."
And all of this comes at a time when the Ravens are hitting new lows with a young coaching staff during this four game losing streak, while former coach John Harbaugh is the leader for NFL Coach of the Year with the upstart Giants. And with the Ravens pushing back on the obvious notion they should be shedding salary with a bloated roster and terrible cap situation through these same media types,. Al the while successful exec on other NFL teams know what really makes sense for the Ravens by Tuesday afternoon ( selling at the deadline).
The loud truths about the realities of this roster are being shouted by those in the media not constrained by having to protect sources ( and former Ravens players and coaches at that ).  And with all attention being paid on team president Sashi Brown and general manager Eric DeCosta as they assumed even more power and control of the entire organization after replacing a super-established coach with a big voice with a rookie struggling to find his, we get always-ambitious "reporting" about Jackson's ankle injury. The another wave after his thumb was crushed by a pass rusher as soon as he dropped back for the first time upon returning from the significant ankle absence.
As we discussed at length with Bomani Jones on “The Daily Flock” the number of people Jackson actually confides in seems to grow smaller by the years (link to the show is below),. He is going make the decision he needs to make, at the appropriate time, in the best interest of his health and career based on the information available whenever he is close to being cleared to play again.
That's a good six weeks down the line; what all logic and stats and game film is telling you is a Ravens season far more lost than last year’s. Jackson has not played a full game since Brazil in Week 3, which is also conveniently left out of the "reporting" on him. And he reached a point where his future is in no way guaranteed given the poison pills he adroitly negotiated into his contract (no-tag clause, no-trade clause, $84M cap hit) coming to pass while this front office is under scrutiny and this roster is under scrutiny like never before.
He worked long and hard for the right to get to this point where he controls his own destiny through arduous negotiations going back to the conclusion of his third season in the NFL. The idea that he is telling people right now he will be back in December to save the season - and his teammates are taking it as fact - is preposterous. (Watch Flowers's expression when they ask him about Jackson's future last week - I'd trust that.
The idea he is making those decisions now given all the variables laid out above paints him as far less shrewd than he is, and if this feels a lot like the same ‘ol pressure trying to be applied on him from the same ‘ol places playing the same ‘ol games,, you aren't alone. It was just a few weeks ago that Ravens rookie coach Jesse Minter, was facing pointed questions after calling a high-ankle sprain “day-to-day” for nearly three weeks before changing his tune only after Jackson met the media to talk about it.
There has been a different sort of standard that has applied to this quarterback all along.
And it has much to do with the fact he employs no agent, and not even a marketing guy or business manager. Jackson doesn't play the PR game and at this I suspect he never will.
Team Jackson has no one willing or interested in getting in the muck with the types who sling this stuff and live in the muck, which inherently means that those who do will double and triple down on getting their narratives pushed by the scoop jockeys. NFL teams are loaded with them – nepo babies and climbers and wounded execs looking for sympathetic figures in the media who will launder their reputations and push them for jobs and help them create narratives that are incredibly important to their careers and job security.
I lived in that world for 15 years; I know exactly how the sausage is made and who plays the game at the dirtiest and shadiest levels. The stories are uniquely driven by the “sources” of such veiled speculation (then packaged as “reporting”), which is serving the self-interest of those pushing it to whomever will print it first or Tweet it first, with no pushback.
The fact that Jackson has amassed NBA levels of power and control and leverage over the 2027 Baltimore Ravens offseason and roster decisions and, in many respects, their very direction is truly unique ( Domonique Foxworth explained Jackson’s unicorn status ), And it bedevils execs and agents and media-types around the league who cannot control this situation nearly in the way they do most others.
So here is all you need to know about what’s next for Jackson: He will be back when he feels like himself and able to do everything he needs to do to protect himself, especially behind one of the worst offensive lines in the NFL. Only if it also truly makes sense in the standings and, I suspect, only if this looks like a football team that could muster anything in the postseason.
It won’t matter what Minter says in the interim or what the talking heads say between now and then. But rest assured that Minter, who would not even comment last week on if surgery has taken place, will continue to call it a decision where the player and doctors and team all agree it’s right for him to play.
“I think it's just a decision for his best interest,” Minter said often in October during the ankle injury. “That's really what every decision is always going to be about."
Jackson…

title: Report: Lamar Jackson Informed Ravens Teammates Of Intent To Return In 2026
full_text:
The Baltimore Ravens are in the midst of an historically horrific four-game losing streak in which their offense has averaged just under 11 points per game and the defense is allowing nearly 30 points per game.
While it doesn't feel like there's much to be hopeful about as it pertains to the Charm City franchise, the face of it isn't ready to throw in the towel just yet. According to a report from NFL Network's Ian Rapoport , star quarterback Lamar Jackson told his teammates that he plans to return this season, with the hope of leading them on a late-season push for the postseason.
In his first game back after missing three games with a high ankle sprain, the two-time league MVP suffered an injury to his right thumb on the first play from scrimmage in a Week 8 loss to the Buffalo Bills . Per Rapoport's source, the three-time First Team All Pro selection underwent surgery to repair a fracture and dislocation in his injured throwing hand.
The Ravens placed Jackson on injured reserve, along with primary backup Tyler Huntley, who suffered a season-ending turf toe injury in the same game and half against the Bills. Thankfully, the typical recovery for Jackson's injury is at least six weeks, although it could take up to nine weeks.
Jackson's message to the team that was paraphrased to Rapoport was, "Just stay alive."
After starting the season winning four of their first five games, the Ravens now sit at 4-5 and currently sit outside of the current playoff picture at the bottom of the AFC North division standings. With eight games and a bye week remaining on their schedule, in order to return to the postseason after just falling short last year, they'll need to start stacking some wins.
The earliest Jackson is eligible to return is Week 14, when the Ravens host the Tampa Bay Buccaneers, following the team's Week 13 bye. That will be five weeks post-op and at the earliest possible end of the spectrum for his potential return.
Fortunately for the Ravens, unlike their last four opponents, who all possess winning records, their next four all have records under .500. It's a far less arduous stretch, and they brought in much-needed reinforcements at quarterback by trading for veteran journeyman Jacoby Brissett to steady the ship on offense and take some pressure off their struggling defense.
If the Ravens can rattle off four straight wins or at least go 2-2 over that span, they'll be in a great position to make Jackson's push to return worthwhile. It'd be just in time for their final four games, all of which are against AFC North rivals, including a pair of bouts with the current division-leading Pittsburgh Steelers.
The first team standing Baltimore's way is the winless Los Angeles Chargers, who just dropped their eighth straight to start the season in a 44-22 blowout loss to the Houston Texans in Week 9, which might have them consider giving their face of the franchise a much-needed mental reset.
In his second game back from a bye, the Chargers' two-time Pro Bowl QB, Justin Herbert, continued to look like a shell of himself as he was sacked a career-high eight times, added to his league-leading interception total and might've suffered a fractured finger on his left non-throwing hand.
This matchup between  two ailing and surprisingly underperforming teams will take place under national spotlight on Monday Night Football. It has all the makings of the ultimate GBOT (get back on track) for the Ravens on both sides of the ball.
On offense, Brissett helped lead the Arizona Cardinals to an impressive upset win over the Chargers in Week 1 and is poised to beat them again after they just allowed C.J. Stroud to carve them up through the air for almost 400 passing yards and five touchdowns. Defensively, this is the perfect oppertunity for the pass rush to get going, for the secondary to make plays on the ball and front seven to dominate the line of scrimmage.
If the Ravens want keep any glimmer of hope of still being alive and in contention for the postseason by the time Jackson is able to return to action, they can't afford to lose to the only winless team in the league. It might end up being a battle of backup quarterbacks if the Chargers decide to sit Herbert so he doesn't embarass himself or get further banged up in primetime.
Josh is a writer for Baltimore Ravens On SI focusing primarily on original content and reporting. He provides analysis, breakdowns, profiles, and reports on important news and transactions from and about the Ravens. His professional resume as a sports reporter includes covering local events, teams, and athletes in his hometown of Anchorage, Alaska for Anchorage Daily News. His coverage on the Ravens and other NFL teams has been featured on Heavy.com/sports, Maryland Sports Blog and most recently Baltimore Beatdown from 2021 until 2025.

title: The Ravens Shunned Experienced Coaches After Firing John Harbaugh. So Far, That Looks Regrettable
full_text:
The Ravens ran a funky head coaching search.
They gave a nominal look at former Browns head coach Kevin Stefanski, a two-time coach of the year, but people close to that coach all along felt like Baltimore wasn’t really interested and he quickly ended up in Atlanta. After general manager Eric DeCosta won the power struggle with potential Hall of Fame head coach John Harbaugh following a terrible 2025 season, the NFL believed Baltimore wanted a young guy.
Owner Steve Bisciotti defended DeCosta’s personnel record to a ridiculous level (“he’s batting .800”) and made a point of letting his fans know DeCosta and team president Sashi Brown had wide swath over the coaching search. The Lombardi Trophy expectations were still the same (“pursuing championships,” Brown said) but they seemed to wanted a guy with roots in their building all along. Even when Buffalo surprisingly fired Sean McDermott – who had won at least one playoff game five straight years – Baltimore made no effort whatsoever to even reach out.
“Not a phone call – nothing,” said one league source with direct knowledge of the situation.
It was going to be Minter and it was Minter – seen as a product of their front office and “winning culture” from his days as a young assistant in Baltimore. The question always lingered around the NFL – was that the right dynamic? Should they really have one of only two staffs in the entire league without a former NFL head coach on it ? And with Harbaugh clearly making a push for NFL Coach of the Year with the Giants (5-2-1 in first place)– a team short on proven starpower and one of the youngest teams in the NFL – execs around the NFL are talking about Baltimore’s lack of direction.
If the team had the alleged roster DeCosta thought it did – with two-time MVP Lamar Jackson having total leverage over the team in 2027 ) would a bunch of novice head coaches be able to get them to click immediately, and take them beyond where Harbaugh could? Shouldn’t experience have been more the rule, if not for the head coach than for the bulk of his staff? Did Brown and DeCosta prize consolidation of power and lack of pushback from first-time coaches over truly trying to seek the best and brightest available to get the team over the top?
With the Ravens likely already having played their last truly meaningful game of the season already and a season spiraling wildly out of control , doing things on offense and defense that are unprecedented in franchise history (in the worst way possible), it’s a disaster. There is a cogent case to be made that DeCosta should have been fired after offensive-line debacle he authored in Buffalo in Week 7.
It would be a surprise if the Ravens (4-5) did the right thing and sold at the trade deadline and it would be even more surprising (with two AFC wins against teams that have three total wins between them) if they salvaged this season. And there is a growing sense that the profile of this staff does not mesh with what was an overwhelmingly veteran roster (in fact, too old and too overpaid at too many key starting spots).
One NFL GM told me over the summer: “Older team, heavy expectations, really young staff. That’s a weird mix.”
I’ve heard variations of this from several people around the NFL I’ve probed about the Ravens in recent weeks. And it makes total sense, and, frankly, made total sense all along.
“Look, that’s an older team, a team that can’t get over the hump, a lot of guys who are in their last year there,” said one longtime NFL personnel executive who has watched the Giants and Ravens closely, among others. “They are used to being coached by experienced coaches, and doing things a certain way.
“You bring in a bunch of young guys, a lot of them have never done it before, you set yourself up for problems. You bring in a bunch of college coaches – that’s not the same thing. Those guys are recruiting, there is so much they do … it’s just not the same thing as what goes on in the NFL. The players see everything. They are going to get away with as much as they can, and that’s what you’re seeing out there …
“You’re seeing it, really, on defense more than anywhere else, and trust me, that’s a big problem in that building right now. They all see the same thing we do. That’s Jesse Minter’s side of the ball. And then look at New York. Total opposite.
“They have a young team, bunch of college kids, don’t know how to win yet. They got a guy who is super experienced and knows how to win. They know the kind of staff he’s going to bring, and the young players see that. That defense is overachieving. It’s the opposite of Baltimore. They’ve got big problems. The film is bad.”
Another NFL GM told me: “A lot of us were saying it when they set up the interviews. Minter was their guy. DeCosta wanted young guys he could control. Now they have to try to fix it.”
Minter is going to have to learn to juggle running a defense and coaching the entire football team at the same time. Declan Doyle still doesn’t even know here he should be calling plays from ( try it from the sidelines, rook). The choking that began under Harbaugh immediately met new lows under this staff.
We’ll never know what might have been with a staff led be proven winners. That’s never where this was going. But there is no denying the impact Harbaugh immediately made with the Giants , and no denying just how massive Minter’s learning curve has proven to be.
Jason has covered sports professionally for newspapers, websites and broadcast networks since 1996 and have covered the NFL extensively for The Washington Post, CBS Sports and The NFL Network from 2004-2025.

title: Ravens Midseason Report Card: Grading The Front Office, Coaches, Offense, Defense And Special Teams
full_text:
The Baltimore Ravens have been trying to convince their fans for years that they are a premier organization despite mustering one meaningful playoff run in all of Lamar Jackson’s 20s and despite churning through coordinators and since Eric DeCosta took over as general manager and despite missing the playoffs last year and looking like an afterthought by Halloween this year.
Terms like “Play Like a Raven” and all of their claims about their “winning culture” are landing with a thud both with fans and a growing number of former star players and coaches lashing out at this regime on social media and on “The Daily Flock Show” (Wink Martindale and Marvin Lewis, for starters).  They have the NFL’s worst projected 2027 salary cap situation and a remarkably-bloated payroll in which most of their highest-paid players are their least productive players.
It’s a total mess,  their 4-5 record flatters them (they had arguably the easiest schedule in the NFL the first six weeks), and they have four straight losses (outscored 117-43); they have scored 14 points or less in four straight games for the first time ever, while allowing 33 or more in three straight. The idea that Jackson is going to come back from a consecutive major injuries and try to rescue them in mid December given his dubious contract situation ( quite a bind DeCosta put the franchise in) , strikes the NFL at large as truly laughable.
It’s hard to find much to be bullish on nine games into a new staff that lacked any semblance of what any Super Bowl coaching staff would ever look like (it actually has more in common with tanking Miami than any in the NFL ), working for a front office that scapegoated a slew of former coaches only for its roster to be utterly exposed for yet another year.
Yeah, John Harbaugh had to go because the message had worn out, but the league knew Jesse Mintner was almost certain to get this job, no one with former head coaching experience was a part of their finalists and now the Ravens are the worst second-half team in the NFL – that’s coaching and that’s on DeCosta and Sashi Brown who oversaw this, and owner Steve Bisciotti who gave them free reign.
Brown said when Minter was hired: “We're at an important time for our locker room. We know we have the talent to go out and pursue championships now. When we set out to find our new coach, we wanted to make sure that we were very serious about bringing a great leader, but also a great person to this organization, to our locker room, and we found that in Jesse Minter, ”
The locker room is a bigger disaster than ever, Minter was openly wondering who his leaders were by October, he has made zero adjustments to change games or the direction of the season. The roster is bad, keeping Marlon Humphrey for $19.3M instead of paying him $4M to go away was always kinda nuts ( we tried to help them in April ), running a $370M payroll with almost no playmakers on either side of the ball is a bitter pill for fans and doubling down on a bad situation by sending a second-round pick for a concussed offensive lineman was silly in real-time .
The injuries are tough but this is an attrition sport.  He was billed as a defensive savant who would fix their coverages and bring the best out of a secondary literally loaded with DeCosta’s first-round picks. They have the second-worst opposer passer rating in the second half and his dime coverages were destroyed by bad QBs and the one thing he couldn’t do was blow a double-digit second half lead in his first home game given that DeCosta’s rosters have made a nasty habit of doing it and it was a big reason why Harbaugh and former defensive coordinator Zach Orr were fired.
We all know how that played out against the lowly Saint and then got way too close for comfort against the lowly Titans.
Minter has been demonstrably worse than Orr was last year The lack of second-half adjustments has been staggering and the fact that he allowed an offensive staff with zero coaches with a proven coordinator pedigree to be constructed around him was a big fail. The fact he has a 4-5 record is keeping him from an F but the reality is, he is so overmatched trying to be an NFL head coach he has turned into one of the worst defensive coordinators in the NFL (the fact the Chargers defense he left is markedly better than this one in Baltimore should be giving the honchos in The Castle significant pause).
He needed more help all along and it was clear after 3-4 games he was over his head and Martindale and'or Lewis should have been on this staff.
It was an A with Jackson against really bad teams for a few weeks, but it’s been a total failure without him and when we are heading to Week 10 on what was supposed to be a loaded Super Bowl team and literally two people on offense are meeting or exceeding expectations (Zay Flowers and rookie guard Vega Ioane), that's a D at best.
Flowers is somehow more of a one-man show now more than ever. No one else on the team has 300 receiving yards, no one else gets YAC and the Ravens have produced 10 total points in the second half the last four weeks. Rookie coordinator Declan Doyle needs to get out of the press box and down to the sideline and someone needs to tell him that trying to script the entire game before it starts isn’t the answer, either.
Oh, and Derrick Henry is averaging a ridiculous 3.4 yards/carry the last four weeks and the run game is cooked with Jackson making it go. The decision to give Mark Andrews the money Isaiah Likely wouldn't take before hitting the open market would be enough to get DeCosta fired in a truly competitive front office but the owner claims he "bats .800" with transactions, so whatever.
None of their highest-paid players are performing anywhere close to how they are being paid.  They are already making excuses for Hendrickson’s staggering lack of fourth-quarter production after anointing him THE CLOSER . Even Kyle Hamilton has had a muted presence, he hasn’t been deployed to help a limp pass rush enough and hasn’t showed up in the pass game hardly at all.
Minter was supposed to be the guy to develop all these draft picks. After proving he can lead the NFL in second-half points allowed through nine weeks he needs to show that TJ Tampa can be a starting corner and figure out if Trenton Simpson or Teddye Buchanan can wear the green dot next season and get second-round pick Zion Young on the field much more. This was supposed to be the group that hit the ground running with Minter running a defense very close to Mike Macdonald’s Baltimore defense that led the NFL in points allowed, sacks and takeaways in 2023.
The Ravens have been on the look for a weapon in the return game for years … that continues. They continue to succumb to silly penalties on teams at the worst times. With an undrafted rookie QB playing on a badly taped ankle on a short week in the rain against the NFL’s second-best scoring defense they failed to provide field position.
Oh, Tyler Loop, a 2025 draft pick, has yet to establish himself as an NFL kicker – on field goals or kickoffs – and was probably getting benched for Jake Moody if he didn’t hurt his groin. The rookie punter will be a work in progress. This was an area in which Harbaugh, a former special teams coach, took a lot of heat but it remains an area of concern.
Jason has covered sports professionally for newspapers, websites and broadcast networks since 1996 and have covered the NFL extensively for The Washington Post, CBS Sports and The NFL Network from 2004-2025.

title: One Ravens Player Who Should Surprisingly Be Traded Before the Deadline
full_text:
There is no ideal time to get out of the Trey Hendrickson contract. Only a half season into what amounts to a two-year, $60M deal it looks pretty disastrous.
And, like oh so many of the contracts executed by failing general manager Eric Decosta , it carries nasty cap and cash ramifications for a team in salary-cap hell because of terrible contract situations with Mark Andrews, Marlon Humphrey, Roquan Smith, John Simpson and others. All the while Tyler Linderbaum and Isaiah Likely and Charlie Kolar and Pat Ricard left as free agents.
That’s bad business. And worse football.
Oh, and unlike every other NFL team with an elite quarterback, they can never get Lamar Jackson extended when they should when the market resets, so his $84M cap hit in 2027 hangs over everything ( he controls their offseason ) while their season spirals to the abyss. This is a mess. It runs years deep into the future and every effort should and must be made to start getting out of it (the entire league sees this for what it is ). And, believe it or not, there is also a case to be made that moving on from Hendrickson – one of the more consequential signings in recent franchise history.
This season is over – not even the Ravens themselves can seriously believe Jackson is going to swoop into this tragedy in all three phases of football and bail them out against all odds in December – and, this I can tell you without a doubt, the conversations about their horrific cash/cap outlays in future are well underway. No one could dare sugarcoat that (especially with Jackson having all contract leverage with the no-trade and no-tag provisions).
Given all of that, here’s why I’d advise getting out of Hendrickson now by any means necessary.
This was really a play for 2026, trying to win right away despite the most inexperienced (and as we’ve come to find out, naive, coaching staff in the NFL (even Miami’s head coach had been a college head coach before, and this staff has more in common with Miami’s than any in the NFL ). Hendrickson was their parachute when the front office had second thoughts about trading two first-round picks for Maxx Crosby (turns out he was worth it) to address years of a suspect pass rush.
Hendrickson was lingering on the market because he was 32, he can’t play the run and that will only get much worse at that age. He has been injury prone lately and he spent a lot of time finding reasons not to play for the Bengals in recent years. His financial ask was seen as to steep according to execs from multiple teams who were exploring pass-rush options, and when DeCosta pounced executives around the league began calling this out. DeCosta, meantime, tried to sell his fans on a master plan to and Crosby and Hendrickson .
Hendrickson looked like a $30M a year guy in Week 1 against the hapless Colts, hurt his finger and has not shown up in the fourth quarter all season. Hailed as a closer, undrafted special teams rookie Ethan Burke has more sacks than him in the fourth quarter. He isn’t even in the top two on the team in sacks and this pass rush is impotent (3.5 sacks leads them). His 12% pressure rate in the fourth quarter is a try-hard guy, not a game-wrecker and 2027 it a retool year no matter how they try to spin it.
“This isn’t going to age well,” said one longtime NFL personnel executive who has watched Hendrickson closely. “You make a move like that, something they never do (big free-agent signing), Year One, he’s supposed to pop.
“Come in, take the game over, make the young guys better.  You see the same thing I do ... They talked him up like the guy who changes your defense when he walks in the locker room and they still blow a lead every time they get it with this guy  … This is worse than (former defensive coordinator Zach) Orr’s tape, and they stuck him with (aging quasi-pass rusher Kyle) Van Noy.
“This is a disaster, man. Don’t let anybody tell you anything different. I watched his tape. It gets worse every week … They have the hand bandaged up like an amputee. The guys (broadcasting the games) in the booth can’t miss it. That’s all you’re going to hear about now.”
Indeed, overmatched rookie head coach Jesse Minter, when asked about mustering two sacks in the last three games while allowing 33 points or more in all of them, immediately brought up Hendrickson’s finger procedure from early in the season. They had seven total pressures as a team with their season on the line against Jacksonville at home, mind you, and THE CLOSER had none.
“We have one guy really kind of playing through having one free hand,” he said. So all the more reason to sit him – better yet: man up and trade him – and play the kids after four straight horrific losses with Hendrickson doing nothing to help the NFL’s worst second-half defense (while leading the league in choking).
Mike Green is one of few ascending young defensive players on this roster, he should be playing more and while he isn’t special against the run he is a helluva lot better than Hendrickson (especially playing with one hand). They both primarily want to line up over the left tackle. One is young and cheap and the other makes $29M more next year.
Does having Hendrickson coming off a washout first season here set to be the second-highest paid player on the team next year make sense when you know Steve Bisciotti is going to want to cut payroll after DeCosta lit $370M on fire this year and couldn’t keep them truly in the hunt past Halloween? Does having him blocking guys like Tavius Robinson (on IR for weeks and still more sacks than Hendrickson) in 2027 make sense? And what about the growth of DeCosta’s latest day-two pass rush reach (my does the epic list of failures here run long ) Zion Young, and Green, too?
And if you are scoring at home, the Ravens are getting real low on draft capital after panic moves for Cam Jurgens (we told you that was an all-time laugher in real-time ) and Jacoby Brissett. They need picks, badly. And with DeCosta’s draft record so poor, they really need all the picks they can get. And with so many bad contracts they don't have many they can get anything back for.
As one GM said: "(Hendrickson contract) looks terrible now, and it was questionable when they did it, especially after the Crosby thing ... Could (Hendrickson) get one, year, $30M, fully guaranteed, right now, coming off this, if he was a UFA (unrestricted free agent)?"
Yeah, trading him now will only save $2M against the cap next year, but every penny helps especially if they have to carry Jackson into the league year at $84M. This team is stuck with basically $100M in cap/dead cap tied up in Andrews, Humphrey, Simpson, Smith, Ronnie Stanley, Derrick Henry, Rashod Bateman no matter what they do (designating two as post-June 1 cuts would help some, but not all that much).
If they wait to make a move on Hendrickson until 2027, you are looking at a $25M cap hit and if they deal him now and admit defeat, that number would be $16M for 2027. He hasn’t been the kind of guy who can put together a full season to be worth $30M a year for a while now, and even these masters of gaslighting till have a hard time pretending they have a Lombardi roster next year.
Is that a risk the Ravens should be willing to take again in 2027 with that $29M fully guaranteed? I sure wouldn't.
Jason has covered sports professionally for newspapers, websites and broadcast networks since 1996 and have covered the NFL extensively for The Washington Post, CBS Sports and The NFL Network from 2004-2025.

title: What We're Hearing About the Ravens Ahead of the NFL Trade Deadline
full_text:
The Ravens are a team many opposing front offices are enjoying watch squirm, with their reputation for hubris and stubbornness – much like the Orioles – catching up to them.
And with the franchise carrying one of the least enviable payroll, roster and contractual situations into the trade deadline next week, they are going to get solicited for select veterans. Whether they think its beneath them or not.
At 4-5, in a four-game losing, allowing 33 points or more in three straight games with one of the worst defenses on the planet and going four in a row failing to score even 14 points for the first time in franchise history with a rookie coordinator they called a genius all summer, they are going nowhere. Two-time MVP quarterback Lamar Jackson has them completely by the throat with how his contract is structured ($84M cap hit next season with a no-trade and no-tag provision) and they not only have the worst salary cap situation in the NFL right now, they have by far the worst projected cap in 2027.
And there are no easy solutions until or unless they get Jackson extended, and even a trade before June 1 would wreck their cap ($74M cap hit), and a trade after June 1 means they are carrying him into the League Year in March counting $84M against the cap and giving them scant chance to build a roster. NFL GMs are baffled by their trade for Cam Jurgens as we reported on in real-time , and two who have looked at their cap situation believe they are essentially handcuffed in 2027 no matter what they do at this deadline.
“It’s not the worst I’ve ever seen,” one GM said, “but the quarterback (Lamar Jackson) makes it unique. They are at his mercy, really ... They have a bunch of really bad contracts they’re going to have a hard time getting out of. They’re pretty screwed. It’s really bad.”
Our friend Mark Levin, who helped Jackson negotiate his contract extension (and explained the uniqueness of that process on the “The Daily Flock” in May ) while running the salary cap and administration department of the NFL Players Association, is studying the situation for us as well. Levin oversaw the cap for the Washington Commanders prior to that and is a unique expert on these matters and went over every key Ravens contract with us this week.
“It’s definitely a mess,” he said when asked him for some historical perspective on how the Ravens cap currently looks for 2027 and 2028. “I don’t think that I could say I’ve never seen anything like it … But this is not going to be an easy fix. They're in a really tough spot.”
The Ravens can’t restructure their way out of it, the voidable years bills are coming due whether they cut their legion of bad players on bloated contracts or trade what they can, and the league is watching closely while the coaches they fired are exceeding expectations with the Giants and Browns. So what do other execs think that means for the deadline?
The general consensus is that, given general manager Eric DeCosta’s track record and how they are trying to sell this season as not the disaster that it is, and the fact they have some injuries to hide behind, it’s viewed as unlikely they sell close to as aggressively as probably warranted. Owner Steve Bisciotti would have to be fully on board, and DeCosta has already made desperate moves, giving away fourth-round value just Friday to complete a trade for benched journeyman QB Jacoby Brissett.
“DeCosta won’t sell,” said a high-ranking official from a team that has faced the Ravens this season and does not think highly of their talent or contract situation whatsoever. “To him that’s a sign of weakness … He started making panic moves in October. Those guys are completely full of (garbage).”
The GM said: “What do I think he’s going do? He just added Brissett. That’s telling you, isn’t it? … Nobody he thinks he’ll really be a seller. I don’t see it.”
As to who the industry believes the Ravens should move – Derrick Henry top the list . After 17 carries for 57 yards Thursday; right at the abysmal 3.4 yards/carry he has averaged the last four weeks behind a broken offensive line while leading the NFL in carries at age 32, this is over. Multiple execs told me the Ravens could get a fourth-round pick for him, most likely, perhaps with contingencies for more based on his production with the new team.
“It’s not going to work for him there without Lamar,” the exec noted. “They can’t win up front.”
Henry would still count $15M in dead cap next year even if dealt.
The contract makes this complicated – DeCosta really did a number here. Stanley is struggling with penalties and he doesn’t seem comfortable in this new offense and has played unsure. But left tackles with his pedigree aren’t everywhere and there are plenty of contenders who could find a spot for him and maybe some even wondering how he might fare on the right side if need be. Without having to worry about protecting Jackson’s blindside anymore now would be a great time to find out what young tackle Carson Vinson could do.
Our pal Marty Hurney, longtime NFL GM, who joined us on “The Daily Flock” this week, believes the Ravens could get a fourth-round pick for Stanley (assuming teams are okay with medicals; a big issue for him in the past).  Other execs have implied the same, but this is another player the GM has made a favorite over the years, so there is skepticism he’d do what needs to be done. Like the rest of this, we only saw this coming back in the spring ( as explained on April 13) .
Oh, and Stanley will count $28M in deal cap in 2027 if dealt, so there’s that.
He was a bottom 10 starting corner in the NFL last year by any measure and rather than pay him $4M to leave DeCosta paid him $19.3M to obliterate the locker room and secondary yet again. Pays to be a made man! Spoke to a member of the Jaguars organization a little but before Thursday’s game. Here’s what he said:
“We are coming right after 44 (Humphrey). (Head coach) Liam (Coen) is going to attack him. He has a target on his back every week … Everybody threw on him and the other guy (Nate Wiggins) all last year. What are they doing over there?”
Humphrey was beat for 50 yards by a blocking tight end off the jump. Nobody is paying him $7.5M for the rest of the season. I suggested a total salary dump in exchange for reserve QB Joe Milton before the season – that’s how devalued this player is everywhere except in Owings Mills (Jerry Jones might have taken on the salary). And he’ll count $12M against the cap in 2027 even when he’s gone as a free agent (good luck with the comp pick there).
Maybe he wants to stay on this sinking ship in what the 40-year-old said was almost certainly his final NFL season. He is incredibly close with defensive coordinator Anthony Weaver, and loved his first sting in Baltimore, but brings elite leadership and is a world-class teammate and on a functional defense as part of a decent rotation, he can provide value.
“Who wouldn’t want Calais on their football team,” the exec said, noting the return would be minimal.
Campbell would not count against next year’s cap if traded.
The GM said: “He doesn’t do much for me. They like him a lot more than we ever did … I guess you could something for him.” Hurney told us on “The Daily Flock ” this week getting anything for Bateman would be addition by subtraction. A real front office would explore it vigorously and maybe let fourth-round pick Elijah Sarratt actually be active for some of this embarrassing defeats.
Bateman would count $8M in dead cap next year is dealt.
The Ravens are stuck with Mark Andrews ( he can't even handle a direct snap now ) and will have to pay him $5M guaranteed next year no matter what and eat $16M in dead cap to cut him. DeCosta giving him Isaiah Likely's money really blew up in his face.
Roquan Smith being still due $10M this season negates any chance of moving him unless the Ravens took on a significant chunk of that total. “More than half, for definitely,” the GM said to have any chance to trade him. He’d…

title: Ex-Ravens DC Zach Orr Was Flogged Then Fired After 2 Seasons. Jesse Minter's Defense Is Significantly Worse
full_text:
The Baltimore Ravens gushed about what a remarkable defensive mind Jesse Minter was when they hired him at age 42, with just two years of experience as an NFL defensive coordinator, to replace John Harbaugh, who is building a credible case for the Hall of Fame and might be the NFL Coach of the Year this season.
They hailed him as a genius of sorts and leaned into to any and all comparisons to true unicorn Mike Macdonald, former Ravens coordinator who went 10-7 as a rookie head coach in Seattle and won the Super Bowl last season. They hailed the fact Minter had Ravens roots – serving as a young assistant in Baltimore before – and therefore was an extension of their culture and winning formula and understood all the vast intricacies of what made them such a first-rate organization.
You see, what owner Steve Bisciotti and team president Sashi Brown and general manager Eric DeCosta were pushing out highly accomplished veteran coaches to hire young, cheap and malleable replacements, the implication was they had all the answers within their front office; these bright young minds coupled with DeCosta’s Lombardi-worthy roster would immediately put them over the top.
“Exciting time for us,” Brown said when introducing Minter as head coach. “Thirty years in the books of Ravens football history here in Baltimore, and we're at an important time for our locker room. We know we have the talent to go out and pursue championships now. When we set out to find our new coach, we wanted to make sure that we were very serious about bringing a great leader, but also a great person to this organization, to our locker room, and we found that in Jesse Minter.”
And indeed, Minter has made a remarkable and indelible imprint in his first nine games on the job  - the season is effectively over in November after four straight ugly defeats, and this product is less professional-grade than before (three QBs hurt on about 12 snaps has to be a record). Minter actually increased the franchise’s already record rate for blowing double-digit, second-half leads to lose. Minter, unquestionably, has made the defense - his calling card and the one thing his very presence was supposed to make demonstrably better – a failure in ways beyond what his predecessor, Zach Orr, dragged for two years by critics before getting fired, could muster.
Minter to this point has been unfit to perform either duty he was hired for, things are only getting worse, and everything about his messaging and lack of accountability and pathetic lowering of standards from week to week to try to obfuscate from just what an abomination this is should be beneath this once-proud franchise. Instead it captures exactly what DeCosta and Brown have constructed – with the worst cap situation in the NFL for years to come it will get worse . And if the Ravens allow him to keep wearing both hats, and if they abstain from gutting this roster at the trade deadline like any competent staff would spend every waking hour trying to do , it will only reveal even further how detached from reality they are.
“I believe in our guys,“ Minter said when asked about the trade deadline Thursday. “I think that there's a lot of things that we need to look at and improve on, but I do think that we have a team ... In really all three phases, there's spurts of good enough football. There is a real inconsistency, I would say, at all three levels, all three phases. And again, some of that is due to whatever, but that is what it is … I do think there's a good opportunity for this team."
SPURTS OF GOOD ENOUGH FOOTBALL IS THE NEW “PLAY LIKE A RAVEN.”
That’s the best they can offer. Lamar Jackson props them all up, or they fail. Will they allow Minter to be unmasked at two jobs instead of one and will they keep this Frankenstein roster through the deadline and run it back in 2027?
Minter’s defense is quite likely going to get worse, given it already has shown strong quitting tendencies (as former Ravens luminaries have pointed out on social media and as former coordinator Wink Martindale made very clear on “The Daily Flock Show” ). Minter got exposed by Trevor Lawrence on throws of 10 yards or more (8/10 for 193 yards and TD) and passes to the middle of the field (12/14 for 154 yds and TD).
Minter had no solutions; nothing even remotely close (it’s the roster and the culture).
He can’t get $19M corner Marlon Humphrey to cover a glorified tackle eligible 50 yards downfield or a first-round safety, Maliki Starks, who he was supposed to turn into a star in Year Two, to ever make a play on the ball or be the last line of defense when desperately needed. They jumped offside to give Jacksonville a critical fourth-down conversion before falling apart to give the game away in the first half (the penalties are shameful and they lead the league pre-snap – no surprise to regular readers . Their $60M fully guaranteed “closer” Trey Hendrickson was held without a pressure, hurry or hit, let alone a sack, and he can’t play the run and will be 33 next season.
Well, at least he had that revenge game against the Bengals! (If the Raiders keep Maxx Crosby, and Lamar decides to stay in Baltimore, best not dress him for that game with Vegas. Mad Maxx has every reason to hold a grudge against this front office).
And Orr didn’t have a $150M defensive roster and an alleged All-Pro edge rusher; he had Kyle Van Noy and Dre’Mont Jones past their prime. Let’s compare the 2025 and 2026 defenses (and, again, these numbers will get worse this season):
Points/Drive Allowed: 2.20                 2.31
TD% Allowed: 23%                 24%
Opposer Pass Rating: 89.6                 96.1
Pass Plays 25+ (thru 9 G): 17                    18
Yards/Attempt: 7.0                   7.6
INT% : 1.8%                1.4%
Sack %: 4.8%                5.9%
Pressure Rate: 31.7%              35%
Hold up, Orr gets killed for having to blitz to generate any pretend pass rush at all with a decidedly cheaper and lesser roster and he has to survive virtually all of last season without Nnamdi Madubuike after the September injury, and he still outclasses his successor? How's that happen?
Minter is scared to call a game like a big boy and bring any heat, he has Hendrickson and Madubuike and Mike Green in Year Two (another alleged breakout) and Calais Campbell is back and instead of fixing their massive hole at hole in the second round DeCosta give Minter another edge presence, Zion Young, who they called a pass rusher and we told you he was not. (Then DeCosta trades a potential top 40 pick in 2028 for whatever is left of Cam Jurgens, while concussed, right before the Eagles were benching him ).
But this is a first-rate operation. Surely not just an attempt to stay in power.
And Minter barely has a better sack rate or pressure rate than Orr despite all of that, and he wants to play dime all the time and zone it up because he is prettified of allowing big plays … and he has arguably the worst second-half big play defense in the NFL despite all those 10-point leads and has allowed more passes of 25 yards or more at this stage of the season than Orr despite not playing a playoff team schedule like Orr did and getting mostly garbage QBs so far.
This is a complete and total disaster, folks, and he is trying to push some narrative about SPURTS OF GOOD ENOUGH FOOTBALL. (Am I the only one who immediately flashes to Richard Hell And The Voidoids ? Probably)
When are these spurts and how long do they last? How do we make the more consistent?
They never seem to occur when ish gets real. Not for his garbage defense. Not nearly enough.
Zach Orr wasn’t the problem, just like Chuck Pagano and Dean Pees, brought in to help him, weren’t the problem. And Minter, with a staff that includes his dad but no former NFL head coaches ( by design ) ain’t fixing it, either. Marvin Lewis came on “The Daily Flock” and told you the pieces don’t fit the defense and the message isn’t getting through with repeated communication breakdowns. And the…

title: Ravens Coach Jesse Minter Must Cede Play Calling Duties: And 3 Other Takeaways From Thursday's Debacle
full_text:
The Baltimore Ravens will need a full reboot on defense for 2027, and they have truly needed one since losing the AFC Championship Game in 2023, and Thursday night’s shameful display should provide all the data points any reasonable front office would need to start dismembering this roster ahead of next week’s trade deadline.
The defense is a joke, allowing over eight yards per play in the first half and free runners all over the middle of the field and no semblance of a pass rush. Rookie head coach Jesse Minter looks like a foil for a power-hungry front office, and pushing out John Harbaugh to hire someone failing miserably as a head coach and a defensive coordinator is quite a trick. Baltimore lost for the fourth straight game, with undrafted rookie Joe Fagnano pretending to play quarterback this time; they head to Week 10 with two AFC victories all season (horrible Colts and Titans) and they have become an utterly noncompetitive football entity.
Losing Lamar Jackson for the season (he isn’t coming back to play meaningless games after going to IR with a thumb injury) isn’t the problem The defense that is stocked with bad football players (far too many either overpaid by failed GM Eric DeCosta or over-drafted by him or both). Minter has made them worse than they were under scapegoat coordinator Zach Orr the last two years and there is no reason for hope.
Malaki Starks, a supposed difference maker, got destroyed when he actually had to show up in coverage, on a 50-yard TD pass to Parker Washington that made it 17-3 at the end of the first half and effective ended this game. The final was 33-10 at M&T Bank Stadium, Baltimore (4-5) has now won three times in its last 12 home games and is 6-9 since last Thanksgiving and has been utterly noncompetitive against winning teams for years.
“Obviously, the results are not acceptable,” Minter said amid many rambling answers in which if he wasn’t excusing a lot of this garbage he was coming closer to it than he should.
Here’s what we learned from this slopfest, in which Kyle Hamilton left and did not return (Minter said he didn't have an update):
Derrick Henry running the Wild Cat is cute, but Jacoby Brissett, who just lost his job to Gardner Minshew and couldn’t function against the woeful Cowboys defense is fixing nothing. The Ravens have a lot of time between now and Tuesday afternoon’s deadline to make the decisions that need to be made.
Henry has to go . Ronnie Stanley, a middling left tackle nearing the end of his career, should go if at all possible . Calais Campbell, 40, is wasting the final year of his career here. Rashod Bateman should have been gone years ago. DeCosta having the guts to lecture the media and fans on how Marlon Humphrey (he is getting clowned by former Ravens players and coaches all over the country) was a $19M corner was something. Humphrey got picked on immediately in this game and has to be benched for TJ Tampa ( no one is trading for Humphrey , who got beat by a blocking TE for a 50 yard gain to open the game, seriously).
This is an unserious franchise that seems to take its fans for fools. I expect zero accountability from the failed GM or his boss, the billionaire owner who couldn't be bothered to do much during the coaching search. But if they don’t starting trying to reposition this franchise before they host the Chargers on Monday Night Football, it’s a new low.
Minter delivered a dissertation about this team not being as awful as it clearly is when asked about direction at the deadline, which sums up their general MO when it comes to what they sell in Owings Mills, and reality.
If your players are going to quiet quit from week to week, and the Ravens won’t admit defeat that they put together a cheap and naïve coaching staff (only the Ravens and Dolphins had no former NFL head coaches employed ) and they won’t bring in former head coaches to help Minter, then it's time to let defensive coordinator Anthony Weaver do the job and call the defense.
Minter has been a barely-functional head coach. He needs to learn how to have a spine and hold players accountable and establish protocols and standards in practices and games. He can’t be trying to fix a defense he keeps breaking at the same time. Pick a lane, but Minter has been an unquestioned disaster to this point.
They gave up 223 yards in the first half in the rain, at home, and had an 11% pressure rate (impossible, right?) with their alleged “closer,” $30M a year pass rusher Trey Hendrickson made no impact, again. This after having Josh Allen and Joe Burrow have perfect passer ratings in the second half against them the previous two weeks, and Deshaun Watson overcoming a 10-point lead in the second half to blow that game.
DeCosta wanted a novice after winning the power struggle with Harbaugh after last year’s pathetic season. He got it. The middle of the field was open the entire game and the defense has no soul.
Part of the reason Minter looks out of his depth is because he can’t command a presence from this team and get them to focus and show attention to detail. Not with this crew.
They had a silly penalty on a return on special teams to back up Fagnano way deeper than he needed to be. They jumped offsides on a fourth-and-short when this was still a football game to give Jacksonville a big first down. They had false starts on successive plays in the first half, with veteran tight end Mark Andrews ( a colossal DeCosta mistake who did nothing of note again and botched a direct snap) committing the second one – he leads all tight ends in that category and in drop percentage.
In a desperate spot to start the second half … we got yet another brutal false start to further compromise a QB who was not ready for this assignment. But when your most overpaid players are also your worst players, and they are never held to account, then why wouldn’t these issues permeate the entire roster ? A fumble on a kickoff return was a nice touch, too.
"It's ownership of players and coaches that keep happening … the pre-snap penalties are unnaceptable," Minter offered. Funny thing is they are acceptable but the biggest culprits - Andrews and Stanley - are made men from the GM and beyond reproach, apparently.
After the rookie offensive coordinator badly embarrassed himself and the entire organization with ridiculous play calling Sunday in playing a key role in his quarterback room getting decimated, Doyle finally grasped the severity of the situation Thursday.
He was committed to Wild Cat and gimmick plays and throws behind the line of scrimmage. He leaned heavily into tackle eligible and 13 personnel (three tight ends), trying to bleed the clock and keep this game as close as he could for as long as he could. Made sense, especially with Fagnano’s right ankle heavily taped in the rain.
Still wasn’t nearly enough, but at least he tried this time. Once the Jaguars opened up a 14-point lead Fagnano had to drop back (he threw one pass beyond the line of scrimmage in the first quarter) and he was under constant duress and it just got uglier from there.
Fagnano is incredibly raw and limited and even with a rudimentary game plan and all that scheming, in a short week he had no chance against this defense. Fagnano was quite poor in the second half. Brissett will start in primetime for this fallen franchise next.
Jason has covered sports professionally for newspapers, websites and broadcast networks since 1996 and have covered the NFL extensively for The Washington Post, CBS Sports and The NFL Network from 2004-2025.

title: Four Ways Ravens Offense Needs To Adjust Without A Mobile Quarterback Moving Forward
full_text:
The Baltimore Ravens will be without the greatest dual-threat quarterback in NFL history for the foreseeable future and potentially the remainder of the 2026 season. On their first offensive play in a Week 8 road loss to the Buffalo Bills , two-time league MVP Lamar Jackson suffered a thumb injury that will require surgery.
This setback officially landed him, as well as his primary backup, Tyler Huntley, who suffered a significant turf toe injury in the same game, on injured reserve on Thursday . Both signal callers will require surgery to address their respective physical ailments.
While the Ravens are slated to start undrafted rookie Joe Fagnano against the Jacksonville Jaguars on Thursday Night Football on a short week, they are reportedly finalizing a trade to acquire journeyman veteran Jacoby Brissett from the Arizona Cardinals.
Bringing in the well-traveled career backup and occasional spot-starter gives the Ravens a proven commodity under center with ties to the coaching staff, as he played under current quarterbacks coach Israel Woolfork last year in Arizona. What it doesn't provide is a player at the position who is anywhere near a threat in the run game, like Jackson or even Huntley.
This means that the Ravens and first-year offensive coordinator Declan Doyle will need to adapt their plan of attack moving forward to better suit the strengths of their current quarterback room with Brissett and Fagnano, who is also more of a traditional pocket passer. Here are four key adjustments they need to make to give the offense its best chance to thrive without the greatest force multiplier in the game for the time being, and possibly the rest of the season.
The Ravens' rushing attack has struggled mightily to run the ball with any consistency and gain consistent traction on the ground over the past three weeks after posting a season-high 208 rushing yards in their first game without Jackson, following his high ankle sprain. They've averaged just 82 rushing yards during their three-game losing streak and will need to make five-time Pro Bowl running back Derrick Henry even more of a focal point of their offensive approach moving forward. The future Hall of Famer has been the subject of several trade rumors since Jackson's injury, but with him gone, Henry is the last star left standing in the Ravens' backfield.
No matter who is under center for this team for the rest of the season, Henry should be carrying the ball early and often, especially now that the offensive line is getting healthier and building more cohesion, with first-round rookie Vega Ioane slated to return from a one-week absence and two-time Pro Bowl center Cam Jurgens getting more acclimated since being acquired via trade.
Despite not having Jackson's electric mobility at their disposal, they still have several playmakers on that side of the ball who can make explosive plays in space with the ball in their hands. At the top of that list is two-time Pro Bowl wide receiver Zay Flowers, who, even after being held without a catch for the first time in his four-year career last week, still ranks eighth in the league in receiving yards. Since losing veteran blocking specialist tight end Durham Smythe to a season-ending torn Achilles, trying to run the ball or just simply operate out of multiple tight end sets, especially out of condensed formations, has been inefficient and downright futile far too often.
The Ravens should still keep the under center element in their offense to preserve and amplify the threat of play-action, but as far as personnel packages go, they should look to spread their formations out with multiple receiver sets. It'll force opposing defenses to have more ground to cover, lighten the boxes Henry has to run into at the line of scrimmage, and get more explosive wideouts such as veteran Rashod Bateman, rookie Ja'Kobi Lane and third-year pro Devontez Walker the ball more.
After having three quarterbacks go down in one game due to poor pass protection just four days ago, including the face of the franchise, the Ravens' offensive line can't be trusted to hold up for deep dropbacks or handle basic stunts, twists and blitzes until they prove otherwise. Doyle should be dialing up quick-developing plays and overemphasizing the necessity for his quarterbacks to not hold onto the ball too long after seeing two of them get strip-sacked this past Sunday. His screen designs and sequencing have been one of the most impressive aspects of his new offense this year. Leaning more into getting his dynamic receivers, running backs and tight ends in space with convoys in front of them should increase even more.
While the soon-to-be 34-year-old Brissett isn't nearly as fleet of foot as the Ravens' injured first and second-string quarterbacks, he is among the best in the league at using his legs to pick up first downs on sneaks. Baltimore's struggles to convert on third and fourth and short are a major reason why they've struggled to sustain drives and finish them in the end zone without Jackson under center, dating back to last year.
Brissett leads the NFL with 17 quarterback sneaks, four more than the Bills' Josh Allen, and is responsible for picking up 16 first downs and scoring a touchdown rushing through eight games. Having him lined up behind Jurgens, who successfully ran the famous 'Tush Push' play with Jalen Hurts and the Philadelphia Eagles, should be the Ravens' go-to play anytime they find themselves needing two or fewer yards to move the chains. Against the Jaguars this week, with Fagnano on a bad ankle, the Ravens should line up one of their tight ends under center in those situations.

title: NFL MNF Game Predictions Back Bills' Elite Offense over Vikings' Vaunted Defense
full_text:
The Buffalo Bills ' offense is facing arguably its toughest test yet .
According to the experts, however, no test is too daunting for Bills' quarterback Josh Allen, a five-time MVP finalist.
The Bills, who lead the NFL in scoring average (33.3), will visit the Minnesota Vikings on Monday Night Football . In addition to boasting the league's No. 2 overall defense (271.6), the hosts are No. 1 against the pass (154.9).
"As a competitor, you're like, 'yeah, heck yeah, I want to play the best,'" said Allen. "I want to go out there and prove why we are what you say, the No. 1 offense. I know it's statistically speaking, but that's still a chip on our shoulder. We want to go out there and be the best offense that we can be. We've got a great opportunity against a fantastic defense."
Even with home-field advantage and a vaunted defense, the Vikings are betting underdogs for the November 9 primetime affair. The Bills enter as a 3.0-point road favorite per DraftKings .
As for what the experts are saying, Sports Illustrated's prediction panel is backing the Bills to win by a 3-to-1 margin. Six of the eight panelists have picked Buffalo to prevail in Week 9 with national staff writer Gilberto Manzano and senior writer Conor Orr being the two defectors. Note, SI selections are straight up.
Although it already seems like an eon ago, the Bills answered the Bell in Week 1 against the Houston Texans and what many were billing a "Super Bowl" defense. Buffalo scored 36 points on the road with Allen passing for 334 yards.
When it comes to Monday night's assignment in Minnesota, Bills' first-year head coach Joe Brady, who doubles as the team's offensive play caller, advised his troops to focus more on their operation than the opposing defense.
"We got to take care of the football. We got to play our style and not necessarily be reactive to it," said Brady.
The Bills' offense could be without the starting left side of its line with both tackle Dion Dawkins and guard Alec Anderson questionable to play . On the positive side, Allen has plenty of his weapons healthy and available .
Meanwhile, the Vikings are starting backup quarterback Carson Wentz with Kyler Murray unavailable.

title: Bills Can Realistically Trade for One of These Safeties, Remain Salary Cap Compliant
full_text:
Where there's a will, there's a way.
The Buffalo Bills aren't exactly flush with salary cap space, but that fact should not prevent them from potentially pulling off a trade ahead of Tuesday's NFL deadline.
If the Bills indeed believe that upgrading their defensive secondary will aid them in their Super Bowl chase, then general manager Brandon Beane seemingly has the means , in terms of draft capital, to pull off a trade.
"I got all the confidence in our personnel staff that if they feel like there's something that needs to be added to our football team, that they'll do what they need to do, and if they don't, we'll be good to go as well," said first-year head coach Joe Brady this past week.
While trading for a cornerback is worth exploring, the consensus seems to be that the Bills will be best served by upgrading the safety position after cutting ties with Chauncey Gardner-Johnson .
"Bills have scanned the safety pool of late," according to ESPN's Jeremy Fowler .
The Jacksonville Jaguars already took one option off the market on Monday morning, trading for Atlanta Falcons' veteran Jessie Bates. With the Jaguars sending a 2027 second-round pick and a 2028 fifth-round pick, the Falcons are reportedly paying most of his remaining salary that carries a $6.5 million cap hit.
That particular strategy is one avenue for Beane to travel. He can also create room by restructuring a high-paid veteran on a multi-year contract.
The Bills carry an estimated $3.8 million in salary cap space (per Spotrac). That ranks 27th on the circuit, but it's enough, with some creative accounting, for Buffalo to swing a trade for one of the safeties rumored to be available.

title: Four Bills' Players Key to Victory vs. Vikings on Monday Night Football
full_text:
The Buffalo Bills are just hours away from making their second appearance on Monday Night Football —and third in primetime overall—during the 2026 NFL campaign as first-year head coach Joe Brady’s squad is getting set to take on the Minnesota Vikings at U.S. Bank Stadium in Minneapolis at 8:15 p.m. ET.
Currently undefeated on the road thus far with a mark of 3-0, the AFC-leading Bills will look to continue their winning ways against a Vikings’ team that entered Week 9 sitting atop the NFC at 6-1 alongside the San Francisco 49ers.
However, despite dealing with injuries at the quarterback position right now on the offensive side of the ball, Minnesota will undoubtedly present plenty of challenges with their top-ranked defense that quarterback Josh Allen and Co. will have to overcome throughout the night.
Some national outside observers expect Allen to have no problem in doing so .
But, it’ll take more than the gunslinger’s seemingly superhuman efforts to overcome the NFC North-leading Vikings on their home turf, even though he does have a good history of playing well at that particular venue . . . just ask Minnesota’s former linebacker Anthony Barr .
So, with that in mind, here are four key players who will need to step up in order to help Buffalo come out of the Upper Midwest unscathed under the primetime lights.
Although Bills’ running back James Cook III has never played in the building that his brother, Dalvin Cook, once ran amok in during his six seasons with the Vikings from 2017 to 2022, he’ll have a chance to showcase the Cook name in a big way at U.S. Bank Stadium on Dalvin’s behalf on Monday night.
Despite leading the lead in several critical categories, Minnesota is actually allowing 116.7 yards per game on the ground to opposing teams entering the interconference matchup with Buffalo, which ranks 17th in the NFL according to FOX Sports ’ database.
So, given that their No.1-ranked pass defense ( 154.9 YPG ) will surely look to stir things up when quarterback Josh Allen drops back to throw the ball , it’ll be important for the Bills to establish a solid running game with Cook, as well as Ray Davis and Ty Johnson.
Buffalo’s bellcow runner, who entered Week 9 ranked fourth in the NFL in rushing with 707 yards, has a huge opportunity ahead of him in primetime.
Whether it be veteran Christian Benford or stellar rookie cornerback Davison “IGB” Igbinosun , the Bills will need to keep close tabs on Vikings’ superstar wide receiver Justin Jefferson on Monday.
And, although Jefferson is currently on pace for the lowest output of his seven-year career at the moment with an average of just 55.8 receiving yards per game, new Vikings’ starting quarterback Carson Wentz recently vowed to put the ball in his top playmaker’s hands against Buffalo.
So, with that in mind, the Bills must find a way to slow down that connection by any means necessary.
Buffalo held Baltimore Ravens’ wideout Zay Flowers without a catch last week, but was that just fool’s gold ?
Bills Mafia is about to find out.
Buffalo’s backup swing tackle Tylan Grable has done well during his relief work behind preferred starting right tackle Spencer Brown over the past couple of games, and it looks like there’s a chance he could have to shift over to the left side on Monday night.
Fellow starting tackle Dion Dawkins missed practice all week due to a rib injury that he apparently sustained against the Ravens in Week 8, so his status is definitely up in the air even though it appears that he’s going to push to play.
Regardless of who is in the lineup, though, they’ll need to do a great job of protecting the blindside of Buffalo’s former 2024 MVP quarterback, especially considering that Vikings’ pass-rusher Dallas Turner, who is just behind Buffalo’s Gregory Rousseau in the sack department with a total of six takedowns through seven games, prefers to rush from that side of the field.
Turner is also second behind only Rousseau ( 14.4% ) in pass-rush pressure rate at 14.3% according to FTN Fantasy .
Whoever is blocking him along Buffalo's offensive line, as well as fellow pass-rusher Andrew Van Ginkel ( 6.5 sacks ), must be on their toes all night long.
Although the picture may seem a bit murky to some at the current moment in terms of his running mate at the third level of Buffalo’s defense, Cole Bishop is going to be an integral part of any sort of turnaround that there might be for Jim Leonhard’s unit over the final 10 games of the regular season.
And, that’ll be the case on Monday night against the Vikings, especially when he’s tasked with covering tight end T.J. Hockenson on occasion.
Despite wideout Justin Jefferson expected to see an uptick in targets, as previously mentioned, Bills’ fans should also keep a watchful eye on Hockenson in primetime.
The eighth-year veteran tight end has tallied 219 of his 295 total receiving yards this season over the past four games, so it appears he may be hitting his stride.
Bishop must be at the top of his game on the road in Minneapolis. Although he finished with just two tackles last week, he did have a key forced fumble on a sack against Baltimore. Those big plays must continue on Monday.
