title: Colts Position Grades: Young Defense Shows Life in Week 9 Loss
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts have now lost five straight games, falling 27-23 to the Dallas Cowboys in another disappointing showing at Lucas Oil Stadium.
In a surprising twist, the defense actually looked serviceable on Sunday. The offense? Not so much.
What's frustrating is watching these young defenders finally step up while the franchise is being torn apart, largely because of how poorly this defense has performed.
But once again, Indianapolis walks away with another loss, falling to 2-7.
Here are my position grades from Week 9.
Daniel Jones finished 20-of-34 for 180 yards, one touchdown, and an interception. But his 15.4 QBR tells the real story.
Jones earned a team-low 36.7 offensive grade, per Pro Football Focus. Interestingly, he graded significantly better against the blitz (69.6) than without it (30.4).
I'm going to defend Jones here. He's never been a quarterback who can consistently elevate a struggling supporting cast, but give him weapons, a rushing attack, and decent defense, and he can win games.
Unfortunately, Indianapolis just traded away one of the best offensive linemen this franchise has ever drafted.
This is the season from hell, and Jones isn't the biggest problem. But he certainly didn't play well Sunday.
Something looks off with Jonathan Taylor.
JT managed just 46 yards on 13 carries and lost a costly fumble. Meanwhile, rookie Seth McGowan continues to impress, rushing for 45 yards and a touchdown on six attempts.
Both were effective in pass protection, but Taylor needs a resurgence. Maybe Tuesday's trade deadline will finally quiet the noise surrounding him.
Where is the separation? This unit combined for 121 total receiving yards.
Ashton Dulin provided the lone explosive play, turning a screen into a 55-yard touchdown. Otherwise, this receiving corps was painfully average.
With Alec Pierce eventually returning, this group still has potential. But right now, nobody is consistently stepping up.
Tyler Warren continues working his way back from injury, hauling in four passes for 44 yards.
The entire group contributed in pass protection, and while the others weren't involved much offensively, tight end was far from the problem.
Surprisingly, this unit wasn't terrible.
Indianapolis allowed two sacks and roughly 10 pressures, with respectable performances in both pass protection and run blocking.
Not dominant, but certainly not the reason Indianapolis lost.
The Colts generated three sacks and consistent pressure on Dak Prescott, but the run defense remains a problem.
Javonte Williams rushed for 101 yards, while Dallas totaled approximately 179 on the ground.
The pressure was encouraging. The inability to stop the run wasn't.
Bryce Boettcher and C.J. Allen are finally finding their footing.
The young duo combined for 22 tackles, providing some much-needed consistency in the middle of this defense.
Neither was spectacular, but both continue showing why they deserve opportunities moving forward.
Dallas threw for 335 yards, and CeeDee Lamb absolutely torched this secondary.
Sauce Gardner held up relatively well early before surrendering a critical 46-yard completion to Ryan Flournoy.
This was a bend-don't-break performance, but allowing that much production through the air isn't acceptable.
Cam Bynum delivered one of his better performances, earning the team's second-highest coverage grade.
Meanwhile, Hunter Wohler led Indianapolis with an incredible 16 tackles.
The young safety is making the most of his opportunity, and this group was one of Sunday's brighter spots.
Spencer Shrader is officially back.
The Colts kicker drilled all three field goals, including bombs from 59 and 50 yards.
Rigoberto Sanchez was reliable, kickoff coverage improved, and Anthony Gould and Seth McGowan provided encouraging returns.
The most frustrating part of Sunday's loss wasn't even the final score. It was watching a defense that has been historically bad at times finally show signs of life, only for the offense to completely disappear.
Indianapolis has now lost five straight, and with Tuesday's trade deadline approaching, this roster could look even worse by next Sunday.
Michael Greene is a graduate of Indiana University and the Scouting Academy. He's in his first year covering the Indianapolis Colts and NFL, with a unique focus on fantasy football.

title: Week 9 Stock Report: Rookies Shine Despite Fifth Straight Loss to Cowboys
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts suffered their fifth consecutive loss on Sunday, falling 27-23 to the Dallas Cowboys to drop to 2-7 on the season. Despite another disappointing result, several young players continued to show encouraging signs, while others had performances they'd like to put behind them.
Here's a look at whose stock is trending up and whose is heading in the opposite direction following Week 9.
Caden Curry continues to make the most of the extra opportunities he's earned in the last two weeks.
Curry recorded his first pro sack and recovered a fumble against Dallas, becoming the first Colts rookie to record a sack and fumble recovery in the same game since Josh Mallard in 2002. His ability to consistently make plays around the football has been an encouraging development for a defense searching for reliable contributors.
Curry has proven to be an excellent find in the seventh round of last year's draft as he's beginning to establish himself as a player worth giving more runway too the rest of the season.
Fellow rookie defensive end Jaylahn Tuimoloau also turned in an impressive performance against Dallas.
Tuimoloau also recorded his first career sack and generated four pressures, continuing what has been an encouraging stretch for the second-year pass rusher. Tuimoloau has steadily worked his way into the defensive line rotation and is beginning to show why Indianapolis invested a second-round pick in him, even if results weren't immediate.
With the Colts potentially giving more opportunities to their younger players down the stretch, Tuimoloau has an opportunity to build on his recent progress.
Seth McGowan rushed for 45 yards on just six attempts, averaging 7.5 yards per carry while scoring his first career NFL touchdown, building on what is turning into an impressive rookie campaign.
His 36-yard run was the longest rushing play of the afternoon for Indianapolis and demonstrated the explosiveness he can bring to the backfield. With Jonathan Taylor's future in Indianapolis increasingly uncertain with the trade deadline on the horizon, McGowan could have an opportunity to step into a much larger role. His performance was an encouraging development for the Colts' future at running back, regardless of if Taylor is a part of that future.
CJ Allen is making a strong impression after stepping into a larger role in the Colts' linebacker corps. The rookie followed up his first NFL start with a second straight game with double-digit tackle numbers.
Allen has demonstrated an encouraging level of confidence and awareness despite being thrown into a difficult situation. Even in a defense which has struggled throughout this season, Allen's presence is clearly felt when he's on the field. His ability to contribute immediately is particularly important for a defense that has dealt with injuries and significant personnel changes. Indianapolis could have an important building block in its young linebacker.
Jonathan Taylor endured a difficult afternoon. The veteran running back finished with 46 rushing yards on 13 attempts, averaging just 3.5 yards per carry, while also losing a key fumble late in the game.
Although Indianapolis' offensive line deserves some responsibility for the team's recent rushing struggles, Taylor hasn't been able to consistently generate the production expected of him. His future is also becoming an increasingly prominent storyline with Tuesday's trade deadline approaching. If Sunday's performance was his final appearance in Indianapolis, it wasn't the finish anyone envisioned.
Bernhard Raimann had an unusually difficult afternoon against Dallas. Indy's $100-million left tackle committed three penalties that contributed to several frustrating offensive sequences. One illegal formation penalty erased an eight-yard completion to Deion Burks on third down, while a fourth-quarter holding penalty turned a manageable third-and-six into a much more difficult third-and-16.
Raimann has established himself as an important piece of the offensive line, but Sunday's performance was a step in the wrong direction for the veteran tackle.
Josh Downs had a particularly disappointing afternoon against Dallas, finishing with three receptions for 24 yards on six targets. More concerning were his two drops, including a critical third-down opportunity late in the fourth quarter that forced Indianapolis to settle for a field goal.
The Colts needed their receivers to make plays in a close game, and Downs failed to deliver when his team needed him most.
Downs' ongoing trade situation has also added another layer of uncertainty to his future in Indianapolis. With the deadline approaching, his stock has taken a hit at an unfortunate time .

title: Colts Trade Candidates Did Themselves No Favors Ahead of Deadline
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts entered Sunday's matchup against the Dallas Cowboys with two of the NFL's most notable trade candidates still on their roster.
With the Nov. 10 deadline approaching, the organization had one final opportunity to evaluate its options and potentially strengthen its negotiating position before the 4 p.m. EST cutoff.
However, Sunday's performances for some notable trade targets did little to help their respective trade cases. Both players entered the week amid considerable speculation about their futures in Indianapolis, but neither gave interested teams much reason to increase their offers.
Josh Downs had an opportunity to make a positive impression on potential suitors Sunday, but his performance against the Cowboys did little to accomplish that.
Downs finished with just three receptions for 24 yards on six targets, while dropping two passes on third down that could have helped extend drives.
The struggles are becoming increasingly difficult to overlook, particularly given the circumstances surrounding his future in Indianapolis. Since his trade request became public, Downs has appeared to be mentally elsewhere, and his recent performances have done little to suggest he's fully focused on helping the Colts turn their season around.
The two games since his trade request became public have produced just seven catches for 47 yards and one touchdown. While Downs has continued to receive opportunities in the offense, he hasn't done much with them. His inability to consistently create production has become an increasingly difficult problem for a player attempting to demonstrate his value to potential new teams.
To his credit, Downs didn't shy away from his mistakes after Sunday's loss.
"I stunk today," Downs admitted. He also pushed back on the suggestion that the trade situation had distracted him, insisting he had practiced well throughout the week and was focused on his responsibilities.
#Colts WR Josh Downs, asked if his trade request weighed on his performance: “I don’t really have an answer for that. …” Asked if he expects to be in Indy after the trade deadline: “I’m not worried about that right now. I got some things I gotta fix …” @TheAthleticNFL pic.twitter.com/jR4AdF4dfz
Still, the optics aren't good. Downs has appeared increasingly disconnected from the team's situation since his trade request became public, and his latest performance only adds to the perception that a change of scenery might be best for both sides.
That doesn't necessarily mean his trade value has disappeared. Downs is still a young receiver with established NFL experience and a skill set that could appeal to teams looking for help in the slot. However, Indianapolis reportedly initially sought a third-round selection before informing interested teams that it had received an offer in the fourth-round range.
For a receiver hoping to attract a stronger return, Sunday's performance was hardly encouraging. Between his declining production, the two costly drops and the uncertainty surrounding his future, Downs hasn't done himself many favors heading into Tuesday.
Taylor has arguably been the biggest name on the NFL's trade market over the past several weeks, with multiple contenders reportedly exploring the possibility of acquiring the Colts' superstar. Following the firing of general manager Chris Ballard and the subsequent trades of Quenton Nelson and DeForest Buckner, Taylor emerged as one of the most attractive potential additions available ahead of the trade deadline due to how valuable he could be to a team looking to contend for a Super Bowl.
The Colts reportedly sought a first-round selection or a package comparable to what the Carolina Panthers received for Christian McCaffrey in 2022. The New York Giants were among the teams showing significant interest, reportedly offering a 2027 second- and fifth-round pick before ultimately pulling that offer off the table. With Indianapolis unwilling to settle for less than its desired return, Taylor's future has remained one of the biggest unanswered questions heading into the deadline.
Unfortunately, his performance against Dallas didn't exactly strengthen the Colts' negotiating position. Taylor finished with just 13 carries for 46 yards, averaging 3.5 yards per attempt, while adding five receptions for 18 yards. His most costly mistake came early in the fourth quarter when he fumbled near the Cowboys' 20-yard line, eliminating a prime opportunity for Indianapolis to take the lead.
The disappointing outing continued a recent decline in production for Taylor. He's rushed for just 258 yards over his last four appearances, averaging 4.3 yards per carry without recording a 100-yard performance. He's also now gone 16 consecutive games without reaching the century mark on the ground, an unusually lengthy drought for a player who has established himself among the league's premier backs.
Taylor has maintained that the trade speculation hasn't affected his preparation, emphasizing throughout the week that his focus remained on helping Indianapolis win. However, following Sunday's loss, he acknowledged the uncertainty surrounding his future when asked whether he had played his final game with the Colts.
"I'm not sure. I know as much as you," Taylor said. "If it is (my last game with the Colts), I'm very grateful for the city of Indianapolis."
Taylor also accepted responsibility for his costly fumble, explaining that he needed to do a better job securing the football regardless of the circumstances.
"No matter what happens, I gotta make sure if it touches my body, if it touches my hands, I gotta try to clamp down on it immediately," Taylor said.
There's little question that Taylor remains an attractive option for teams looking to strengthen their backfields for a postseason run. He's still just 27 years old, has eight rushing touchdowns this season and is under contract through 2028 after signing a two-year, $44 million extension in August.
However, his recent production and ball-security issues haven't necessarily given interested teams additional incentive to meet Indianapolis' asking price.
For a player who has been the face of the trade deadline this season, Sunday's performance was an unfortunate opportunity missed. Taylor hasn't erased the value he's established throughout his career, but he didn't do much to justify an already ambitious asking price.
The Colts have less than 48 hours to determine how they want to proceed with the remainder of their roster. Indianapolis has already informed interested teams that Daniel Jones will not be traded, but the futures of Jonathan Taylor and Josh Downs remain uncertain as negotiations appear to have stalled .
Despite the amount of speculation surrounding potential deadline activity, ESPN's Stephen Holder reported Sunday that the next few days could be relatively uneventful for the organization.
According to Holder, a source believes the deadline is "pretty likely to be anticlimactic," when it comes to the Colts.
League source on trade speculation surrounding the Colts: "This [trade deadline] is pretty likely to be anticlimactic." Obviously, situations are fluid and deadlines spur action, so time will tell. But I am personally adjusting expectations.
Additionally, per The Ringer's Tom Pelissero, Indianapolis has already informed quarterback Daniel Jones, another player recently rumored to be the subject of trade talks, will not be traded before the deadline.
The Colts informed QB Daniel Jones on Saturday they’re not trading him by Tuesday’s deadline, sources tell @ringer @netflixsports . Teams called and the Colts listened. But they never had any intention of moving him. Despite speculation, Jones is staying in Indy. pic.twitter.com/Ew0cVkmEuW
That doesn't mean Taylor or Downs are guaranteed to remain in Indianapolis. However, the Colts must determine whether the offers currently available provide enough value to justify moving on from either player or whether keeping them…

title: Why Colts' Decision to Keep Daniel Jones Despite Trade Interest Feels Like Malpractice
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts have been shopping their roster ahead of the 2026 NFL Trade Deadline as they prepare for a rebuild for the first time in a decade.
Longtime franchise pillars in left guard Quenton Nelson and defensive tackle DeForest Buckner were the first to be dealt for draft capital , but the Colts have been playing hard to get when it comes to the rest of their top trade assets.
Running back Jonathan Taylor headlines all trade rumors ahead of the NFL's November 10th deadline, but wide receiver Josh Downs and defensive tackle Grover Stewart have also been among the most mentioned in various rumors.
However, perhaps the Colts' most shocking trade candidate that's been revealed in recent weeks is quarterback Daniel Jones.
Jones has by no means been the sole reason that the Colts have gotten off to a brutal 2-7 start to the season, though he has been a big contributor to such dysfunction. Jones is one of just two starting quarterbacks in the NFL who have thrown more interceptions than passing touchdowns through nine weeks.
The Colts' seemingly punted on the 2026 season and transitioned their priorities to the future once they traded Nelson and Buckner, but instead of moving on from the Jones experiment mid-season, they've continued to roll with him.
And again, this isn't all on Jones.
The Colts have provided him the worst wide receiver room in the NFL, and Shane Steichen's offense has been broken as a result. Indianapolis kicked off the 2025 season with historic efficiency under Daniel Jones for the first time, and this perfect marriage of scheme and personnel netted immediate results.
However, one year later, the Colts' perfect situation has devolved into a subpar supporting cast, and Jones has reverted to his usual self.
Jones's return from his infamous Achilles tear has naturally played a big part in his regression, though it's evident through nine weeks that a less-than-ideal supporting cast is what has been the main reason.
So, given the circumstances, why has Jones received any trade interest at all?
The Colts' starting quarterback received calls from the Minnesota Vikings and Baltimore Ravens because of the aforementioned perfect situation he thrived under just a season ago.
Teams believe that Jones can be a succesful game-manager so long as he has the necessary help, so reaching out about a likely late-round pick for his services feels like an easy choice.
Nobody predicted that Daniel Jones of all people would warrant trade interest, but desperation forces organizations to take a shot on quarterbacks any chance they can justify it.
The Colts were gifted a golden opportunity to cut their losses with the Daniel Jones experiment, but a recent report from The Ringer's Tom Pelissero claims they are keeping Jones around for the foreseeable future.
The Colts informed QB Daniel Jones on Saturday they’re not trading him by Tuesday’s deadline, sources tell @ringer @netflixsports . Teams called and the Colts listened. But they never had any intention of moving him. Despite speculation, Jones is staying in Indy. pic.twitter.com/Ew0cVkmEuW
On the surface, this makes sense.
The Indianapolis Colts will be among the worst teams in the NFL come 2027, so having a veteran bridge quarterback for a big-time transition period would do more good than harm.
The Colts' 2027 season will likely be dead on arrival no matter who is brought in this coming offseason, but at least a veteran presence can help bridge the gap and further the development of the promising young pieces still on the roster.
It makes even more sense once you consider Daniel Jones's contract.
Jones is on the Colts' books for one more season, and his $38 million salary, coupled with his $10.5 guaranteed money for injury that is due until March, makes for an ideal mid-tier bridge option at the position.
In theory, this would provide the next front office with a viable option for the regime's first season.
For example, the Miami Dolphins similarly blew up their roster last season and then turned around and signed Malik Willis to a modest 3-year, $67 million deal.
However, the state of the Indianapolis Colts' organization is much more complex than your typical rebuild. Not only that, but Jones has played so poorly as of late that he no longer warrants mid-tier money.
The added layer of the Colts reportedly telling Jones they weren't trading him on Saturday, the day before Week 9's slate of games, doesn't make their decision look any better. Had a contender's starting quarterback gone down the day after, they could have been a potential new suitor for Jones's services.
Then again, if the Colts are ultimately planning to make Jones their tank commander for 2027, then this is some subtle 4D chess on display.
I would argue that rolling with Anthony Richardson for the rest of the season would be the best course of action , because if he plays well enough to bring back on a cheap one-year deal for 2027, then parting ways with Jones would be that much easier.
And if not, second-year quarterback Riley Leonard is waiting the wings.
I understand the vision of giving the next general manager an option, but that logic fails to hold up once you consider teams are willing to give up draft capital for a player that could very well be cut in the offseason, or does it?
The Colts can save $38 million if they make Daniel Jones a post-June 1st cut designation, so there are numerous avenues to parting ways on the table, but continuing to roster Jones when it's beneficial for both parties to part ways feels like a big misstep.
While it appears that way on the surface, the Colts actually would save more money with the June 1st designation than they would by trading him midseason. Indianapolis would save just $11.6 million in 2027 by trading Jones, given that he carries $36.9 million in dead cap over 2026-27, according to Spotrac.
Adding a late-round pick instead of freeing up $25 million would actually be the malpractice on display.
Indianapolis desperately needs to part ways with any contributor from their failed construction under Chris Ballard, and although Jones was among the last to join the wave, he, too, shouldn't be part of the plan moving forward, but it appears he will be, and it makes sense why.
Colts' Owner/CEO Carlie Irsay-Gordon looked to have won the trust of the fanbase after she seemingly accepted the organization's immediate fate and fired Chris Ballard , and then doubled down by trading Quenton Nelson and DeForest Buckner, but has since failed to prove that her version of the Colts is any different than her late father's, Jim Irsay's, most recent teams.
Irsay-Gordon and her sisters, co-owners Kalen Jackson and Casey Foyt, deserve some grace and patience as there's still a long ways to go before the rebuild officially kicks off, but they need to maximize this year's trade deadline if they want the Indianapolis Colts to be taken seriously anytime soon.
Noah Compton is the Publisher of Indianapolis Colts On SI. Noah is from the Indy area and has been covering the Colts since 2022, including stops at FanSided, The Blue Stable, and SBNation.

title: Colts' Loss to Cowboys Confirms Rebuild Can't Come Soon Enough
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts fall to 2-7 after losing 27-23 to the Dallas Cowboys at home .
With less than 48 hours remaining before the NFL Trade Deadline arrives , the Colts are one step closer to establishing their new core of the future.
Indianapolis has until 4 PM EST on Tuesday, November 10th to strike deals for running back Jonathan Taylor and wide receiver Josh Downs, amongst others, and while the Colts reportedly prefer to keep the latter of which, their loss to the Dallas Cowboys is just further proof that they'd be better off cutting their losses and starting anew.
With that said, I'm taking the opportunity to break down my biggest takeaways from the Colts' loss in question.
The Indianapolis Colts took no time to trade franchise pillars LG Quenton Nelson and DT DeForest Buckner , but they've since held off from trading the rest of their roster.
Part of this is due to the reported belief that Colts' CEO/Owner Carlie Irsay-Gordon prefers to keep Jonathan Taylor around to kick off the impending rebuild in question, but it's also because their season was technically over yet.
Sure, it was obvious to some of us that the Colts' season was over even before they began their fire sale, but for all intents and purposes, Indianapolis still had a statistical chance to make the 2026 playoffs.
After they fell to 2-6 in a loss to the Jacksonville Jaguars in Week 8, it seemed like the Colts would come to their senses and bench their top remaining trade candidates for the foreseeable future as they look to strike a deal.
Jonathan Taylor, Josh Downs, and Daniel Jones have become the headliners for the Colts' trade deadline sale, but numerous other veterans, such as Grover Stewart and Mo Alie-Cox, are likely being called about as well.
Instead of going out there and leaving no doubt in their last game before the deadline, the Colts' top three trade candidates did nothing to help their case.
If anything, Taylor, Downs, and Jones have drastically hurt their personal stock, and now the Colts have lost some leverage as they enter crunch time in negotiations.
In the last two weeks, here's how the trio in question performed:
Daniel Jones: 39-62 (62.9%) for 324 passing yards, 2 TDs, 3 INTs, and sacked 5 times Jonathan Taylor: 21 carries for 69 rushing yards and 2 fumbles Josh Downs: 7 receptions on 11 targets (3 drops) for 47 receiving yards and 1 TD
The Colts should have shut down Jonathan Taylor and Josh Downs until their future was determined, and Daniel Jones should have been benched weeks ago .
Dragging these trade talks out has not only allowed for poor performance to hurt the players' stock, but it's also given potential suitors more time to address their shortcomings via other avenues and/or allowed teams who maybe shouldn't have been all-in to come to their senses and pull out of negotiations altogether.
That's not to say the Colts won't be able to net worthwhile compensation for any of these players come deadline day, though it does put them at a disadvantage.
This is the bed Indianapolis made for themselves, and now they must sleep in it.
The Shane Steichen era is officially 27-33 through 3.5 seasons, and the Indianapolis Colts are 2-14 in their last 16 games dating back to last season.
The Shane Steichen experiment has looked to have run its course on numerous stops throughout the season thus far, but nothing the Colts have done since firing longtime general manager Chris Ballard suggests Steichen will be able to right the ship in Indianapolis.
Of course, Colts' head coach Steichen is not fully to blame. The whole reason Ballard has been the lone decision-maker fired so far is because the Colts were finally willing to admit his vision was nothing more than fool's gold.
The Colts' shortcomings can all be attributed to Ballard's failed tenure as general manager, but in the three weeks he's been out of the building, Steichen and Co. have done nothing to prove they deserve one last shot in 2027.
Indianapolis finally looked competitive for the first time all season against the Dallas Cowboys, especially since franchise cornerstone and team captains Quenton Nelson and DeForest Buckner were traded, but it still wasn't enough.
Shane Steichen is undeniably one of the NFL's most creative playcallers, some even consider him an offensive mastermind of sorts, but unfortunately for Indianapolis, his tenure as a first-time head coach for the Colts has only suggested that he can't get the job done here.
The rest of the Colts' season should be treated as an extended preseason.
With so many moving parts on the roster, the only development worth monitoring is that of the Colts' young players. Not all will prove to be building blocks of the rebuild, and that's why giving them as much opportunity as possible down the stretch should be the top priority moving forward.
Indianapolis didn't spearhead this as soon as they traded Quenton Nelson and DeForest Buckner as they probably should have, but they've slowly but surely ramped up the young portion of their roster's workload, and it's quickly paid dividends.
For starters, second-year defensive end Jaylahn Tuimoloau has really come into his own as of late. He has registered his first two career sacks in back-to-back weeks, and truly looks to have unlocked part of his pass-rushing game that was previously thought to not be there.
And that's not the only positive development we've seen across the defensive line.
Recently-extended defensive tackle Adetomiwa Adebawore has evolved into a legitimate star across the interior. The fourth-year defensive lineman leads the Colts in sacks and pressures through eight weeks, and remains a productive player despite taking on double-teams at the highest rate in his career thus far.
Furthermore, third-year edge defender Laiatu Latu remains a hot-and-cold pass rusher, but his flashes are too intriguing to give up on him just yet.
Rookie defensive end Caden Curry has also burst onto the scene as of late. After proving to be a hard-nosed special teams contributor to begin his career, the Greenwood, Indiana product has earned serious playing time as a rotational player across the Colts' defensive line.
Curry logged his first sack and third fumble recovery of the season against the Cowboys, and now it looks like the Colts may have found a gem on Day 3 of the NFL Draft.
Moving back one level of the defense, rookie linebackers CJ Allen and Bryce Boettcher look like the exact players the Colts envisioned they'd become.
Allen, in his second start and first as the green dot of the defense, registered 10 tackles against the Dallas Cowboys, which makes two consecutive games that he's logged double-digit tackles. He also added one tackle for loss and one pass break-up.
Meanwhile, Boettcher's 12 tackles were the second-most on the team. The Colts' second of two rookie linebackers may need to clean up his fundamentals, but he no doubt flies around the football.
Finally, second-year safety Hunter Wohler looked like the same player against the Cowboys that he has in the Colts' past two training camps. In his first start, Wohler led the Colts' defense in tackles with 16, though his below-average coverage ability reminded us that he's got a long way to go before he can considered for a full-time role.
On the offensive side of the ball, seventh-round pick Seth McGowan continues to look like a legitimate NFL running back. McGowan lead the Colts on the ground against the Cowboys, outrushing Jonathan Taylor to the tune of six carries for 45 rushing yards (7.2 ypc) and his first career rushing touchdown.
The Indianapolis Colts still have a lot of work to do, but at least their young core is softening the blow in the meantime.
Noah Compton is the Publisher of Indianapolis Colts On SI. Noah is from the Indy area and has been covering the Colts since 2022, including stops at FanSided, The Blue Stable, and SBNation.

title: The Good, the Bad and the Ugly from Colts’ Wild Loss to Cowboys
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts dropped their fifth game in a row with a 27-23 loss to the Dallas Cowboys in what was a highly entertaining yet sloppy game of football. The defeat means Indianapolis has now lost 14 of its last 16 games across the last two seasons.
That said, despite the negative result, there were some notable outcomes for a team heading towards a rebuild .
Here’s the good, the bad, and the ugly from what was arguably the most entertaining game of the Colts’ season so far.
The Colts’ pass rush was almost nowhere to be found in the early portion of the season. On Sunday, it came alive.
Indianapolis edge defenders Laiatu Latu, Caden Curry, and Jaylahn Tuimoloau all recorded sacks. Latu forced a fumble simultaneously, which set Indianapolis up with a short field in the first half. Curry and Tuimoloau’s sacks were each player’s first of their respective careers.
Additionally, while he won’t get credit on the stat sheet, recently-extended defensive tackle Adetomiwa Adebawore made some key plays in pass rush to help set his teammates up for success. He finished with two tackles, three QB hits, and a batted pass.
Despite losing their sack leader in DeForest Buckner in a trade two weeks ago, Indianapolis hasn’t skipped a beat getting after the quarterback.
The most encouraging development for the Colts on Sunday was the involvement of their young players.
It was a Jaylahn Tuimoloau coming out party against the Cowboys. The second-year defensive lineman is really putting it all together this season, and it was only a matter of time before he found his first career sack. Tuimoloau added a batted ball as well and had a few nice reps in run defense.
Hunter Wohler, while he struggled in pass coverage, was an enforcer against the run. He finished with a team-high 16 tackles.
Tyler Warren came alive in the second half after zero targets in the first 30 minutes. The former first-round pick finished with four catches for 44 yards and picked up a couple key first downs as well.
All in all, a solid day for the second-year players who saw the field.
In addition to the second-year guys, Indianapolis got plenty of contributions from their 2026 rookie class.
CJ Allen logged double-digit tackles (10) for a second straight game and nearly snagged his first career interception. The second-round pick really makes his presence felt. Caden Curry logged his first career sack and recovered a fumble. Seventh-round pick Seth McGowan rushed for 45 yards on six carries and found the end zone for the first time as a pro.
Bryce Boettcher was everywhere as well, joining Allen in the double-digit tackle department with 11.
While the immediate future is likely to be ugly, the Colts have a chance to work with some of these young players and really develop them into assets they can utilize in future seasons.
Just wasn’t meant to be for the Colts’ defense against the run.
Javonte Williams led the way for the Cowboys with 101 yards. Former Colts running back Tyler Goodson picked a great day to rush for a career-high 77 yards on 11 attempts, good for 7 yards per carry. As a team, Dallas managed 5.3 yards per carry and posted just under 180 yards on the ground.
While there were some nice plays made in run defense by a few Colts youngsters, the overall product wasn’t there. Bryce Boettcher, while always aggressively flying around, wasn’t consistently in the right place to make a play. Wohler brought some physicality as a tackler and Tuimoloau got into the backfield a few times, but the defense struggled collectively to stymie Dallas’ rushing attack.
A welcome-to-the-NFL type of afternoon for the rookie.
Jalen Farmer was put through the wringer on Sunday, being responsible for a couple lapses in protection that resulted in sacks. It was clearly a day full of growing pains for Farmer, who’s very clearly the weak link up front for the Colts’ offense.
Replacing an All-Pro-caliber left guard like Quenton Nelson was always going to be a tough task, and it’s too early to throw the towel in on Farmer. But so far, the rookie from Kentucky has done little to convince Colts’ decision makers that he’s their best option at that spot moving forward.
The Colts’ passing attack is reaching unwatchable levels of poor.
Quarterback Daniel Jones managed 180 passing yards and a touchdown, completing 59% of his passes. That said, the stats are a bit inflated by a 55-yard screen pass that Ashton Dulin took to the end zone in the third quarter and a few long drives late in the game.
Additionally, Jones hardly pushed the ball down the field and threw mostly passes at or near the line of scrimmage, a sign of just how handicapped the passing game is without Alec Pierce.
When Pierce went down with a heel injury in Week 2, Indianapolis lost a significant piece of their offense. Without him, there is no deep threat, making the passing game too one-dimensional.
To make things worse, Indy’s best receiver who’s healthy, Josh Downs, is mentally checked out after requesting a trade earlier in the season. That leaves Dulin, a 34-year-old Keenan Allen, Laquon Treadwell, Anthony Gould and Deion Burks at wide receiver. That’s not a group that you’ll ever find consistency with.
Warren, arguably the Colts’ best pass catcher as a whole, wasn’t targeted until the third quarter.
It’s easy to put the blame on Jones, but his supporting cast did him no favors. If that does end up being Jones’ last game in Indianapolis amid trade speculation ahead of the Nov. 10 deadline, Colts fans will be left with a sour taste in their mouths over the quarterback.
Cornerback is a cruel position.
Despite a valiant effort trying to contain the white-hot Ceedee Lamb, Sauce Gardner’s game won’t be remembered for how he held his own against one of the league’s best receivers.
Instead, he’ll be remembered for allowing the 46-yard deep ball to Ryan Flournoy that set Dallas up for their go-ahead touchdown with less than two minutes to go.
Gardner has quietly been very solid in 2026, but his mistakes have been magnified due to the impact they've had on games.
While he may not have given Indianapolis the kind of return they were hoping for by trading away two first-round picks a year ago, Gardner is the only Colt under contract through 2030. He has ample time to make it up.

title: Colts vs. Cowboys Best Bets: Finding Value in the Chaos
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts are falling, and falling quickly. But while this team continues to spiral, we’ve still been able to find value in lines and player props that Vegas is pricing incorrectly.
We’ve managed to capitalize on the chaos, going 15-7 on Colts-specific bets. With Dallas coming to Lucas Oil Stadium on Sunday, it’s time to hunt for value.
The past week was dominated by trade speculation involving nearly every talented player left on this roster. But for now, guys like Jonathan Taylor and Josh Downs are still Colts.
After neither was moved this week, I expect some of that noise to settle down. These guys are still here to make plays and put production on tape, and I expect a much more active offensive showing than we saw in Jacksonville.
On the other side, the Cowboys passing attack with Dak Prescott, CeeDee Lamb, and George Pickens could tear this Colts secondary apart.
Here’s what I like for Week 9.
The rookie is heating up, and I love the juice McGowan has brought to this offense lately.
He has cleared this line in four of his last five games, including 29, 46, and 27 rushing yards over his last three. It’s becoming clear Shane Steichen wants to find ways to get the ball in his hands.
McGowan has also flashed as a kick returner, averaging 27.9 yards on 24 returns. That’s what playmakers do — find a way to get the football and make something happen.
I’m riding the hot hand here.
This game feels like a pretty big tell for where Taylor stands with this franchise.
He was held to just 23 yards on eight carries and failed to reach the end zone against Jacksonville. But even after that performance, Taylor still has eight rushing touchdowns through eight games.
Dallas is also exactly the type of defense I want to target with him. The Cowboys allow an NFL-worst 152.8 rushing yards per game, while ranking 30th in missed tackles and 27th in rushing touchdowns allowed.
The new-look Colts offensive line now has a full game together. I’m betting on a Taylor rebound.
Allen has quietly been one of the most consistent pieces of this Colts offense.
He has cleared this line in four of his last five games, posting 67, 82, 45, and 63 yards in those four hits. With the rest of this receiving corps dealing with injuries, trade speculation, or inconsistent production, Allen remains Daniel Jones’ most reliable veteran target.
Dallas allows the 26th-most receiving yards to wide receivers.
This one almost feels too easy.
Lamb already has six receiving touchdowns through eight games, and now he gets one of the league’s most vulnerable secondaries. Trevor Lawrence did whatever he wanted through the air last week, and Prescott should have plenty of opportunities to do the same.
The matchup gets even better when you look at coverage tendencies.
Lamb has the second-largest disparity between his man and zone coverage grades this season, favoring man coverage. Indianapolis runs man at the ninth-highest rate in the league.
Lamb should get plenty of chances.
McGowan and Allen give us two strong yardage plays, while Taylor and Lamb are my favorite touchdown spots.
The Colts might be difficult to trust right now, but that doesn’t mean we can’t keep finding value in the chaos.
Good luck and bet responsibly.
Game odds refresh periodically and are subject to change. If you or someone you know has a gambling problem and wants help, call 1-800-GAMBLER.

title: Grading ESPN's Trade Proposals for Colts' Taylor and Downs
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts have already shipped out two of their biggest names, and with Tuesday's trade deadline approaching, the future of Jonathan Taylor and Josh Downs remains uncertain.
But how much more talent can Indianapolis afford to lose?
ESPN recently gathered eight experts from ESPN and NFL Network to pitch realistic trades they would like to see completed before Tuesday's 4 p.m. ET deadline.
Two of those proposals involved Taylor and Downs, and both could have serious implications for the Colts' rebuild.
Let's break down the offers and grade them from Indianapolis' perspective.
Vikings receive: RB Jonathan Taylor
Colts receive: 2027 second-round pick, 2027 third-round pick, two 2027 fifth-round picks (one acquired from the Giants).
Judy Battista compares this package to the compensation San Francisco surrendered for Christian McCaffrey in 2022.
She argues that Minnesota needs Taylor's explosive playmaking ability alongside Kyler Murray, especially with an offense that has struggled despite having Justin Jefferson and Jordan Addison.
I couldn't agree more. Pairing Jonathan Taylor with that Vikings defense would make Minnesota an absolute nightmare, even with some of Murray's inconsistencies.
For Indianapolis, though, this is where things get complicated. Taylor has 610 rushing yards and eight rushing touchdowns through eight games, and he's still the centerpiece of this struggling offense.
Four draft picks would certainly help accelerate the rebuild, especially considering the Colts don't own their 2027 first-round selection.
But I'm not sure I'm comfortable moving one of the league's best running backs without getting a first-rounder in return.
This is probably the best package Indianapolis could realistically expect outside of a first-round selection, and it's difficult to ignore that much draft capital.
Chiefs receive: WR Josh Downs
Colts receive: 2027 fourth-round pick.
Jeremy Fowler argues that Kansas City desperately needs another playmaker, while Indianapolis could strengthen its rebuild by moving a receiver who has already requested a trade.
From Kansas City's perspective, this is an absolute steal.
Downs would be unreal with Patrick Mahomes. His route running, reliable hands, and ability to create separation could make him one of the most dangerous slot receivers in football.
But for Indianapolis? I’m not a fan of this deal.
Downs leads the Colts with 330 receiving yards through eight games, and without him, this passing attack might become completely nonexistent.
If Indianapolis is fully committed to tanking the rest of this season, fine. But if Shane Steichen wants any chance of producing an effective offense, Downs is arguably one of the best cards left in his hand.
I understand the contract situation, and just like Nelson and Buckner, there are difficult decisions ahead. But unlike those two veterans, Downs is still young enough to be part of whatever this franchise is building toward.
There are ways Indianapolis could keep Downs beyond this season, although it's unclear whether that's a direction either side wants to pursue.
A fourth-round pick simply isn't enough for me to justify losing one of this offense's few remaining playmakers.
Michael Greene is a graduate of Indiana University and the Scouting Academy. He's in his first year covering the Indianapolis Colts and NFL, with a unique focus on fantasy football.

title: Colts Continue to Be Delusional About Daniel Jones
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts have been at the top of NFL news with the NFL trade deadline approaching on Tuesday, November 10th.
Jonathan Taylor and Josh Downs are at the forefront, but now Daniel Jones is in the fray for QB-needy teams with the mid-point of the NFL season approaching.
Initially, it was all about the Minnesota Vikings being a suitor since Kevin O'Connell had a previous connection with Jones from his brief time there in 2024.
Now, per The Ringer's Tom Pelissero, the Colts have shut the door on dealing off Jones despite a 2-6 record in a completely lost season.
The Colts have received calls on QB Daniel Jones ahead of Tuesday’s deadline, but they’ve told interested teams they aren’t trading him. More in The Sweep: https://t.co/2WjDotrPhy pic.twitter.com/LYOgpVd3gL
The Colts have already traded Quenton Nelson (Seattle Seahawks) and DeForest Buckner (San Francisco 49ers) to signal a rebuild.
It makes sense if the Colts were to retain Taylor and Downs. Taylor is one of the franchise's greatest players and is still in prime form at 27-years-old.
As for Downs, despite requesting a trade, he's shown to be one of the best slot receivers in the league on any given game day, and is only in his fourth NFL season at 25-years-old.
In short, both of these players could be vital for the rebuild if they aren't traded.
As for Jones, there's no chance that he's a part of that strategy, yet the Colts and head coach Shane Steichen continue to campaign for him to remain under center and not trade him.
#Colts HC Shane Steichen, asked if Daniel Jones is held to a softer standard: “It goes back to the preparation and the command he has of the offense. …” “You want to have accountability, but like I said, I feel in this situation that he gives us the best chance to win.” pic.twitter.com/2jsFHaf1Jk
Quite frankly, Indianapolis should do whatever they can to trade Jones at this point, especially considering that he's suddenly not in the Colts' plans for the future.
Along with that, Jones has shown zero ability to be stable under center this year, and has looked arguably worse than at any point during his veteran NFL career.
Through eight games, Jones has 162/268 completions (60.4 percent), six total touchdowns (five passing), nine interceptions, and four fumbles. The honest truth is that Jones has simply been awful.
Tack on that Anthony Richardson Sr. threatens a defense more than Jones, and that the Colts would save $11,600,000 in 2027 by trading him (Over the Cap), it makes even more sense to get him off the roster.
The NFL is full of smoke screens around the trade deadline on an annual basis, so one might look at Pelissero's update as a ploy from Jones' camp, or the Colts, to drive up a better deal.
However, Pelissero is arguably the closest insider to the Colts franchise, so when he reports something from Indianapolis, it can be trusted to the highest degree.
This is why I said the earlier reports re: trade talks for Jones were likely from his camp. Pelissero is very plugged into the Colts, and it seems like Indy wants to keep him at least the rest of the season. https://t.co/ORYDeYD4qD
Anything can happen as the NFL trade deadline approaches, but seeing how committed Steichen is to Jones, paired with the Pelissero update, it appears that the Colts are sticking with the struggling quarterback for the rest of this season.
For any Colts fans who hoped that Richardson would get a chance to start, that reality looks to be an afterthought.
Even if Jones continues his erratic play for a bare Colts offense, I can't imagine he'll be benched so Richardson can finally get a look as the starter under center.
Until Tuesday, fans should cast their eyes on Taylor and Downs, because it's clear that the Colts are committing to Jones for the rest of the 2026 season.

Drake Wally is a Senior Writer for the Indianapolis Colts On SI. His works have also appeared on Bleacher Report, MSN, Yahoo, and SBNation. He also co-hosts the Horseshoe Huddle Podcast.

title: Week 8 Film Review: CJ Allen's First Start Provides Hope for Colts' Future
full_text:
It's fair to say that nearly halfway through his rookie season, CJ Allen's path to consistent playing time  has been arduous.
Lauded early on by recently fired general manager Chris Ballard as a "special dude" , Allen had to fight through injury and questionable personnel decisions to receive his first opportunity in the starting lineup.
"He stands for all the right stuff. He's an athletic, fast MIKE. He'll be a green-dot guy for us from the get-go. I mean, he's a face of the program type of guy. He's a really special dude now,' Ballard said about CJ Allen after drafting him 53rd overall in the 2026 NFL Draft.
Unfortunately for the Georgia product, his first shot at significant playing time ended in a monumental drubbing at the hands of the Jacksonville Jaguars .
However, as I will cover throughout the rest of this article, little of the blame should be attributed to Allen . Granted, anytime a defense gives up thirty-five points to an opposing offense, there will be some mistakes committed by its spine.
Nevertheless, for a rookie making his first start against Trevor Lawrence and the Jaguars , I came away impressed with his play, especially against the run. In my opinion, there weren't many coverage reps that showcased specific proclivities in that department.
It'll likely require a much different game script than the one the Indianapolis Colts found themselves in last Sunday to see meaningful coverage reps for the young rookie.
pic.twitter.com/acV9dbeQRX
One of the more memorable plays from CJ Allen's first start was this sack coming off a play action drop back.
The reason Allen gets a free run at Trevor Lawrence is because of the stunt game up front executed by Adetomiwa Adebawore and Grover Stewart. Tomi starts from a 4i alignment on the right side of the formation and hesitates at the snap to allow Stewart to collision the right guard. This sets Adebawore free to loop back around and preoccupy the center and left guard. In some defenses this is simply called an "Indian" stunt.
Grover does a fantastic job occupying the "whole man" of the right guard and not allowing him to get hands on Allen, who has a chasm in the B-gap to run through.
One reason I wanted to highlight this play is because of the way CJ Allen finished the sack. Time and time again the Colts have failed to finish sacks on the rare occasion they've generated pressure.
Highest pressure rate this season, per @NextGenStats : 1. Vikings – 45.8% 2. Jets – 41.3% 3. Rams – 41.0% 4. Broncos – 40.3% 5. Packers – 40.2% Lowest pressure rate: 28. 49ers – 32.0% 29. Eagles – 31.5% 30. Cardinals – 31.5% 31. Saints – 31.4% 32. Colts – 26.5%
pic.twitter.com/3CHdHmcYdI
This play looks to be an outside zone run by the Jaguars that gets blown up by Grover Stewart getting his helmet on the outside shoulder of the left guard and not allowing the center or guard to climb to either linebacker. We also get a gap exchange between Akeem Davis-Gaither, who immediately scrapes to the playside C gap, and Laiatu Latu, who knifes inside the left tackle's base block, forcing Bhayshul Tuten to cut back into CJ Allen.
Allen does a great job recognizing fast flow away from him and beats the climbing backside guard to the spot. He's able to "get skinny" and dip his shoulder underneath the bigger offensive lineman to penetrate the cutback lane.
I'd like to see the rookie finish off Tuten in the hole, rather than allowing him to fall forward after an awkward tackle attempt. However everything else about this rep, from the play recognition to the block avoidance was stellar.
pic.twitter.com/D0ANl2JFwz
The Jaguars motion to an offset I set out of 13 personnel and end up running what I'm effectively calling "double iso". Since the Colts are in an under front, the center and playside guard double Grover Stewart at nose, leaving the offset tight end isolated on CJ Allen. Another tight end wraps into the C gap and is isolated on Cam Bynum.
CJ Allen knows he needs to "take grass" on the tight end, so he attacks downhill and collisions the lead blocker. He does so with his outside shoulder on the inside half of the blocker to "spill" the ball carrier to a teammate. The violence with which he attacks downhill ensures the lead blocker can't get vertical displacement, and allows Mooney Ward a nice clean picture to fit into when Tuten hits the hole.
pic.twitter.com/dBxf4VBabG
The Jaguars run outside zone towards CJ Allen this time. The right tackle completely washes Allen out of the run fit, and he fails to make the tackle from behind once the running back breaks into open space.
The issue here is allowing the offensive linemen to get frame to frame with him. Once Cole Van Lanen was able to square the rookie up and get his hands inside his chest, he was never going to be able to deconstruct the block.
This Bhayshul Tuten touchdown was the result of several catastrophic breakdowns in the Colts defense. That happened far too many times on Sunday, and wasn't always due to the failures of one player. That is yet another unfortunate trend that has permeated throughout the Colts' 2026 season.
pic.twitter.com/RH1ESLBvnX
The final play I chose to highlight was this lead toss play. I think Allen may be looking for play action or even be boot/counter/reverse responsible. Either way, after widening with the fast motion of the receiver, he's a tick late getting back over the top, and gets cut off by the right guard.
The second play I highlighted showed Allen getting skinny and giving the blocker less surface area to get hands on him. I'd like to see something similar in this instance. Instead he allows the blocker to completely drive him out of the play as he fights to get over the top.
Like with any player, there are certainly some reps that CJ Allen would have liked to have back. But on the whole, I thought he showed substantial promise in his first career start.
There will probably be times throughout his career where he has difficulty tracking the ball carrier through the hole due to his lack of elite size, but the speed in which he attacks open space and his tenacity coming downhill stood out on film. On several plays Allen's pre-snap communication revealed he had a good idea of what run play was coming at him, and the majority of his post-snap reactions were evidence that the rookie has played high level football for a long time.
Akeem Davis-Gaither, the Colts' primary starting linebacker thus far, was downgraded to out for Week 9, so CJ Allen is slated to assume green dot duties for the first time in his career.
Indianapolis' second-round pick provided another reason for fans to turn one eye towards the future last Sunday, even as Indy's season as a whole took another turn towards going completely down the drain.

title: 3 Instant Observations on Jaguars Trading for Davon Godchaux: How Rest of Deadline is Impacted
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars aren’t done.
A few hours after the Jaguars made their trade deadline blockbuster for star Atlanta Falcons safety Jessie Bates III, the Jaguars have reportedly made another move.
According to Netflix’s Tom Pelissero, the Jaguars will be sending a 2028 sixth-rounder to the New Orleans Saints for veteran defensive tackle Davon Godchaux, a pick that can reportedly become a 2027 sixth if certain conditions are met.
So, what do we make of the Jaguars making the move to land the big man in the middle of the defense? We break it down below.
Before we get into where Godchaux can help the Jaguars, we should first discuss what this move really says. It became clear after the big trade for Bates earlier in the day that the Jaguars were not going to pull off some master blockbuster move for a defensive tackle like so many had been hoping, and perhaps even expecting. The Jaguars had been linked to defensive tackles for weeks, but dealing such a big package for Bates suggested that the Jaguars took their swing on defensive linemen, but it didn’t take and they instead pivoted to their safety need. The fact that they made a cheap move to land a rotational run-stuffer just a few hours later suggests this is the case.
Godchaux is about as ho-hum as you can get in terms of adding a veteran defensive lineman. It is not the type of move that really moves any needle, even if it does help the team’s depth situation at defensive tackle. The Jaguars were likely always going to have to go this route at defensive tackle after the Bates move, so it isn’t surprising to see the Jaguars make this kind of addition. A dream scenario would’ve been Bates and a blue-chip defensive tackle, surely. But it just wasn’t going to be overly realistic, and a Bates + Godchaux haul does make the Jaguars a better team today than they were when they left the field in Baltimore a few days ago.
It is clear what the Jaguars like about Godchaux and where they think the 10th-year veteran can help them. It was always going to be easier to find a rotational nose tackle to help ease the loss of Davon Hamilton than it was going to be to find an impact pass-rusher at the defensive tackle spot, and that is exactly what the Jaguars have done with this move. Jacksonville got solid play from the backup nose tackle spots with Matt Dickerson and Albert Regis against the Baltimore Ravens, but neither is an exact replacement for Hamilton as a two-gapping run-stuffer. Now, Godchaux is far from being Hamilton, but he is at least a similar style of defensive tackle.
Godchaux should be able to give the Jaguars some solid reps in a rotation against the run, though it is important to keep expectations realistic. He will not take games over like Hamilton, and he also will not give the Jaguars the same pass-rush value from nose tackle that Hamilton was giving them this season. But he should at least improve their nose tackle depth for the next two months, which was their ultimate goal with the move.
The Jaguars have now added to both the safety and defensive tackle rooms, giving away second-, fifth-, and sixth-round picks in the process to land the two defenders. It feels like we can expect the Jaguars to be mostly done at the deadline now as a result and, hey, Brian Thomas Jr. is still on the squad. Since the Jaguars have been able to fill their two biggest needs on defense without giving away Thomas in order to help get picks to offset the packages given away, there doesn’t seem like there is much reason left to trade Thomas this season. Had the Jaguars needed compensation from a Thomas deal to land Bates or a defensive tackle, perhaps it would be a different story, but they didn’t need to do that.
If the Jaguars get offered a second-round pick for Thomas, that would feel hard to pass up, but this was always the case. Anything less, and it feels like the Jaguars would be making their roster and depth chart worse without the reward that would make it worth it. Since the Jaguars don’t need to make such a move to land defensive reinforcements, the Jaguars should hold onto Thomas for the rest of the season and then reevaluate his trade market once next offseason begins. If he has value now, he should have value then.

title: The $6.5 Million Reason Jessie Bates Cost the Jaguars a 2nd-Round Pick
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- It is becoming clearer and clearer why the Jacksonville Jaguars had to pay such a big price tag for their pre-trade deadline blockbuster.
The Jaguars traded a 2027 second-round pick and a 2028 fifth-round pick to the Atlanta Falcons Monday for former All-Pro and Pro Bowl safety Jessie Bates III, a big price for any safety.
But according to reports, it seems like there are a few different reasons for a second-round pick being included. 6.5 million of them, to be exact.
One big reason the Jaguars had perhaps not been seen as true buyers for some of the market’s elite players was their cap space. with the 25th-most cap space in the NFL at just over $4.6 million. Bates is due $6.5 million alone for the rest of the season, so this is a deal the Jaguars financially couldn’t make work without some restructure and cap gymnastics, the likes of which the Jaguars have already been tapping into for some time due to the past regime’s dead cap issues.
Simply put, there was no way the Jaguars could make this trade without the money aspect changing. And with all of the restructures the Jaguars have already done over the last two reasons, it stands to reason that perhaps they feel like they have nearly tapped out that option. As a result, the way to make this trade work was to have the Falcons eat some, if not all, of the $6.5 million Bates is due for the next few months.
According to multiple reports, that is exactly what the Falcons will be doing. But for the Falcons to take on money for a player they are sending elsewhere, it is clear that the trade package would have to be sweet. Throwing in a 2nd-round and a 5th-round pick for a player on an expiring deal certainly qualifies, and it clearly helped the Jaguars land Bates.
There are also other cap-strapped contenders who might have been looking for a safety like Bates at the deadline,  Add in all of these variables and it is not hard to see why the direction of any Bates deal eventually went to a second-round pick.
Most safeties do not get traded for such a high pick, let alone safeties who are only under contract for another two months. But the Jaguars are not most teams, and Bates is not most safeties. Even with his expiring deal, he has been one of the NFL’s most productive safeties for his entire career, and he has made some genuinely game-changing plays for the Falcons as recently as the past few weeks.
If the Jaguars are able to extend Bates and make some noise in 2026 with him helping lead their defense, it is easy to say that a second-round pick would be a fine cost to pay. It is still a high cost, of course, but the context of what the Jaguars needed to do to make such a move happen at least explains the inflated price tag.
Jacksonville paid a premium price for their new defensive weapon. Now, it is time for him to throw himself into the scheme and the Jaguars’ winning ways and prove why he was worth such a price.

title: 3 Instant Takeaways on Jaguars’ Deal For Jessie Bates: Why the Blockbuster Works
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars have taken their big swing.
The Jaguars have reportedly landed Atlanta Falcons safety Jessie Bates in a pre-trade deadline blockbuster. According to ESPN’s Adam Schefter, the Jaguars have traded a 2027 second-round pick and a 2028 fifth-round pick to the Falcons for the former All-Pro and Pro Bowl safety.
So, what do we make of the move to boost their defense ? We break down our immediate takeaways below.
The Jaguars paid a big price to land Bates, that is for sure. A second-round pick (thought it will almost certainly be a late-second) and a fifth-round pick aren’t killer on most trade value charts, but it is a lot to give up for an older safety who has already been in the NFL for nearly a decade. It is also a lot to give up for a player who is on the final deal of his contract and could easily become a free agent by March. If Bates isn’t on the Jaguars’ roster past 2026, giving up a second would look rather silly unless a Lombardi Trophy comes with it.
So, why the second? For starters, Bates is still supremely talented, and the Falcons are still technically in the NFC South race despite getting boat raced by the Cincinnati Bengals. There is also the fact that in a trade market where several contenders are in need of safeties that Bates was likely at the top or near the top of every single needy team’s list. , for example, that could certainly drive the price up for a team like the Jaguars. That is just a hypothetical, but it makes sense for that to be the case.
Jaguars general manager James Gladstone has proven that he can build productive draft classes without topics before. He has had just two picks in the top-two rounds of the draft since he was hired due to the Travis Hunter trade, and both Hunter and 2026 second-rounder Nate Boerkircher have worked out well. The Jaguars didn’t give away all of their draft capital, just part of it. They can work with that, because that is what they have been doing already.
Last year, the Jaguars faced serious injury questions at the wide receiver position as they looked to go on a second-half run. Their solution was to add an experienced veteran on an expiring contract in wide receiver Jakobi Meyers, trading a fourth- and a sixth-round pick for a move many people thought could be a rental. Meyers has been anything but a rental, though, with his addition changing everything about the Jaguars’ offense. As a result of his immediate impact and fit on and off the field for the franchise, Meyers didn’t have to wait long before signing a three-year extension and becoming a key Jaguars centerpiece and veteran leader moving forward.
Fast forward to this season, and the Jaguars have been hit by injuries once more, but this time at safety. With veteran leader , the Jaguars needed to add some experience to keep the unit together before the important late-season stretch. Bates, like Meyers, is a respected and productive veteran with a ton of experience, an expiring contract, and a chance to carve out a long-time role in Jacksonville moving forward. The focus will be about 2026, but I highly doubt the Jaguars gave up a second-round pick without some intentions of picking up contract talks relatively quickly with Bates. It happened last year, and it should happen again.
With James Gladstone using a second-round pick to land Bates, it sure makes some kind of splash along the defensive line seem less likely. Perhaps Gladstone would be willing to touch his first-round picks, but there isn’t another available defensive tackle in the NFL worth making that kind of deal for now that Jeffery Simmons is off the market. Derrick Brown would likely cost a first if he was available, but it is hard to see the Jaguars making that kind of grand move without a second-round pick. This also seems like a package that would’ve been used for a guy like Moro Ojomo.
With that said, the Jaguars still have the capacity to add to the room. Christian Barmore would likely only cost a Day 3 pick, and cheap veteran nose tackles would not cost an arm and a leg. The Jaguars have made things work with their current defensive line in terms of pass-rush, and they could turn to a platoon to replace Davon Hamilton if no trade is made. I do not think the Bates trade takes a defensive lineman off the market at all, but I do think the Jaguars are no longer big game hunting for one.

title: Where the Jaguars Stand 48 Hours Before the NFL Trade Deadline
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- 48 hours to go.
In 48 short hours, the NFL trade deadline will officially be here and we will know if the Jaguars made any moves after a 6-2 start as they gear up for an eventual playoff win.
So, where do things stand for the Jaguars with 48 hours until the big day? We break it down below.
There is not much that has changed on the Brian Thomas Jr. front over the last month. It looked like the Jaguars were pulling the plug on working him through his issues when they benched him during the second-half of an important AFC South game against the Houston Texans in Week 2, but the Jaguars rolled him back out as a top-three receiver on the depth chart in each of the first two weeks after the bye.
Thomas has seen two targets in that span, both coming against the Colts last week. He didn't see a target against the Baltimore Ravens and seems more like an auxilary piece in the Jaguars' offense along Parker Washington, Jakobi Meyers, and the tight ends and running game. But despite all of this, Thomas has remained with the Jaguars.
A few teams still make sense as those who could be interested in Thomas. The Kanas City Chiefs are the name that has been connected to the Jaguars' star receiver the most, though it is clear they have yet to come close to a price that would make it worthwhile for the Jaguars to deal the former first-round pick. The Jaguars really like Thomas as both a player and a member of their locker room, and it doesn't look like they would deal him for just any
The Jaguars have one of the NFL's top-rated defenses in really every metric, and they are coming off a fairly dominant defensive performance against Derrick Henry even without Davon Hamilton in the lineup. But it is because of the loss of Hamilton that it seems like the Jaguars would be wise to cast a wide net on defensive tackle targets. It made sense to do so even before Hamilton was injured, but the fact that he is out for the year now suggests the Jaguars need to make a move to truly be a Super Bowl contender.
That is at least one school of thought. The Jaguars could roll with Matt Dickerson and Albert Regis, along with Austin Johnson, at the nose tackle spot for the next nine weeks while Arik Armstead, Ruke Orhorhoro, and sometimes Travon Walker provide the pass-rush inside. It is a different team without Hamilton, but the Jaguars' front is a big reason they have been arguably the NFL's best team over the last two seasons.
The defensive tackle market is also a factor. Big names like Jeffery Simmons and DeForest Buckner came off the board a few weeks ago, while other big names like Derrick Brown and Moro Ojomo might not even be available. There are a few high-floor options, but one of the few impact players who seems to surely be on the market is New England Patriots defensive tackle Christian Barmore.
Jacksonville could also use help at safety due to injuries. Eric Murray is out for the year and Caleb Ransaw is on injured reserve, leaving the Jaguars' depth thin at the position. Antonio Johnson is one of the team's best defenders, while Rayuan Lane and Kaevon Merriweather have flashed in expanded snaps. But to prepare to face the likes of Caleb Williams and CJ Stroud in big games over the final two months, could the Jaguars want to add a veteran like Jessie Bates or Budda Baker?

title: 4 Thoughts on the Jaguars Entering the Trade Deadline: The Brian Thomas Jr. Stance
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- It could be a very interesting next two days for the Jacksonville Jaguars.
Well, it will be an interesting next 50 hours or so for all 32 teams as the NFL Trade Deadline approaches with speed. But the Jaguars are an especially interesting case considering their spot as a contender in the AFC at 6-2, and considering they have some clear needs at a few defensive spots.
So, what do we make of the Jaguars and where they sit entering the trade deadline's final two days? We have some thoughts.
Perhaps I am being stubborn. And I did say a few weeks ago the Jaguars should trade Thomas due to his declining role. But the vast majority of Brian Thomas Jr. trade reports this weekend have felt like ... nothing much to me. We have all seen the case of the Jaguars being stubborn about Thomas before; the team itself has even pushed back on Thomas trade noise in the past. We have also seen reports of other NFL teams believing that a Thomas trade will eventually happen despite the Jaguars' stubbornness.
The latest report that seems to be getting traction is one from Adam Schefter this morning where he says the Jaguars appear to be set to listen to offers. To that point I contend... why wouldn't they? When have the Jaguars not listened? Would they not listen on virtually anyone at the deadline, because that is what teams do? Were they not expected to take any phone calls for the next two days? It very much so feels like a situation that hasn't changed, and people are frustrated at the lack of change.
Schefter: Sounds like Jaguars will listen to trade offers for Brian Thomas Jr. before deadline.
This isn't to say Thomas hasn't seen his role decerease since the start of the season. He has caught one pass since Week 4, and it stands to reason he could help another offense in the NFL more than he is currently helping a Jaguars offense that is doing just fine without a big impact made by Thomas. But for now, this all feels like ... just not much.
I know that some fans thought a team like the Jagurs might want to make a trade before the Sunday games to keep a target from getting injured, but that doesn't really happen outside of the weird Marvin Harrison Jr. trade from last month. Ultimately, most trades before the deadline happen either right on Tuesday or on the day after the Sunday games and, in some cases, after the Monday Night Football game.
I think if we see the Jaguars make a trade, we see it happen close to Monday evening/Tuesday afternoon. Get the player in for Wednesday and go from there to see if they can get them ready to play in Week 10 against the Tennessee Titans on the road. That is only in the event the Jaguars do pull off a trade, of course, but my prediction is that we do see at least one.
I think the Jaguars are going to be in the defensive tackle and safety market , and there are three teams I think they are going to have to compete with for targets.
I am normally very much so i nfavor of teams taking massive swings with draft picks. I loved what the Rams did during their Super Bowl windows. I thought the Travis Hunter trade was a good one. And I think the Chicago Bears made the best move of the year grabbing Jeffery Simmons. With that said, not every blockbuster is built the same, and there is one popular blockbuster hypothetical thrown out there that I just would not do: a king's ransom for Philadelphia Eagles defensive tackle Jalen Carter.
I have not really considered Carter much as a potential option for the Jaguars. Partly because I do not think the Eagles would want to have to deal with the dead cap that would come with trading Carter, and partly because Carter is just a player I would not put together a Simmons-like package for. My feeling is there has to be some reason the Eagles would be selling. It made sense for the Titans to; Simmons is gonna be a few years into his 30s the next time they sniff .500. But the Eagles should have a window. If they would be comfortable with moving on from Carter, I believe there likely would be a reason. He is an elite talent, but I would look elsewhere.
