title: Raiders Stock Report: Risers & Fallers After Loss to 49ers
full_text:
The Las Vegas Raiders got off to another slow start in Week 9, falling behind early to a San Francisco 49ers team that did not need any help to have a successful day. Week 9 was a mistake-filled performance for the Raiders on both sides of the ball.
Week 9 would have been the team's worst overall performance this season, if not for their subpar outing against the New England Patriots a few weeks ago. The Raiders' road matchup against San Francisco was disappointing, but not totally unexpected.
Sunday went about as expected for a Raiders team that struggled with the New York Jets last week. The 49ers looked like an elite team coming off their bye week. Las Vegas looked outmatched physically and mentally.
Below are the players who are rising and falling following the Raiders' Week 9 loss to the 49ers.
There are few positives that can be drawn from the Raiders' loss to the 49ers, as the game was not all that close. The stats will not show it, but in a limited sample size, Jeanty looked closer to full health than he has at any point this season. Giving Jeanty the first half of Week 8 was a good idea.
Jeanty averaged over four yards a carry and likely would have gotten more attempts had the Raiders not fallen behind by so many points so quickly. Jeanty's ankle injury shortly before the start of the regular season will go down as one of the unfortunate events of the 2026 season.
After Mike Washington's success last week, if there was any question of whether or not the Raiders' rushing issues were because of Jeanty, Sunday confirmed it has more to do with Jeanty and Washington's supporting cast than with them.
The Raiders' defensive backfield issues mean the unit will keep getting targeted. This will test the unit, but also give them opportunities to make plays. Stukes has been a much-needed addition to Las Vegas' defensive backfield, but has had expected growing pains.
Overall, Stukes plays generally well. In Week 9, he intercepted Brock Purdy in the second half, giving the Raiders a chance to mount another comeback. Stukes' development is one of the positives for Las Vegas.
Las Vegas' tight ends have been their most dependable position group this season. I believe they have the best group of tight ends in the league. However, both Bowers and Mayer had costly fumbles on Sunday . Had the Raiders scored on those plays, they would have had a chance.
The Raiders need more at cornerback, but it will not come this season. The unit has struggled mightily over the past few weeks, and it seems to be snowballing. It's easy to point to Stokes' struggles or Porter not being fully healthy.
However, the unit as a whole is struggling. It would be easy to fix one cornerback who is struggling, but they all are at one point or another weekly. Sunday was another example, as Purdy completed eight of his 12 first-half passes for 123 yards and a touchdown.
Las Vegas' defensive backfield has long been an issue, but it appears their dependence on inexperienced defensive backs is proving costly. Although it has been costly, Las Vegas' front office and coaching staff are banking on it being a positive for those young defenders' development.
The Raiders have a long way to go. This offseason will be primarily about fixing the unit one way or another. The progress Las Vegas made on its roster this offseason was good enough to help them surpass last season's win total before even getting halfway through this season.
The front office should be commended for that. Although hoping the struggles their defensive backfield has had this season will help their individual and collective development, the Raiders must do what they can to fix the unit, as it is simply not good right now.
More is needed in a lot of regards. It will be up to the Raiders' front office to have another big offseason full of notable signings to help the team succeed.
Ezekiel is a former Sports Editor from the Western Herald and former Atlanta Falcons beat writer.

title: 3 Instant Observations From Raiders' Week 9 Loss vs. 49ers
full_text:
The Las Vegas Raiders were on the road again in Week 9, this time against the San Francisco 49ers. The Raiders faced a 49ers team fresh off its bye week. The extra week of preparation, combined with Week 9 being a home game, gave San Francisco many of the intended benefits early in the game.
The Raiders started another game slowly. After winning the toss and deferring until the second half, which is usually the better option for them, Las Vegas' defense allowed a 12-play, 69-yard drive that was reminiscent of much of the unit's outing against the New York Jets last week.
Las Vegas' offense followed up by gaining seven yards in three plays, then punting the ball after an opening drive that took one minute off the game clock. Predictably, the 49ers marched down the field to jump out to an early 14-0 lead, and the Raiders had to play catch-up the rest of the day.
Below are a few of my instant reactions to the Raiders' Week 9 loss to the 49ers.
The Raiders escaped their Week 8 matchup against the Jets with a win. The fact that they had to escape against the Jets was telling. The success of Geno Smith and the Jets against the Raiders' defense last Sunday, while the 49ers had the week off, foreshadowed their Week 9 slate.
The 49ers are better at everything than the Jets are, especially on offense. San Francisco used a nearly carbon-copy game plan, attacking a vulnerable Raiders defense on the ground and through the air . Las Vegas allowed the Jets to run for 140 yards in the first half.
In Week 9 , the 49ers nearly ran for 100 yards in the first quarter alone. Las Vegas' inability to stop the run only makes things harder for a questionable defensive backfield. This has been on full display throughout the season, especially over the past two weeks.
Entering the season, it was no secret that the Raiders still had plenty of work to do on their roster. That was the case even after their slew of offseason roster additions. In terms of roster-building, few teams in the league were more active than Las Vegas.
However, few, if any, rosters in the league needed as much work from top to bottom as the Raiders' roster did following their 3-14 campaign under Pete Carroll. Las Vegas' Week 9 loss to the 49ers further confirmed that the Raiders are better than they were last season.
Halfway through the season, the Raiders are no longer the league's worst team worthy of the No. 1 overall pick. Yet they are much closer to the two-win Jets, the New Orleans Saints, the winless Los Angeles Chargers, and the one-win Miami Dolphins.
Still, that is technically progress, which is all anyone asked of the Raiders this offseason. Their five losses this season are just the result of calculated risks Las Vegas' front office had to take while addressing some positions more than others.
Because of how the league is set up, no team is good at every position. The Raiders are simply in their first season after beginning to turn things around, roster-wise. No one is surprised that Las Vegas has lost to the teams they have. It is just tough to see it be as bad as it has been at times.
The Raiders were never expected to contend for a playoff spot this season until they started 3-0. They are still in the playoff hunt, but at 4-5, with games against the Seattle Seahawks and Denver Broncos coming up, Las Vegas will soon have to make some tough decisions.
Those decisions will have to come at several positions, and regarding how to progress through the rest of this season. Las Vegas' rebuild is just getting started; their five losses are what early-stage rebuilds look like.
However, Las Vegas' front office and coaching staff should consider that development on game days is more productive than practice.
As losses begin to pile up, the Raiders brass must look at the full picture and not let a perceived shot at the playoffs lead them to make the wrong decision for the team's future beyond this season.
Ezekiel is a former Sports Editor from the Western Herald and former Atlanta Falcons beat writer.

title: Why Raiders Splitting RB Carries Is a Good Thing
full_text:
The Las Vegas Raiders are looking for answers when it comes to their ground game.
Las Vegas ranks 31st in the NFL in EPA per rush and rushing yards per game, ahead of only the Green Bay Packers. For an offensive staff that found success in Seattle and hopes to bring that to Las Vegas, things have not gone well.
The biggest issue with the Raiders' rushing attack is that former top-10 draft pick Ashton Jeanty has not lived up to the billing through his first two seasons. He has been impactful as a receiver, but he has not powered the run game.
Enter Mike Washington Jr., a fourth-round rookie who blew NFL fans away with his impressive Scouting Combine performance in February. Washington has shown some flashes when he gets the ball, which has led to an increase in carries.
The Raiders are 4-4 and trying to play their way into a Wild Card spot. That won't happen if they can't run the ball more efficiently.
The answer is for them to continue splitting carries between Jeanty and Washington.
In the first four games of the season, Jeanty had 78 carries, while Washington had 24. In the next four games, Jeanty has had 30 carries, while Washington has had 41.
It's obvious the Raiders are trying to get Washington going to spark the ground game because Jeanty can't currently make that happen. But there's a reason for that.
Jeanty suffered an ankle injury a few weeks before the regular season began, and it's evident that the injury has lingered into November. He has not been able to plant and cut to make defenders miss, which is his biggest strength.
Jeanty's game is predicated on patience and forcing missed tackles. If he can't do that, he won't be able to get to the second level or move the chains. That's why the Raiders have emphasized getting Washington the ball in the backfield, a more decisive, hit-the-hole-and-go type runner.
Klint Kubiak has been smart about how to approach a struggling run game. If Jeanty is not going to be an effective rusher, the Raiders will give Washington more opportunities in the backfield while Jeanty continues to be impactful as a receiver.
The Raiders should keep the two running backs splitting carries, because it's the best thing for the offense -- and Jeanty's health. It will benefit the team in the long run.
Carter Landis studied journalism at Michigan State University where I graduated in May of 2022. He currently is a sports reporter for a local television station, and is a writer covering the Las Vegas Raiders

title: What Raiders Must Repeat Offensively To Take Down 49ers
full_text:
It took some time, but in their Week 8 matchup against the New York Jets, the Las Vegas Raiders got back to playing winning football. It was admittedly a sloppy first half for both teams. The Raiders ground out a hard-fought second half to beat the Jets, ending their four-game losing streak.
It was far from pretty, as is the case sometimes in the National Football League. The Raiders still found a way to win a game they would almost certainly have lost last season. Las Vegas continues to take care of business in games they are "supposed" to win.
Yet Week 8 reconfirmed that there are no guarantees, and the margin of error is as slim as the blade of grass between Jeremy Chinn's cleats and the sideline on his game-sealing interception. They now turn their attention to the San Francisco 49ers as they hit the road in Week 9.
San Francisco is the better team by most metrics, but metrics don't win games. Sunday will come down to execution and the Raiders' ability to compensate in areas where they are clearly overmatched.
For that to happen, Las Vegas must fine-tune and speed up what worked last Sunday. Ideally, that would start with continuing to find success on the ground. Even if they only get two or three yards per carry, if it leads to a manageable third down, Las Vegas' offense is in business.
If the Raiders have to feed Mike Washington again in Week 9, so be it. Ashton Jeanty out of the backfield has helped keep the Raiders' passing attack afloat at times. If Las Vegas can keep finding ways to get Jeanty the ball in space, the offensive line's run blocking becomes less of an issue.
Finding a way to potentially get Jeanty and Washington on the field at the same time, somehow, along with the likes of Tre Tucker, Jalen Nailor, and a healthy Jack Bech, would add another dimension to the offense that could help negate some of the issues the unit has had against top competition.
Las Vegas must keep throwing a mix of running backs at opposing defenses, no matter how slow the progress may feel at times. All of the Raiders' running backs bring a unique skill set, most of which is largely unknown under Kubiak's offense, to their upcoming opponents.
In Week 8 , veteran quarterback Kirk Cousins sparked the offense's best third quarter of the season. Since they won, the offense's second-half performance against the Jets may have been the best second half of the season too. Cousins jump-started it all right out of the gate.
The Raiders' best third quarter of the season began with Cousins' dart to Bowers, which opened things up for the unit in the third quarter and for the rest of the game. The third quarter will once again prove vital for Las Vegas against a talented 49ers team in Week 9.
“I think the first play of the second half might have been the throw to Brock [Bowers], and I thought that was a key play in the game and a great call by our coaches, and that whole drive, to finish that drive, it got us right back in the game, which we needed, very important. If you punt and they go down and score, it could be a whole different story,” Cousins said earlier this week.
“So, it’s very important, and we’ve got to be really strong in the third quarter the rest of the way. And I felt we have continued, last week in the fourth quarter, continuing to play well in the fourth quarter. But it’s a four-quarter game. You’ve got to do it, all four of them.”
Raiders' offensive coordinator, Andrew Janocko, looks forward to the challenge of beating one of the league's best.
“I think we do our film study. They’re going to do their film study on us. We’re going to find new and unique different ways to attack defenses. It’s a new play caller, so it’s a new system. As far as what we saw from last year, I know that some of the players are the same, and they’re retooled too," Janocko said earlier this week.
“They’ve gotten some new pieces. They’ve gotten some guys back from injury, so that’s something that we look forward to going on the road and using as a good measuring stick."
Ezekiel is a former Sports Editor from the Western Herald and former Atlanta Falcons beat writer.

title: How Raiders Can Turn Tide Against Elite Opponents on Sunday
full_text:
The Las Vegas Raiders are a consistent football team, though not in the way you think.
With a 4-4 record, the Raiders have beaten four teams with losing records and lost four with winning or .500 records after eight games. On Sunday, they return to the Bay Area for the first time since relocating to Las Vegas to face the 6-1 San Francisco 49ers, who are coming off a bye week.
While the 49ers, despite many injuries, have maintained their own level of consistency and success, they can be beaten (just ask the Atlanta Falcons two weeks ago). Head coach Klint Kubiak and his franchise need a signature win, and they hope to do that this weekend in Santa Clara.
Kubiak was once a key piece of the 49ers' success as their passing game coordinator in 2023, the year they lost in overtime to the Kansas City Chiefs in that season's Super Bowl. However, while his experience was meaningful, it comes down to this game being a player's one.
"Yeah, they’re a top offense in the league, top defense in the league," Kubiak said. "Extremely well coached, great talent everywhere. That experience was very meaningful for me. But a couple years removed from that, and on Sunday it’s a players’ game.”
San Francisco is indeed a top-five scoring offense at 28.1 points per game and sixth in the NFL in points allowed per game at 19.9. Next Gen Stats puts the 49ers at +0.18 EPA per play, the third-best in the NFL, while allowing the fourth-fewest rushing yards per game at 89.0.
This is a terrific team with exceptional core talent, including linebacker Fred Warner, edge rusher Nick Bosa, running back Christian McCaffrey, tight end George Kittle, and star quarterback Brock Purdy. Not to mention that they recently acquired Pro Bowl defensive tackle DeForest Buckner, who began his career with the 49ers a decade ago.
I would argue this is arguably the Raiders' staff's most challenging matchup of the season due to how well-coached both sides of the ball are with head coach Kyle Shanahan and defensive coordinator Raheem Morris. Their counterparts are offensive coordinator Andrew Janocko and defensive coordinator Rob Leonard, who provided similar observations.
"Yeah, they do. They’re fundamentally sound, man," Leonard said. "They’re a clean operation, and they got some good players. Quarterback’s playing at a high level, good tight end, running backs, and the offensive line is really good. So, that’s what jumps out to me, how fundamentally sound they are, and they’re able to put a lot of pressure on you."
"It’s a talented bunch. Been together for a long time. Experienced bunch," Janocko explained. "It’s a team that have a lot of familiarity with playing against them last year. They’re well coached, well prepared. They attack the football. They’re very opportunistic. So, it’ll be a heck of a challenge for us against one of the best teams in the league."
While the 49ers do provide a "heck of a challenge" for the Raiders, the latter has three players who can be the biggest difference in this game: quarterback Kirk Cousins, tight end Brock Bowers, and star defensive end Maxx Crosby.
Cousins is seeing a resurgence with Kubiak and the Raiders. The offense has so much potential if Kubiak could put his head down, find a true solution, and learn how to evaluate running backs correctly - something he has struggled with in the past with the Seattle Seahawks.
Morris will find ways to try to blanket or bracket Bowers on the perimeter, but even if that were the case, it may not matter. Bowers has been the best tight end in football this season, and he missed two games at the start. His presence alone gives Cousins and the Raiders' offense a chance for an explosive day against a stout 49ers passing defense.
Then, there's Crosby. We haven't seen a game-wrecking performance from the veteran superstar this season. However, the Raiders will need Crosby to flip the switch this weekend to have a shot at beating the 49ers in a shocking road win.
The Raiders have the tools to get their first win against a team with a winning record this season, putting themselves in the thick of the wild-card race at the halfway mark of the campaign. It will be their biggest challenge yet, something they're embracing to the fullest.
Jared Feinberg, a native of western North Carolina, has written about NFL football for nearly a decade. He has contributed to several national outlets and is now part of our On SI team as an NFL team reporter. Jared graduated from UNC Asheville with a bachelor's degree in mass communications and later pursued his master's degree at UNC Charlotte. You can follow Jared Feinberg on Twitter at @JRodNFLDraft

title: Predicting Raiders' Lineup Moves in Week 9 Against 49ers
full_text:
The Las Vegas Raiders' coaching staff enters their Week 9 game against the San Francisco 49ers looking to build on their win over the New York Jets last Sunday.
In their Week 8 matchup against the Jets, Las Vegas made several notable changes to their starting lineup that proved fruitful. After struggling to find competent play at the right guard position between Jackson Powers-Johnson and Caleb Rogers, the Raiders turned to rookie Trey Zuhn.
The Jets are not known for being a stout defense, but they are serviceable and gave Las Vegas fits for the entire first half, holding the Raiders to 97 total yards. Still, Zuhn looked like he may be the Raiders' best option at right guard for the rest of the season.
Sunday's matchup against the 49ers will be much more telling, as San Francisco's defense is much more of a challenge than New York's. It will be interesting to see how Zuhn does at guard against one of the toughest teams the Raiders will face this season.
Given their success last week, even against the Jets, Las Vegas would be wise to stick with those changes for an additional week to get another look at how well they work. If Zuhn plays well against the 49ers, the starting right guard position is his to lose.
Starting Zuhn at right guard wasn't the only change Las Vegas made against the Jets. They also started rookie running back Mike Washington over Ashton Jeanty. The Raiders cannot afford to sit Jeanty for an entire game, as he is far too valuable catching the ball out of the backfield.
Still, the way they successfully used Washington on the ground and Jeanty through the air against the Jets is worth building upon in Week 9 against the 49ers.
Ahead of the team's road matchup against the 49ers, offensive coordinator Andrew Janocko praised Washington's Week 8 outing.
“He’s somebody that continues to improve, really works his craft. He wants to get better at each and every single thing he does, whether it’s fitting his hands up, his eyes, everything coming out. It’s all the little fundamental things that we talk about. It’s stuff that he wants to get better at, improve on, and that’ll allow him to become a more successful player,” Janocko said earlier this week.
“Running the ball is a full team thing. The greatest thing about football in general is that it’s 11 as one on every single play. So, it takes all 11 for everybody to be successful."
Cornerback Darien Porter returned to practice this week after playing only one play against the New York Jets last Sunday. He is officially listed as questionable heading into Week 9. However, speed is arguably Porter's greatest asset on the field, and he is dealing with a groin injury.
A groin injury can linger. Despite being listed as questionable, Kubiak and defensive coordinator Rob Leonard may decide not to risk damage to Porter's long-term health in a game where they already face an uphill battle.
Las Vegas faced a similar decision earlier this season, when they could have rested running back Ashton Jeanty against a New England Patriots team that was missing more than five players before their matchup ended. The Raiders need Porter beyond just this week.
Resting Porter on Sunday is far from ideal for Sunday's game, but may be best for his career, depending on the severity of his injury and how much progress he made on it during the week. Porter sitting out would offer a valuable opportunity to other corners on the roster.
Porter may very well start against the 49ers. Regardless, rookie cornerback Hezekiah Masses is sure to see significant playing time. Heading into Sunday, Masses could be in for another action-packed day, who has had extreme highs and lows during this season.
“I think it’s always a moving target. See where your team’s at, and who’s playing the best ball at the time. And it’s a 17-game regular season where things change every week. And [there have] been changes at guard," Kubiak said earlier this week.
"[We have] changed up front defensively. Changed at corner, and that’s the NFL. We have a young roster, and we’re going to give guys opportunities and see what fits us best."
Ezekiel is a former Sports Editor from the Western Herald and former Atlanta Falcons beat writer.

title: A Simple (And Logical) Solution to a Clear Dolphins Problem
full_text:
One day after veteran Zane Gonzalez missed a second field goal attempt in as many weeks, Miami Dolphins head coach Jeff Hafley said he and GM Jon-Eric Sullivan hadn't made a decision on their kicker.
We'll make it simple for them: It's time to move on.
The Dolphins will have to make a call one way or another because Gonzalez has exhausted his three practice squad elevations with Miami, meaning he can't kick for the team again in 2026 unless he's signed to the active roster.
And it should be a slam dunk decision, one we're actually surprised hasn't already been made — unless it has been made but Hafley didn't want to reveal it just yet.
It's that much of a non-brainer, at least from where we sit.
Gonzalez's two misses have come in games where the Dolphins gave themselves a chance against quality opponents and they both came at key junctures — a fourth-quarter miss that kept the Dolphins two scores down against the New England Patriots in Week 8 and the miss on the final play of the first half that kept Miami from going into halftime tied 6-6.
As Hafley said after the game and again Monday, the Dolphins have to make those kicks.
Makes on both of those maybe wouldn't have changed the outcome in either game, but it's not like the Dolphins are operating with a big margin for error.
But the biggest reason the Dolphins should move on from Gonzalez is that they should operate with their kickers the same way they have with the rest of the roster, and that's basically treating this season as one big audition for veteran newcomers and a year of development for their draft picks.
Gonzalez has been a solid kicker during his NFL career, but why shouldn't the Dolphins aspire to get better at that position in 2027 and get an early look at somebody with more upside.
The Dolphins already have held tryouts for different kickers this season, and one of them stands out as an intriguing candidate — and it just so happens Hafley and Sullivan are familiar with him.
That would be Lucas Havrisik, who appeared in three games with the Green Bay Packers in 2025 and was 4-for-4 on field goal attempts with a long of 61 yards. Before that, he played nine games for the Rams in 2023 and was 15-for-20.
Or maybe somebody like Tanner Brown, who has never kicked in the NFL but was 25-for-28 for Louisville of the UFL this year with a long of 60 yards.
Brown also was among the kickers who have tried out for Miami this year.
Why not take a shot at one of those unproven young players?
What's the worst that can happen?
The Dolphins have to keep looking for a kicker?
It's not like the one they have now has been overly reliable.
And we could say the same about punter Bradley Pinion, whose 25-yard shank set up a Detroit field goal in the second quarter.
The Dolphins already have brought in punter for tryouts as well, so maybe the time has come to give somebody else a shot.
But the call on Pinion might be tougher because he's already on the 53-man roster. With Gonzalez, it's changing kickers or dumping somebody from the 53 to make room for him.
There's no reason they should do that right now.

title: Miami Dolphins 2026 Week 9 Snap Counts Stories: Secondary Switch, What's Going on With Grant?
full_text:
What stood out regarding play counts in the Miami Dolphins' 19-9 loss against the Detroit on Sunday:
We'll start with the list of inactives, which was highlighted by wide receiver Jalen Tolbert going back to the sidelines and running back Jaylen Wright missing the game with a quad injury.
The only Dolphins player who was active but did not play was backup quarterback Kyle McCord.
Since we've been keeping track every game, the starting lineup was back to seven rookies with fourth-round pick Kyle Louis making his first NFL start. The other six starters were Kadyn Proctor back in action at left guard, Will Kacmarek at tight end, wide receiver Caleb Douglas, linebacker Jacob Rodriguez, cornerback Chris Johnson and safety Michael Taaffe.
-- After Caleb Douglas has the biggest snap count among the wide receivers against New England, this time it was Malik Washington back to having that top spot, though by a small margin (44 to 42).
-- What's notable at wide receiver is Chris Bell having 36 snaps to only 11 for Kevin Coleman Jr., who again was more noticeable with Bell targeted only once for an incompletion where he failed to create separation.
-- Tight end Will Kacmarek, who left the game temporarily after taking a big shot to the side of the knee, played only 20 offensive snaps for a second consecutive game. While there was a contributing factor in this game, we'd still like to see him more after the Dolphins spent a third-round pick on him.
-- We again have a hard time getting Kacmarek being outsnapped by rookie free agent fullback DJ Herman, particularly on a day when the running game didn't have much operating room.
-- As should have been expected, it again was the Ollie Gordon II show at running back, though his snap percentage (72 percent) was smaller than it was against New England. Backups Kaytron Allen (6) and Carlos Washington Jr. (5) combined for 11 snaps.
-- Recent waiver wire pick-up Jared Wayne, who was in the lineup instead of Tolbert, played six offensive snaps and was flagged for two penalties — not exactly a good percentage there.
-- Five players were on the field for all the team's 59 defensive snaps — LB Jordyn Brooks, LB Jacob Rodriguez, S Michael Taaffe, CB Chris Johnson and S Dante Trader. The first four also had 100 percent participation each of the previous two games.
-- Chop Robinson's recent surge was reflected in the face that he got the most snaps on the edge, which hasn't happened this year because that distinction usually goes to Josh Uche. It was Robinson with 39 snaps and Uche to 35, then a major drop for any other edge defender with Rodney McGraw next with 12.
-- While Louis got the start, it should be noted he played only 11 snaps on defense, so categorizing as a starter now would be a stretch.
-- What stood out on the defensive line was the very similar number of snaps between Zach Sieler (42), Zeek Biggers (39) and Jordan Phillips (38), where Sieler usually played far more than his teammates. Given the performance of the defense, this can only be viewed as a positive development.
-- It's not exactly a great sign, however, that 2025 first-round pick Kenneth Grant played only 21 snaps in his fourth game back. This actually was his lowest total since he played 16 snaps against the Bengals in Week 5 in his first game of the season. The Dolphins need more from Grant, period.
-- Another interesting development came at cornerback where JuJu Brents and Jason Marshall Jr. got basically the same work load after Brents had emerged clearly ahead in recent games.
-- Edge Jamree Kromah, who the Dolphins claimed off waivers from the Chicago Bears two weeks ago, made his Miami debut and it consisted of two snaps on defense and four on special teams.
-- Opening-day starter Zayne Anderson was among the seven non-specialists who saw action only on special teams, along with LB Shaka Heyward, LB Jackson Woodard, S Julius Wood, C Andrew Meyer, G Jarrett Kingston and G/T Caedan Wallace.
-- Finally with special teams, rookie Seydou Traore again led the way with 20 snaps, though this time he was tied with Woodard. They were followed with 15 for Louis, Wood and Heyward.

title: Four Losers And Four Winners From Miami's Week 9 Loss
full_text:
Despite an exceptional performance by the defense, the Miami Dolphins were unable to knock off the Detroit Lions, falling by a score of 19-9 as they remain winless at Hard Rock Stadium.
It's no joke what Miami's defense has accomplished since their bye week. This is the first time in the past 30 games that the Lions' quarterback, Jared Goff, has been unable to record a passing touchdown.
Breaking a streak like that doesn't happen by accident. It's just a shame that not only was the offense unable to capitalize on its opportunities, but the special teams also somehow ended up just as ineffective in a game that was this close.
If there needed to be a wake-up call for changes to be made to Miami's special teams, this should be enough justification.
After playing a clean game of football against New England, Bradley Pinion made a pair of mistakes against the Lions — a kickoff that fell short of the landing zone to begin the game, and a punt that went about 25 yards. Not surprisingly, they ended up being catalysts for two field goals. But, hey, at least he can throw a decent football.
Miami didn't believe Riley Patterson was the answer at kicker, so the Dolphins turned back to Zane Gonzalez, who doinked a kick off the upright to close out the first half. It would have tied the game, but clearly asking for consistency at the position has been a bit too much.
And to top it off, allowing Detroit to capitalize on a fake punt to start the second quarter is the icing on the cake.  It seems surreal that, at this point in the season, the Dolphins need to seriously consider a shake-up at both kicker and punter, and their coverage could use some much-needed work as well.
It's another week when Sullivan's picks in the 2026 NFL Draft impressed, and it's making many Miami fans feel like the 2027 draft, which could be a monumental one for the franchise, is in good hands.
Honestly, it's surprising it took Jacob Rodriguez this long to record his first sack, but he did just that in the second quarter, alongside 10 total tackles on the day. Chris Johnson, meanwhile, recorded his first interception of the season, which also happened to be the first pick thrown by Goff in 2026.
That's THREE rookies on this team with an interception (Johnson, Rodriguez, Michael Taaffe). On the other end, Caleb Douglas continues to be as reliable a wide receiver as ever for the offense. Overall, the rookie won big today, which means Sullivan is a winner by proxy.
This might have been the worst collective performance by the offensive line this season. Granted, they faced a pass rush with game-wrecker Aidan Hutchinson. Still, both Jonah Savaiinaea and Austin Jackson looked rough, but it's extra disappointing to see Brewer struggle the way he did.
He looked sharp to start the season, but has been inconsistent as of late, and now there are some fans who are second-guessing the three-year extension. He had trouble standing his ground, being pushed backwards on multiple occasions. On top of that, he was flagged twice for holding — the latter killed the momentum of an otherwise solid drive in the middle of the third quarter.
Detroit wasn't the only team with an effective pass rush. The Dolphins came at Goff with everything they had, resulting in three sacks. Uche was responsible for one of those on Detroit's first drive. The Lions were knocking on the end zone at the 4-yard line, but Uche set them back 6 yards, forcing a field goal attempt instead.
In addition, Uche was able to make contact with Goff's throwing arm, resulting in a wild throw that Johnson capitalized on for the aforementioned interception. This was a pleasant two-game stretch for Uche, with nine tackles, two sacks, and a pass deflection against the Patriots and Lions.
Did the offensive line do Willis any favors? No, not really. But his decision-making, which has been up and (mainly) down this season, was, well, down. There were quite a few general misfires, some overthrows that receivers like Caleb Douglas bailed him out on. But the interception he threw into double coverage might have been one of the worst mistakes he's made on the field so far.
The dual-threat option was nonexistent in this game for Willis, which could be almost entirely due to the nagging groin injury he's been dealing with. If it's this impactful in terms of negating what Willis can do, then maybe Jeff Hafley should consider giving him time to heal and throwing Kyle McCord into the fire in the meantime.
But hey, another nice game for Douglas! Seventy yards off six receptions is nothing to scoff at, and it's not crazy to say he was the sole bright spot of the offense. His 20-yard gain in the first quarter came off a phenomenal snag midair off a pass that was thrown a bit too high.
If it were any other receiver in that situation, it might have been picked off, but Douglas is good enough to make a play like that happen. Believe it or not, this is the first time all season that Douglas was targeted more than Malik Washington — 8 to 3. Unfortunately, it takes more than a rookie wide receiver to carry an entire offense on his back.
Gordon was in a similar situation to Willis — the offensive line didn't help him out in the way they're expected to. So it was a brutal outing for Gordon, with 55 yards on 16 carries. It's not a good thing when the biggest positive is that he kept his cool even through adversity.
What this game really shows is how much De'Von Achane meant to this offense. He could take over a game by himself, as he was physical enough to shake off would-be tacklers in the trenches, even if there weren't comfortable gaps created by the offensive line. Gordon is tough, but he can't do the same thing as consistently.
After a solid performance against Minnesota back on October 4, Biggers was pedestrian against Cincinnati, the New York Jets and New England. However, he was one of many Dolphins in the trenches who teed off on Jared Goff in what should be considered a breakout game for the 23-year-old.
He ended the day with three tackles, a sack, and two QB hits. His sack — the first full sack of his career — came on third down of Detroit's first drive of the second quarter, forcing a Lions punt. It's not a contest, technically, but the 2025 seventh-rounder looked a lot better than the 2025 first-rounder. Just saying.
Jake Gibson is a writer for the Miami Dolphins on SI. A native of Homestead, Florida, Jake grew up a South Florida sports fan and has currently attended five Super Bowls in person.

title: Five Instant Overreactions to the Dolphins-Lions Matchup
full_text:
The Miami Dolphins fought hard, but ultimately lost to the Detroit Lions in a 19-9 bout. There is plenty to analyze in this game from Sunday afternoon, so let's overreact to some of the key developments.
Malik Willis spent much of this game under constant pressure, and while he was able to avoid all but two sacks, he looked almost completely sapped of his athleticism, and his condition appeared to have worsened as the game went along.
Willis has been on the injury report for the last couple weeks with a groin ailment, and it’s pretty clear that it’s impacting his top-end mobility as well as his decision-making. He’s passed up multiple opportunities to run or extend plays, which may be his biggest weapon.
If Willis is banged up enough that it’s changing his calculus inside and outside the pocket, then it’s time to sit him down. It’s less about his performance of late, and more allowing him to get back to a comfortable place so Miami can better evaluate him down the stretch of the season. Plus, an extended look at Kyle McCord could be valuable in deciding whether he’s a long-term answer at backup QB.
One of the lone positives from an abysmal offensive performance is that of Caleb Douglas. The rookie receiver has looked stellar after returning from injury, and made multiple nice plays in this game, the best of which was a full-extension catch where he plucked the ball from the air after a stellar route past the sticks.
Douglas had a fourth-down drop late, but aside from that gaffe, he was easily Miami’s best offensive player. His fluidity and tackle-breaking at  6-4 are both astounding, and he’s risen to the moment as Malik Willis’ No. 1 option. His development is going to be one of the more exciting storylines of Miami’s rebuild, and it wouldn’t be shocking to see him as the centerpiece of an effective Dolphins passing game in the future.
A fun (and successful) fake punt call doesn’t change the fact that the Miami Dolphins’ special teams unit is embarrassing. Missed field goals, kicks short of the landing zone, and shanked punts are all stories that keep repeating themselves. Nothing has been fixed week over week, and we’re at the point where that falls on the coaching staff.
Miami used the last of their practice squad elevations on Zane Gonzalez, and after back-to-back weeks with missed kicks, it would be a massive mistake to bring him back on a regular deal. Furthermore, the social media noise around Chris Tabor’s job security gets deservedly louder and louder, as personnel changes haven’t led to better results. I think a midseason shake-up would be warranted if they decide to go in that direction.
The Miami Dolphins fought hard and remained competitive in a game where they faced the No. 1  offense in the NFL and only put up 228 total yards, and that’s because their defense put up a virtuosic performance.
Miami consistently moved Jared Goff off his spot, sacked him three times in the first half, and forced him to throw an early interception that flipped the field for Miami. Jahmyr Gibbs averaged only 3.7 yards per carry, and Detroit ended the game 3-for-12 on third downs.
Jeff Hafley mixed coverages, threw out all kinds of disguises, and put together some perfectly timed blitzes and stunts. A better offensive performance likely gives this game national recognition as a masterful shutdown of the league’s most effective attack, and it can’t be ignored, regardless of the final result.
With Kadyn Proctor returning from concussion protocol, there was a real opportunity for Miami to flash some of the run-game dominance we’ve seen in recent weeks. However, aside from a few chunk gains, they failed to get anything going.
Ollie Gordon finished with 16 carries for only 55 yards, and Malik Willis was under constant pressure. The only reason the Lions only finished with two sacks is because Willis miraculously avoided several free rushers throughout the game.
The offensive line is a unit defined by its weakest link, and Austin Jackson stuck out in a bad way against Detroit. He was consistently beaten in pass protection, and didn’t do enough in the run game to even it out. Furthermore, Miami’s line has three players in their third year or earlier, and their youth has led to several miscommunications that they’ll need to grow and move on from.

title: Miami Dolphins Week 9 Instant Takeaways: Time for New Specialists, Suggestions for Offense
full_text:
That the Miami Dolphins lost against the Detroit Lions to fall to 1-7 in this rebuilding season wasn't a surprise at all, but how it came about? That was a different story.
Be honest, how many figured the uneven Dolphins defense would be able to stymie for most of the game the vaunted Detroit offense and hold it to only one touchdown? No, if the Dolphins were going  to win this game, they would have to outscore the Lions, with the thought that maybe they could do some damage against what statistically is a mediocre Detroit defense.
Well, the defense did its part only to watch the offense come up woefully short.
It was a brutal game all around for the offense, lowlighted by a whole bunch of penalties, a lot of pressure on Malik Willis, a really poor decision by Willis himself that produced a bad interception, other misfires, a couple of dropped passes, the whole sordid affair punctuated by rookie Caleb Douglas dropping a fourth-and-12 pass that should have been good for the first down.
There are so many things to pick apart offensively, though a lot of the fingers will be pointed at Willis because he's the quarterback and, in a best-case scenario, the quarterback of the future for this franchise.
It was difficult to make the case for Willis after this performance, though it must be repeated that he's operating at a major disadvantage with a really poor supporting cast.
It also didn't help that Willis clearly looked hampered by the groin injury that's had him on the injury report the past two weeks. Then again, if Willis can't scramble, it takes away what should be one of the best parts of his game, and if Willis isn't going be operating at full capacity, head coach Jeff Hafley has go to start thinking about using first-year quarterback Kyle McCord until Willis is right physically.
And for those Dolphins fans who keep calling for McCord, we would warn everyone to be careful what they wish for because McCord is going to be hamstrung by the same issues that surround Willis.
One other suggestion on offense is to be more aggressive, particularly near or in the red zone where we really don't need to see run on first and second down when the running game is struggling.
We also would suggest being more bold in a situation like when the Dolphins were down 9-3 in the third quarter and facing a fourth-and-6 from the Detroit 34-yard line. Settling for a 52-yard field goal attempt that still leaves you trailing even if successful isn't the way to go from this vantage point.
-- We do have to give the Dolphins props for a daring move when they had Bradley Pinion throw a pass out of punt formation, which produced their longest play of the game after it was completed to Kaytron Allen. Incidentally, that was the team's first completion by a punter since 2019 when Matt Haack threw a touchdown pass to kicker Jason Sanders in the famous "Mountaineer Shot" play.
-- That was one highlight for the special teams, which otherwise were brutal again. The Dolphins had a Pinion kickoff fall short of the landing zone, Pinion had a 25-yard punt, Zane Gonzalez missed a chip-shot field goal at the end of the first half, a fake punt allowed, and maybe we forgot something. This is a season for evaluation and trying to find hidden gems for 2026 and beyond, and it says Pinion and Gonzalez just aren't it, and it's time for the Dolphins to look for new kicking specialists.
-- The loss, though, was more on the offense than the kicking game.
-- The offensive line remains a work in progress, and this was a rough game against the Detroit pass rush and it wasn't just Aidan Hutchinson who did damage for the Lions. As has been the case most of the season, it was the right side that struggled and that's Jonah Savaiinaea and Austin Jackson. And Aaron Brewer also didn't have a great game, as he's having a hard time following up on his remarkable 2025 season.
-- This is very disappointing because the hope was the offensive line was going to make this offense run, but it's just not happening.
-- The running game again was sluggish, and there's only so much Ollie Gordon II can do without beter blocking up front.
-- That Dolphins pass rush in the first half was nothing short of dominant, easily the best we've seen all season.
-- There were standouts everywhere in that part of the game, particularly Josh Uche, Chop Robinson and Zach Robinson. Shoot, even Zeek Biggers got involved with the pass rush.
-- The pass rush slowed down a bit in the second half, but that had to be expected and nobody should complain about the performance of the defense in the least.
-- Great to see Chris Johnson come up with his first NFL interception the week after he made headlines and highlights for the wrong answer with his missed sack against Drake Maye. That it was an easy pick after Uche hit Jared Goff's arm made no difference. Johnson has been solid as a rookie, much better than his stats might suggest.
-- Really, there was very little not to like about the defensive performance, which had to overcome a pretty bogus DPI call against Jason Marshall Jr. against Amon-Ra St. Brown.
-- The big number here is the Dolphins holding Detroit to 270 yards, by far their lowest total of the season. The previous low was 355 in Week 2 against Buffalo.
-- This unequivocally was a winning performance by the Dolphins defense; it's just too bad the offense couldn't hold up its end of the bargain.

title: Why the Dolphins Are Off to a Good Start in Trying to Duplicate Detroit's Success Story
full_text:
The Miami Dolphins will be facing the Detroit Lions on Sunday for the first time since the 2022 season, and the Lions sure have come a long way since then.
Still in the relatively early stages of a rebuilding project then, the Lions have progressed to become perennial contenders.
In that sense, the Lions team the Dolphins will face Sunday is pretty much what they aspire to become.
It might not show on the field at Hard Rock Stadium on Sunday, but it says here the Dolphins are on their way toward becoming what the Lions have become.
At the center of the Lions’ rebuild is head coach Dan Campbell, who from the start has possessed an innate ability to lead. That was obvious even when he was interim head coach of the Dolphins in 2015, and it also was apparent even after his first Lions team in 2021 started that season 0-10-1.
While he hasn’t talked about “biting kneecaps” — at least not in press conference — Jeff Hafley sure looks like he possesses impressive leadership qualities.
And if you don’t believe that, just rewatch the postgame video after the Dolphins’ first victory of the season against the New York Jets in Week 7.
Or you could check out the words of Josh Uche when he told reporters, according to Joe Schad of the Palm Beach Post, “I think it starts with the head coach. The energy he brings, no toxicity, it's just all football. All ball, all details, all discipline."
OK, it’s not just about Hafley being a good leader because that will only take a team so far, and the Lions aren’t the Lions simply because of Campbell.
It’s taken a lot of good personnel decisions, and the first one of Detroit’s rebuild in 2021 was taking tackle Penei Sewell with the seventh overall selection in the draft — one pick after the Dolphins bypassed Sewell, who they could have used then and could use now, and instead took wide receiver Jaylen Waddle.
The first draft pick of the Dolphins’ new regime of GM Jon-Eric Sullivan and Hafley kind of looked like what Detroit did, with Miami taking a foundational piece for the offensive line with Alabama tackle Kadyn Proctor.
Through the first seven games of the 2026 season, Proctor absolutely looks the part of somebody who could end up doing for Miami what Sewell has done for Detroit.
Detroit continued their string of big-time draft hits with Jahmyr Gibbs, Jack Campbell, Sam LaPorta, Brian Branch and Amon-Ra St. Brown with later picks, and those players have formed the foundation of a team that was on the doorstep of the Super Bowl in 2023, secured the No. 1 seed in the playoffs in 2024, and is among the leading NFC contenders this season.
The Dolphins’ first draft class under Sullivan and Hafley needs a little bit more time to fully be evaluated, but the prognosis is very impressive with not only Proctor, but Chris Johnson, Jacob Rodriguez, Caleb Douglas and maybe a couple of others as well.
The key for the Dolphins will be to continue making good draft selections, and also solidify the quarterback position, whether with Malik Willis or a draft pick in 2027 or 2028.
In some ways, the Dolphins already are ahead of the Lions because they already have that first win.
However many more are in the cards for Miami in 2026 is debatable, but what’s more important is continuing on that similar Detroit track.

title: Dolphins RB Ollie Gordon II Set to Pay the Price for Taunting Penalty
full_text:
Ollie Gordon II is going to have to pay a price for his taunting penalty in Week 8.
The Miami Dolphins running back was fined $17,911 by the NFL for taunting of his unsportsmanlike conduct penalty in the third quarter of the team's 24-19 loss against the New England Patriots last Sunday.
The penalty, which came at the end of a 5-yard run after Gordon got up and started yapping at Patriots linebacker Robert Spillane, turned a third-and-5 into a third-and-20. The Dolphins couldn't convert, had to punt and the Patriots drove to score what became the game-winning touchdown that gave them a 17-13 lead.
"Honestly, it was one of those things where I took it too far," Gordon told reporters this week, per David Furones of the South Florida Sun-Sentinel. "Just got to be quiet and take it back to the huddle. That's one of the things I got to get better at, instead of dragging it on too long and talking to the other team.
"It's really just knowing when to do it, when not to. Be smart about it, not do it for too long, to be smart with it and not do it every play, like play after play. More like, tone it down some, get back to the huddle. If it is for a little bit, do it quick, get back to the huddle. Nothing too crazy."
This actually was the second time this year that Gordon was fined for taunting because it also happened in the preseason when he was fined $5,962.
Gordon is an emotional player with a big personality, but he's obviously got to be smarter than costing the Dolphins 15 yards because he can't control himself.
He's got the option of appealing the fine, though it might be difficult to get it rescinded since he was flagged on the play.
That should serve as punishment enough.
Some fans suggested benching him for a quarter against Detroit as a way of teaching him a lesson, but we'd question the wisdom of hurting the team that way, particularly since both of his backups (Jaylen Wright and Kaytron Allen) were listed as questionable for the Lions because of quad issues.
Gordon is the second Dolphins player fined during the 2026 regular season after rookie cornerback Chris Johnson.
The first-round pick was fined the same $17,911 amount for a hip drop tackle against Ashton Jeanty of the Las Vegas Raiders in the season opener, but he wasn't flagged on the play, he appealed the fine, and it was rescinded.

title: Breaking Down the Dolphins Saturday Updates for the Detroit Game
full_text:
The Miami Dolphins indeed look like they'll be missing one of their running backs against the Detroit Lions on Sunday.
That's the biggest conclusion we can reach from their weekly Saturday moves, which this time included the practice squad elevations of running back Carlos Washington Jr. and kicker Zane Gonzalez.
Running backs Jaylen Wright and Kaytron Allen, the two backups behind new starter Ollie Gordon II, both are dealing with quad injuries and Washington being elevated means that one or both might wind up missing the game against Detroit at Hard Rock Stadium.
This was a second elevation for Washington, who also spent one week on the active roster before being waived and then re-signed to the practice squad.
Gonzalez was a given, but his elevation was his third and final one, meaning this will be his last game unless the Dolphins sign him to the 53-man roster. Gonzalez missed a 43-yard field goal attempt in the fourth quarter against the New England Patriots last Sunday, and one would think he better have a clean outing against Detroit or the Dolphins will be looking elsewhere for a kicker.
If it comes to that, it wouldn't be a surprise if the Dolphins again go the practice squad elevation route.
The one move the Dolphins didn't make was at the edge defender position, which would seem to suggest that Malik Herring, who was one of the three players listed as questionable along with Wright and Allen, will be able to play despite his neck injury.
The Dolphins have five edge defenders on the 53-man roster with Herring, Chop Robinson, Josh Uche, Rodney McGraw and newcomer Jamree Kromah.
The Dolphins elevated rookie seventh-round pick Max Llewellyn from the practice squad that past two games when Robert Beal Jr. was injured in Week 7 and because Kromah had just joined the team last week. Llewellyn is out of practice squad elevations and the Dolphins would have to sign him to the 53 to use him again or they simply could have promoted Amari Gainer  or Eric Watts if they really needed an edge against Detroit, though a move on the 53 would have been needed for either Gonzalez or Washington because each team can only elevate two players each game.
The Lions also made a series of moves Saturday, the most notable involving linebacker Jack Campbell being placed on injured reserve. He, of course, sustained a serious neck injury in the Lions' victory against the Minnesota Vikings last Sunday.
To take his place on his the 53-man roster, the Dolphins signed cornerback Nick Whiteside from their practice squad.
The Lions also elevated edge Anthony Lucas and running back Jabari Small from the practice squad, with edge DJ Wonnum already declared out for the game and RB Siona Vaki questionable because of a late-week ankle injury.

title: Lions Insider Dishes on How the Dolphins Can Attack, Shock Detroit
full_text:
The Miami Dolphins will face their former interim head coach in Week 9 when they take on Dan Campbell and the Detroit Lions at Hard Rock Stadum.
Detroit will go into the game with a 5-2 record and coming big NFC North victories against the Green Bay Packers and Minnesota Vikings, the latter handing the Vikings their first loss of the season and thus officially preserving the 1972 Dolphins' status as the only perfect team in league history at least for another year.
To discuss this matchup from different angles, as well as the Lions' ascent to perennial contender status after a tough start under Campbell in 2021 with the similarities to the current Dolphins, we called on Detroit Lions On SI Publisher John Maakaron, who earlier in the week also was a guest on the All Dolphins Podcast (check out that episode).
JM: I think the Lions are most vulnerable in the secondary, as they've shown throughout the season.  In particular, the Lions have had trouble covering tight ends, so the Dolphins could exploit Detroit's defense over the middle of the field. Jack Campbell is out, and with that the Lions will have to rely on their backup linebackers in their man-coverage heavy scheme. With D.J. Reed also not expected to play, the Lions will be down their best cornerback. They've had some success as of late in holding the Packers and Vikings' passing attacks, but Reed has been a huge part of that. If Malik Willis can get into a groove, it could be a long night for the back seven.
JM: Miller has been solid up to this point. While there have certainly been growing pains throughout his debut season, the rookie has held his own for the most part. As far as giving him help, nothing is off the table. Last week against a blitz-heavy Vikings defense, the Lions utilized several multi-tight end packages designed to shift the strength of the defense as well as keep the blitzers off balance. If Miller struggles early in 1-on-1 work against Robinson, the Lions could do this once again to get him some help.
JM: That is a very real concern. Dan Campbell discussed that earlier this week, when he noted that the team was split between their empathy for Campbell and his situation but also the urgency to prepare for their upcoming game. The sight of Campbell being injured in that fashion is very jarring, and it wouldn't be surprising to see the Lions come out slow based on the fact that they're coming off of two high-stakes divisional wins (Green Bay and then Minnesota).
On the other hand, Dan Campbell is a master motivator and has traditionally had his teams ready to play in situations where they could be entering a trap game. There's certainly a concern that they could have an emotional letdown, but I would be very surprised if that were the case given Campbell's track record.
JM: The turnaround didn't truly begin until his second year. Sure, there were moments in year one where things were encouraging and looking up. Campbell would have the team ready to play, they would compete until the end and unfortunately they rarely came out with a win amidst some agonizing losses. Then, year two started extremely poorly culminating in that loss to Miami (coincidentally) at Ford Field that put Detroit at 1-6. After that game, though, things turned around drastically as the Lions won eight of their last 10 to finish with a winning record.
Even throughout those early struggles, though, there were always signs that the team might end up being competitive and winning. They were in just about every game, and never went down without a fight. There are elements of that in Miami's current start to the season, and because of that there should be some optimism.
JM: Teams have had some success limiting Hutchinson by making him go through multiple players en route to the quarterback. Oftentimes, there's a chip from a tight end and a back on his side waiting for him should he win his initial matchup. Willis can help himself by using his mobility to evade Hutchinson, who sometimes has a tendency to get too far upfield. In order to avoid him taking over, Willis will have to be quick on his feet and Miami will need to get him some extra help by utilizing chip blocks from tight ends and running backs.

title: The Dolphins Will Pull Off a Major Upset This Season, But When?
full_text:
The Miami Dolphins will face another difficult challenge in Week 9 when they play host to the Detroit Lions, who will bring to Hard Rock Stadium the top-ranked offense in the NFL.
It will be Lions head coach Dan Campbell's first game in Miami since he served as Dolphins interim head coach for the final 12 games of the 2015 season.
Detroit will go into the game as a 6.5-point favorite, according to the Fan Duel Sportsbook, while the Dolphins will be looking for their most significant victory of the season.
Not surprisingly, the national opinion from media members is the Dolphins are going to lose for the seventh time in eight games, and all logic suggest it's a reasonable prediction because Miami simply doesn't appear to have the firepower to stay with the Lions.
But we all know the saying about any given Sunday, and there will be a time this season when the Dolphins win a game nobody expects them to win.
Just think back to that 2019 season we always bring up as a comparison point. After starting 0-7, the Dolphins defeated not one but two eventual playoff teams down the stretch, including the gigantic upset at Gillette Stadium in the season finale.
The Dolphins will have plenty of opportunities in the remainder of the season for a big upset with a schedule that includes games against the Buffalo Bills (twice), Denver Broncos, Chicago Bears, Green Bay Packers and a rematch against the Patriots.
Book it, the Dolphins will record a major upset this season.
And it will defy logic after we really break down the game and the matchups, just like this game against Detroit where it's just really difficult to see how Miami can slow down the best offense in the NFL.
But the games aren't played on paper or computer screens, and there will be a Sunday where Malik Willis has a big game throwing the ball or the defense forces a couple of turnovers.
We just probably won't see it coming.
If you look around the national media, nobody is seeing it happening Sunday against the Lions.
Quite frankly, we don't either. But we'll be wrong one of these Sunday. That, you can count on.

title: Why I Fully Trust Vikings GM Nolan Teasley Ahead of the Trade Deadline
full_text:
The 2026 NFL trade deadline is just 24 hours away, and for the Vikings, it could have a lasting impact for years to come.
Over the last few weeks, the Vikings have been rumored to be looking for a running back, tight end, offensive line, defensive line, and Bigfoot—even a quarterback. How much of that was just due diligence versus legitimate inquiries isn't clear, but at 6-1, general manager Nolan Teasley will have some big decisions to make after Monday Night Football.
Regardless of the outcome against Buffalo (barring some serious injuries), Minnesota will still be squarely in the mix for a top seed in the NFC. In most cases, 7-1 or 6-2 at the deadline would trigger some serious buying, but the Vikings aren't like most teams: their potential needs and unusual front office construction may lead to some problems.
Teasley wasn't brought on until after the NFL Draft, and hasn't been able to make much of an impact on the roster outside of some late-summer signings and around 874 practice squad moves. The deadline would provide him that opportunity, but it would mean having to part with 2027 draft picks before he's even sat in the Vikings' war room.
That situation almost guarantees that the Vikings' first-round pick, or picks valuing a first, won't be on the move. That also means no Jonathan Taylor (womp womp). Really, while the logic for not doing the top-tier trade seems potentially flawed, it's likely for the best. The 2026 defense would be a terrible thing to waste, but the number of question marks for the 2027 squad is virtually limitless.
It seems likely that next year's quarterback isn't on the roster, and the Vikings will have to find one in free agency or the draft. Almost half the starting defense needs new deals (or not), with key players like Andrew Van Ginkel, Blake Cashman, Jalen Redmond and Isaiah Rodgers all on expiring contracts. On offense, Jordan Mason, Aaron Jones Sr. and T.J. Hockenson could all be on the move, and Justin Jefferson's patience may only last so long .
Bringing back even half of those guys would take some serious cash, and the Vikings will need some rookies to come in and contribute right away. There's certainly a world where Minnesota stays competitive in 2027, but given aging, high-priced free agents and an empty silhouette at the most important position in sports, it's reasonable to expect the Vikings to face a steeper hill to climb next season.
As frustrating as it will be to see the Vikings nickel and dime their way through the trade deadline, 2027 is already shaping up to be a huge challenge, and adding more pressure on top of the current issues isn't a path Teasley will be willing to venture down.
Obviously, the counterpoint is that the defense is the best in the NFL this year; defensive coordinator Brian Flores could leave after the season, and adding Taylor, or even a deal for a quarterback, would all but ensure the Vikings did everything they could to make it happen in 2026. It's not every year you start 6-1, but it probably doesn't take long to see that the Vikings have punched above their weight.
The combined record against non-NFC North opponents is 9-25, and while the Vikings shouldn't apologize for winning, you could argue the real team will be revealed in November, with the peaking Packers and juggernaut 49ers up next.
It's rare for the head coach and GM to be on different timelines, and Teasley will be tempted to push the chips into the center of 2026 for an all-out sprint to a Lombardi. Still, he knows that finding elevators at quarterback or running at this point in the game won't come cheap, and overpaying to land them could send the Vikings down the Colts' current unfortunate path just a year after their all-in push.
Managing risk will be the name of the game for Teasley, and while I expect him to add some pieces at the deadline, the splash move won't happen. Whether that's enough to appease fans will be a different story, but improving a bit at the deadline while maintaining at least some flexibility in 2027 is the prudent decision.

title: Vikings’ Present and Future Could Be Defined in Final Stretch Before Trade Deadline
full_text:
If this Vikings season hasn’t had enough drama and intrigue for your liking, this week may finally deliver the adrenaline rush you’ve been chasing.
To say Monday night’s matchup with the Bills and the impact it may have on Tuesday’s 4 p.m. ET trade deadline carry massive implications would be putting it lightly. Are the Vikings truly contenders? Is general manager Nolan Teasley willing to bet it all on a roster he didn't build? Vikings fans and the NFL world at large will get their answers soon.
Let’s break down what’s at stake for a Vikings team looking to embrace the now while planning for the future.
The eyes of the nation will be focused on Minnesota’s battle with Buffalo on Monday Night as the Vikings are set to make their 2026 primetime debut. Leading the way? Carson Wentz, whose last primetime performance came against the Chargers in 2025 and ended in season-ending surgery. Safe to say, Wentz is looking for a much better ending .
Luckily, the Bills’ pass defense should give him plenty of chances to find his star wideouts.
Need to be more consistent in staying on the field and keeping our defense off the field. pic.twitter.com/juk6uh2ycQ
The Vikings will be desperate to prove they belong in contention conversations after an atrocious showing from their offense in Detroit last week. The defense, meanwhile, will look to secure its title as the league’s best unit against a stellar Josh Allen-led offense. But what happens if the offense puts up another dud while the defense shines, whether win or lose?
With some of the team’s best defenders set to hit free agency after this season, Teasley’s trade deadline actions, or lack thereof, may tell the team everything they need to know.
It seems clear to most outside observers that the current model of winning isn’t sustainable, especially as other contenders around the league are already loading up for postseason runs . Eventually, your offense will need to step up and win games, and Monday may be the perfect chance to prove it can. If not, the fanbase and team will be watching Teasley's decisions before Tuesday’s deadline closely.
Make no mistake, the right series of moves could set the 2026 Vikings up for a legitimate run at the Super Bowl. An elite defense, an elite receiver in his prime, talented veterans set to hit free agency, and two of the league's best playcallers. For many, this is enough to go all in on this season and ignore the future.
After all, how often does a team start 6-1?  But for Teasley, the implications go far beyond the now.
It’s important to remember that Teasley was hired more than a month after the draft, an almost unheard-of timeline for a GM hire. With almost no say on the current roster, an impending mess of contracts, salary cap issues, and the desperate need for a quarterback , does it make sense for Teasley to eliminate much-needed draft capital?
The answer to that question depends fully on another: Does the first-year GM see this Vikings team as a contender or pretender?
Teasley is fresh off a Super Bowl victory as the assistant GM in Seattle, so he certainly knows a thing or two about constructing a championship roster. If he goes all in for a splash move (or two) at the deadline, we’ll know he sees the potential for the Vikings to make a run. If he doesn’t, we’ll know his focus is on the future. But the potential fallout of another season without a playoff win could carry massive weight for two of the most important people in the building.
Kevin O’Connell is the first coach since Jay Gruden in 2018 to enter his fifth season without a postseason victory. While O’Connell is beloved by ownership, fans, and players, a potential roster reset may make it even harder for him to find playoff success anytime soon. This begs the question: how long is too long for fans and ownership?
There’s also the Justin Jefferson factor. The wideout is in year seven of his NFL career, with a 0-2 playoff record to show for it. While Jefferson remains the epitome of a selfless leader through adversity, his focus is clearly on winning a championship above all else. At what point does he see that happening elsewhere?
"I feel like we should win every game. That's just the mindset, that's the expectations that I have every time I step foot out there on the field." - @JJettas2 pic.twitter.com/EQkg3esiKu
Needless to say, the Vikings’ performance on Monday Night and the weight of trade deadline decisions could define this team for years to come. Let’s hope Teasley is, in fact, the right man to steer the ship.

title: Vikings Could Be Sneaky Winners From Eagles Benching Tanner McKee in Week 9
full_text:
The Minnesota Vikings are surprising a lot of people by winning games this year. Their 6-1 start to the season is making many fans wonder if the team could be contenders for a deep playoff run this season.
One issue facing the Vikings entering Week 9 is the quarterback position. Minnesota has not gotten stellar play out of former Arizona Cardinals quarterback Kyler Murray, who is set to miss time for the second time this season due to injury .
Carson Wentz will once again step in as the starter, but his backup for the Monday Night Football contest against the Buffalo Bills will be Max Brosmer. The Purple and Gold could use more depth and future potential on the quarterback depth chart.
The Philadelphia Eagles are having a bad season. On Sunday, Philly lost their seventh game of the season. And with the NFL trade deadline on Tuesday, they could be receptive to trading a player like quarterback Tanner McKee.
McKee isn't going to beat out Murray or Wentz, but he would raise the floor of the quarterback room and provide head coach Kevin O'Connell with a passer to develop while his veterans start games this season.
Standing 6-foot-6 and weighing 231 pounds, McKee was a sixth-round pick of the Eagles in 2023. The 26-year-old quarterback started three games for Philadelphia this year, completing 63.2% of his passes and throwing two touchdowns with two interceptions.
More interestingly, McKee averaged 212.7 passing yards per game in those three games. That is significantly more than Murray's 170.3 passing yards per game since joining the Vikings. The potential is there for him to grow into a quality backup.
Philadelphia head coach Nick Sirianni benched McKee after the Eagles went 0-3 with the young quarterback at the helm. The team opted to start Joe Milton on Sunday against the Giants, which resulted in another loss.
Trading for McKee likely wouldn't cost much. He is in the final year of his rookie contract and is set to become an unrestricted free agent at the end of this season. The Eagles would likely love to get an asset in return for him instead of allowing him to walk in free agency.
While the Eagles seem content to move on from McKee, the Vikings should be interested. While this wouldn't be the blockbuster trade that many fans of Minnesota are hoping for, it would be a solid move to show that the franchise is serious about this season and the future of the quarterback position .

title: Vikings vs. Bills: Who Wins and Why in Week 9
full_text:
What happens when an unstoppable force meets an immovable object? We'll find out that answer and more Monday night when the high-octane Buffalo Bills come to town.
The Vikings will get Josh Allen and the Bills for their next game as part of a brutal November stretch. The Vikings enter the matchup at 6-1, but with the loss to Detroit and Green Bay and San Francisco on deck, it's easy to see how things can derail fairly quickly.
The Vikings will again need a demonstrative performance from the defense in order to keep the Bills in check, while the offense will try and find any sort of momentum with a new quarterback under center. It's the Vikings and Bills in Week 9 as the last game before the trade deadline, so let's get into who wins and why.
With Kyler Murray sidelined with a hamstring injury, the Vikings will turn to Carson Wentz against the Bills. Objective No. 1 for Wentz: Get Justin Jefferson the ball. For what likely culminates into several reasons, the Vikings haven't found a way to get their superstar the ball. That's problematic, clearly, but Wentz has generally been better at looking to Jefferson than Murray has thus far. In Wentz' starts dating back to 2025, Jefferson is getting 9.3 targets per game compared to just 7.6 with Murray in their full games together.
Wentz won't be making any plays with his legs in this one, but the 30th-ranked passing defense of the Bills will also allow him to find plays through the air. Buffalo is allowing a 300-yard passer almost every other outing in 2026, and Wentz might have to get darn close to keep pace with Josh Allen on the other sideline.
The 6-1 Bills will be a huge challenge, but it's certainly not because of their defense. The Vikings may struggle to generate a ton on the ground, but Wentz will be given some opportunities to shine . Edge rusher Greg Rousseau and his seven sacks will require constant attention, but no one else on the roster has more than 1.5 of them.
Yeah, this is going to be must-watch TV as the No. 1 scoring offense collides with the No. 1 scoring defense. Something's got to give, and the Vikings are hoping that it's the Bills' juggernaut offense. Josh Allen has scored multiple touchdowns in every game this season, and is a one-man wrecking crew for Buffalo with his 20 total scores.
Brian Flores' unit has allowed just nine total touchdowns in 2026, however, and would be the team that could bring Allen's streak to an end. Still, stopping Allen isn't the only issue for Minnesota. Just a week after getting gashed on the ground to the tune of 230 yards, the Viking defense will have to regroup and find a way to stop James Cook, who boasts an impressive 5.1 yards per carry on the year.
Ultimately, if the Bills get anywhere close to their 33-point-per-game scoring average, the Vikings will be on the fast track to 6-2. The defense will need to get creative to get Allen off his game, and give the struggling offense at least a fighting chance.
