title: 3 Reasons Why Vikings Can Still Upset Bills Without Kyler Murray in Week 9
full_text:
The Minnesota Vikings have the opportunity to get back to their winning ways on Monday Night Football when they host the Buffalo Bills. However, that game will be a great test for the Purple and Gold.
Like the Vikings, the Bills are 6-1 through eight weeks. They have a franchise quarterback in Josh Allen who can put a lot of points on the board, and a dynamic rusher in James Cook to take pressure off the passing attack.
Still, the Vikings have a strong defense and a great kicker to help them in Week 9. Not only that, there are three reasons Minnesota could surprise many fans and leave U.S. Bank Stadium with a primetime victory.
The Bills are giving up the third-most passing yards in the league this year. They are allowing 254.7 passing yards per game, which should help the struggling Vikings' passing attack that averages only 165.6 yards per game.
Buffalo has also given up 15 passing touchdowns in seven games, which is another good sign for Minnesota's pass-catchers. In fact, 15 of their 22 touchdowns allowed have come off a pass play, which should have head coach Kevin O'Connell excited about passing the ball.
The Bills' starting cornerbacks are having a rough year. Christian Benford is allowing a 110.3 passer rating ( h/t Pro Football Focus ), while Maxwell Hairston is allowing a 115.8 passer rating. Even nickel corner Dee Alford is allowing a 97.1 passer rating.
It is time for the Vikings to attack Buffalo's defensive backs.
Buffalo is allowing teams to convert third downs at a 41.94 percent rate. That rate increases to 50 percent when on the road. Meanwhile, Minnesota is converting only 36 percent of its third-down tries this year, but that number jumps to 43.18 percent at home.
If Minnesota can move the chains, control the clock and field position, while playing strong defense and scoring a couple of touchdowns, the Vikings have a solid chance of winning on Monday night.
Carson Wentz is the starting quarterback this week due to a hamstring injury to Kyler Murray. He will need to be on target with his passes to keep drives alive for Minnesota and maintain control of the pace of the game.
The Vikings' defense is allowing 1.4 points per game in the fourth quarter. The dominance that Minnesota has shown in the final period has been mind-blowing, but they will need to score during that time as well.
Thankfully for the Purple and Gold, Buffalo is allowing the second-most points per game in the fourth quarter. The Bills are giving up 10.3 points per game in the final frame this season, which should keep Minnesota within striking distance, even if they're down late.
If this is a close, competitive game , it favors the Vikings. While at home, in a nationally televised game, it would be fantastic for Minnesota to defeat a team like Buffalo and help to silence critics who don't believe the team is a legit threat this year.

title: Justin Jefferson’s Comments Should Like a Fire Under Vikings to Go All In at Trade Deadline
full_text:
The Minnesota Vikings are 6-1 through eight weeks and sit atop the NFC North. The division is highly competitive, with every team having a winning record, so the Purple and Gold will need to fight hard every week to stay on top.
Tuesday is the NFL trade deadline, but the Vikings haven't made a trade. There are several big-name targets that Minnesota could pursue , but for now, general manager Nolan Teasley has not executed any deals.
The clock is ticking for Minnesota to get a deal done to improve its roster before the trade deadline passes. Making a trade would signal to the league that the franchise expects to be a serious contender this season and anticipates a playoff berth.
On Thursday, Vikings superstar wide receiver Justin Jefferson spoke to the press, and his comments about the team being "very, very special" were shared by The Athletic's Alec Lewis on X . His word choices were perfect.
Vikings Justin Jefferson: "I feel like the potential and the guys that we have in that room is something very, very special. I feel like we're wasting that by not going out and executing the plays that we have called."
Jefferson looked at the team's struggles this season and put the responsibility on himself and his teammates to execute better. Of course, the words "potential" and "wasting" were interesting in that quote.
Vikings general manager Nolan Teasley needs to hear those words as a call to action. If the team and its star player are ready to rally around the franchise, he needs to do everything he can to help the team become winners.
That said, making a trade for a player at a position of need would go a long way toward Teasley proving he believes in this team and sees success in its future. Adding a piece to the mix to help make that happen could be the spark the team needs to continue strong throughout the season.
If there was a time for the Vikings to push their chips in the middle of the table, this is the time to do it. Minnesota's defense is incredible; the team is winning games, and the NFC feels wide open for any contender to step up and take it.
Hopefully, Teasley is listening to his players and is willing to do what he can to help the Vikings this season. This team feels special, but something is missing to make it exceptional. Perhaps trading for the right player can make this team a legitimate threat this season.

title: Underrated RB Trade Target Deserves Vikings’ Attention as Deadline Nears
full_text:
The deadline for the Minnesota Vikings to make a trade this season is rapidly approaching. Nov. 10 at 3 pm CT/4 pm ET, so if the Purple and Gold want to make a move, they must act soon .
The fandom seems to have its heart set on acquiring Indianapolis Colts running back Jonathan Taylor . But the outrageous asking price, combined with his lucrative contract, makes it difficult for the Vikings to get a deal done.
Instead, Minnesota should look at another solid running back who won't cost nearly as much to acquire and has a much more team-friendly contract situation: Tennessee Titans RB Tony Pollard.
Pollard is in the final season of his three-year, $21.75 million contract with the Titans. The Vikings should be able to easily work out an extension that fits Minnesota's tight salary cap situation once he arrives.
At 29 years old, Pollard would be the bell cow running back the Vikings are looking for. Since arriving in Tennessee in 2024, he's averaging 15.5 rushing attempts and 2.1 receptions per game. This season, Minnesota's running backs average 22.3 rushing attempts per game, which would still leave plenty of work for backup Jordan Mason.
Starting Minnesota running back Aaron Jones Sr. has been playing through a knee injury while Mason was on injured reserve recovering from thumb surgery. The 31-year-old veteran running back took a pay cut to stay with the Vikings this season, so it is pretty safe to say he isn't in the team's long-term plans.
A future running back duo of Pollard and Mason in Minnesota sounds good. Pollard is one of the few bright spots on a Titans team that has won only one of its first eight games. The team already traded star defensive lineman Jeffrey Simmons to the Chicago Bears, so there's precedent for them to be willing to let assets go.
Pollard is averaging 4.5 yards per carry this season and has scored six rushing touchdowns in eight games. His excellent Pro Football Focus grade of 85.6 ranks him sixth among all qualifying running backs. His 86.5 rushing grade highlights his effectiveness on the ground.
The clock is ticking for the Vikings to get a deal done before the deadline. General manager Nolan Teasley needs to focus his efforts on a player who wouldn't only help the team win games, but also not require significant assets in the future. Pollard should be that player.

title: Every Option the Vikings Should Explore as Kyler Murray Injury News Worsens
full_text:
What started out as a sore hamstring after the Lions game has now been revealed to be a Grade 2 strain for Kyler Murray, according to Tom Pelissero.
Vikings QB Kyler Murray is rehabbing a Grade 2 hamstring strain that will keep him out of Monday night’s game against Buffalo – and potentially beyond. More in The Sweep: https://t.co/2WjDotsn76 pic.twitter.com/FSPegIsdWo
The Vikings had already planned on keeping Murray out for Monday night's contest against the Bills, but it now seems that he'll miss more time as well. Carson Wentz will get the nod at quarterback, but with the trade deadline looming on Tuesday, there's plenty of routes the Vikings can examine for the remainder of 2026.
Here's every possible avenue the Vikings could explore at quarterback, and why they can (or can't) work.
Wentz has already played this for Minnesota season, rallying a Week 1 comeback against the Packers, and keeping things steady in a monsoon at Chicago. There's plenty of folks who think Wentz has actually been the better option all along, and that the Vikings offense will see a boost with him under center.
Wentz is a very different quarterback than Murray, but does different mean better in this case? It's possible. Unlike Murray, Wentz will throw across the middle, find Justin Jefferson, and work on-schedule.
He also plays with his feet in cement, though, and the Vikings interior hasn't exactly been cooking up pancakes up front. The Vikings offense should find some better rhythm under Wentz, but his first test's difficulty will be set to HARD.
With the trade deadline quickly approaching, Wentz will only get one game to audition for the job. The high-powered Bills are sure to put up points, even against Brian Flores, and Wentz will have the task of keeping pace. If the offense stumbles, general manager Nolan Teasley could start working the phones.
If Wentz doesn't show up on Monday, the Vikings may turn their attention outside of the building to fix their offensive woes. The options are plentiful, but really there's only two that make any sense whatsoever.
If Las Vegas falls this weekend to San Fransisco to drop to 4-5, there's a slight chance they may be willing to part with Cousins. A win, however, all but ensures the 38-year-old sticks in silver and black.
Cousins is putting up MVP-type numbers this year, with 19 touchdowns to just five interceptions, making this trade potentially difficult. Still, outside of Wentz and maybe Max Brosmer, Cousins probably knows this offense better than anyone else, and the Vikings should look to add him--maybe even if Wentz looks serviceable.
The Raiders will have little motivation to deal the respected veteran Cousins, even in a loss, and the Vikings would surely have to overpay to get the guy they could've just signed this March anyway. Sunk-costs aside, Cousins is probably the best quarterback for the 2026 version of the Minnesota Vikings.
Herbert is one of the worst quarterbacks in football this season with a league-leading 10 interceptions, but his track record up to this point shows a top-10 guy who just hasn't meshed with his new coordinator.
The Chargers have swiftly declined any and all inquiries up to this point, but at 0-7 with little direction going forward, they'd be foolish to hang up the phone if Teasley starts dangling multiple-first rounders in front of them.
The Vikings obviously have quarterback needs in 2026, but the only quarterback under contract for 2027 is Brosmer , and Herbert would certainly solve that issue. Clearly this season hasn't gone to plan for him, and Kevin O'Connell and the Vikings would need to be certain that this year is simply a speed bump, and not a cliff.
Herbert is a needle mover, and the same just can't be said for Daniel Jones or Geno Smith despite their potential fits and cheaper price tag.
There's always the possibility that Minnesota still believes this thing can get figured out with Murray as QB1 despite his underwhelming start. With Murray now expected to miss at least two weeks, the Vikings could try and keep this thing afloat until his return.
Murray has avoided the big mistakes this year, which obviously helps, but he's also avoided the big plays too. His uber-conservative play has kept games close, but he hasn't elevated the offense in any meaningful way either. Jefferson isn't involved, and the explosive plays just haven't been there.
The good news, though, is that those problems mostly aren't due to lack of ability, and if Murray can settle into the playbook a bit more, maybe those plays start to trickle in.
Many are already out on Murray, believing that a full summer and six games is already enough time to be comfortable with the offense--which he's obviously not. For the few that still think a couple more weeks is all he needs to see things click, it wouldn't be too surprising to see Murray as the signal-caller to start the playoffs.

title: The Best, Worst and Most Likely Vikings Outcomes vs. the Bills in Week 9
full_text:
The 6-1 Vikings are turning to Carson Wentz at quarterback for Monday night's game against Buffalo as Kyler Murray tends to a hamstring injury. It's possible that the move sparks a change in the offense, and Minnesota finally gets some rhythm and life on that side of the ball. Equally possible, though, is that the Vikings are no closer to figuring out their offensive woes as the Bills roll.
Either way, Monday night's outcome will have significant ramifications for how the rest of the season goes in more ways than one. That said, here are the best, worst, and likeliest scenarios for Week 9.
The Vikings are turning to Wentz for the third time in the last two seasons, and maybe this start will somehow be better than his first two stints as starter. Truthfully, Wentz hasn't been terrible during his appearances, throwing for 213 yards per game and a solid 9:5 TD/INT ratio over his seven contests. But he'll need to bring his best to keep pace with the NFL's No. 1 scoring offense.
If the defense does its thing and limits the damage done by Josh Allen and company, and Wentz looks much sharper than Kyler Murray, the Vikings may finally have direction after floating in uncertainty for much of the last few weeks.
It's clear that the offense has not only been lackluster, but is now actively holding the team back from its true potential. A strong statement from Wentz may give the Vikings all they need to push their chips into the center for the remainder of 2026.
The Bills' defense has yielded a 300-yard passer in three games this season, so the opportunity for Wentz and the Vikings' offense to succeed is certainly there.
Offense looks ok? Defense is fine? Surely this can't be the worst-case scenario! While this scenario may not be the worst individual game result, it would make the Vikings' course of action for the remainder of the year dreadfully nebulous.
If the Vikings stumble in a close game, they'll fall to 6-2 with the trade deadline up next, followed by dates with the Packers and 49ers. Another underwhelming performance paired with a strong record sends some mixed signals , but the pressure for the Vikings to still be buyers at the deadline would be immense.
Still, with a tough schedule and no obvious direction after a theoretical defeat to Buffalo, would general manager Nolan Teasley feel comfortable enough to go all-in on the 2026 edition of the Vikings? It's hard to say, and that call would be made infinitely easier by a win or a blowout loss.
That's not to say a big loss is especially helpful, but it may protect the Vikings from suffering the same fate as the now-tanking Indianapolis Colts just a year after their big swing at a title.
Brian Flores and his defense do all they can, but like in Detroit, the levee is going to burst at some point.
Allen is a bit scary, but so is the Minnesota defense. The Vikings have already proven they can handle almost anything, but it's hard to stay on the field for over 35 minutes without some fatigue showing. The defense has allowed just 10 total points in the fourth quarter all season, and seven of those came last week against the Lions. But if Wentz and the offense don't offer any help on Monday, there's only so long Flores can keep Allen and the Bills at bay.
Ultimately, the Vikings probably keep things close for a while thanks to their elite defense and ability to take care of the ball on offense. Wentz will push the ball downfield more than Murray ever did, and there's a good chance the offense looks much healthier. But much like what happened with the Lions, the defense, believe it or not, has a limit. If Kevin O'Connell can't engineer long drives that end in points, the Bills will probably pull away late, which will culminate in a consecutive loss for the Vikings.

title: 3 Most Important Things to Watch for as Vikings Host Bills in Week 9
full_text:
Through nine weeks, the 2026 Vikings’ season has been quite the rollercoaster. A 6-1 start hasn't been enough to silence growing concerns about a struggling offense and the need to find a long-term answer at quarterback .
Now, the Vikings and their top-tier defense prepare to host the Buffalo Bills on Monday Night Football, hoping a QB change provides the spark their offense needs.
Let’s break down what’s on the line under the Monday night lights.
Vikings head coach Kevin O’Connell ended any speculation about the team’s Week 9 QB on Thursday, announcing that Carson Wentz would start , as Kyler Murray recovers from a hamstring injury. Time will tell if this is the boost Minnesota’s problematic passing game needs, but Wentz seems to know his top task: get the ball to Justin Jefferson .
#Vikings QB Carson Wentz says he understands why Justin Jefferson is frustrated about not getting the ball as much as he wants: “Just get him the rock. He's as good as I've been around. ... I want to get him the rock as much as anybody.” pic.twitter.com/TAEk1MgSi8
Jefferson has thrived with Wentz compared to the other QBs he’s played with over the past two seasons, averaging close to 40 more receiving yards with Wentz than with Murray. If the Vikings want to win on Monday, Jefferson will need to be the star we all know him to be, and Wentz will need to take advantage of a defense that allows the third-most passing yards per game in the NFL.
Brian Flores and the Vikings defense facing off against Josh Allen is the reason this game was tailor-made for a primetime slot. Allen needs no introduction, as he’s been one of the league’s top QB’s for close to nine seasons now. The combination of Allen and running back James Cook (brother of former Viking Dalvin Cook) has helped the Bills post the second-most yards per game in the NFL this season.
The Vikings’ defense faced a similar challenge against Jared Goff and Jahmyr Gibbs last week in Detroit and held their own for the first half. Minnesota sacked Goff four times and held Detroit to only six first-half points.
Eventually, Gibbs took over, but the first-half formula could translate to this week, especially if the offense actually helps out this time. The Vikings' defense has proven it can hang with the best, and shutting down Allen and Cook would be another statement for Flores.
Of all the games left on Minnesota’s November slate, their one matchup against a non-conference opponent is admittedly the least consequential from a standings perspective, but it still carries major implications. With the NFL trade deadline approaching on Tuesday, Minnesota’s performance against one of the league’s top teams could give general manager Nolan Teasley confidence in which direction this team is heading.
The Vikings are going to start Carson Wentz Monday night against the Bills. Kyler Murray is dealing with a hamstring injury and is week to week. Could Minnesota look to add a QB before the deadline? My report on our @NFLonPrime postgame show. pic.twitter.com/gQMQBvvWW7
While numerous reports have emerged in recent weeks surrounding potential trade targets for the Vikings, steam has picked up over the last 24 hours around a potential QB acquisition. Two NFL insiders, James Palmer of NFL on Prime and Adam Schefter of ESPN , have hinted strongly that the Vikings may be looking for an upgrade. Schefter stated Friday on his podcast that he’s “watching the Vikings’ quarterback position.” (h/t: VikingzFanPage)
If the Vikings see another strong defensive effort wasted by a poor passing game, Teasley may have no choice but to find a fix to save the season.

title: What Went Wrong with Patriots CB Christian Gonzalez vs. Packers?
full_text:
In a 45-27 beatdown in Foxborough on Sunday, seemingly everything went wrong for the New England Patriots, who couldn't find any solution to a high-powered Green Bay Packers offense.
The blame pie for Week 9's loss has been split in many different ways, from Drake Maye's turnovers, to  Mike Vrabel's seemingly incorrect gameplan and lack of adjustements, and poor defensive scheming. Despite all that went wrong, no individual has been handed more criticism for Sunday's loss than Christian Gonzalez.
The fourth-year cornerback, who just signed a record-breaking extension in the offseason , played without a doubt the worst game of his professional career.
A former All-Pro selection defensive back, Gonzalez earned his stripes as one of the NFL's best secondary players by locking down some of the most skilled wide receivers in the world. Against the Packers, the 24-year-old put up almost no competition to receivers Matthew Golden and Christian Watson.
According to NFL's Next Gen Stats, Gonzalez allowed a combined 187 yards and 10 receptions to the Packers dual receiving threat. Prior to Sunday, Gonzalez's career-high receiving yards allowed was 90 —  less than half of what he let up to Green Bay.
Additionally, Gonzalez only allowed 196 yards in the six other games he played in this season. The 187 yards allowed on Sunday was the third-most by any NFL defensive back this season — an embarrassing statistic for the highest-paid cornerback in the league.
Christian Gonzalez allowed 7 receptions for 105 yards to Matthew Golden and 3 receptions for 82 yards to Christian Watson. Gonzalez is the only defender since at least 2018 to allow more than 80 receiving yards to two different players in the same game. Powered by @awscloud pic.twitter.com/2voC02QTd3
Quarterback Jordan Love threw for 372 yards in his three touchdown and nearly 80% completion rate performance. With more than half of those yards coming in targets attempted towards Gonzalez, it's clear that Green Bay and head coach Matt LaFleur had a game plan to come at the star corner.
LaFleur denied this intentional game plan postgame.
"I wouldn't say we went at him all game, but it was more just attacking the coverages more so than an individual," he said.
In addition to his touchdown allowed to Watson, Gonzalez also recorded a defenive pass interference, just his third penalty of that kind assessed to him in his career.
Watson and Golden, practically toying with the Patriots defense, each set career highs in yardage on Sunday, and are now both within the NFL's top-four players in receiving yards on the season.
One of the major storylines following the Packers offense all season has been their success rate with throwing the football downfield. Love attempts more passes of 20-plus yards than any other quarterback this season. He entered Sunday as the league leader in passing yards, with two top-10 weapons in receiving yards.
Knowing this information about the Packers, it begs the question to defensive coordinator Zak Kuhr, wasn't it obvious that Green Bay would throw the ball deep?
"We knew that was going to be the key to the game – eliminate the big play," said veteran safety Kevin Byard III. "We didn't do good enough today, at all."
What makes Gonzalez's performance more puzzling is how he was targeted. The Patriots have notoriusly been one of the best man coverage teams in the NFL, calling man coverage schemes more than every team, but two. On Sunday, the Patriots ran more zone than expected, and were often beat.
Gonzalez — known to be one of the best man-to-man cornerbacks in the NFL — let up a surprising 101 yards in man coverage. His catches allowed didn't come from losing a step, or not making plays at the ball (which is how most cornerbacks are beaten in man coverage), but instead he simply wasn't where the play needed to be made.
Some of his mishaps came in unfortunate circumstances, like a trip that caused Watson to break free, or a poor defensive read by Byard, who was supposed to provide safety help on the touchdown Gonzalez allowed.
Not being close enough to his receiver is what caused yesterday's putrid performance from the Patriots defensive cornerstone. He allowed far too much space between himself and his defenders, and was often taken advantage of for it.
The Patriots most heavily-targeted defensive back seemed to not have taken his career-low performance to heart.
"I had a bad game" said Gonzalez. "So, I'm not shaken up by it. I'm not too worried about it. I'll move on and be ready for next week."
Patriots HC Mike Vrabel starts off his quote on CB Christian Gonzalez with: "You can't take a nap in this league." Asked him to clarify what he meant by that in this specific instance. "You just can't take a play off or think that they're not going to challenge you or throw the…
Again, one piece of the blame pie certainly belongs to Kuhr, who may have instructed Gonzalez to give the Packers receivers an extra yard or two in coverage. But there's no doubt that if Gonzalez looked like the superstar cornerback he's always played like, New England would've found themselves competing to the very end.
"When your best players don't play good, you don't have much of a chance in this league," said Vrabel. "So, we expect a lot more. He expects a lot more. We need more from him and everybody else."

title: Patriots Get Tough News on Ben Brown's Knee Injury Heading into Week 10
full_text:
FOXBORO — Mike Vrabel said one day after the New England Patriots' 45-27 loss to the Green Bay Packers that they were "wearing out the MRIs."
That doesn't seem like a surprise, as the Patriots got banged up beyond belief in Sunday's drubbing of a game. Several key players, including Rhamondre Stevenson, Brenden Schooler and Carlton Davis, would leave with lower body injuries. Starting left guard Ben Brown, who was only in the game after injuries have decimated the offensive line to this point, also was ruled out with a knee injury.
Asked on Monday if there was an update on Brown's status heading into this week, the outlook for the 28-year-old guard didn't appear that good.
"(He) probably won't make it this week," Vrabel said.
After Brown left the game, Walter Rouse came in to replace him. In totality, the Patriots offensive line really struggled to make things easy for Drake Maye in the pocket. He was sacked four times and was under duress for most of the evening .
It's been a tough year for Brown health-wise. After repping as one of the top backups during the summer, he got banged up during a preseason game that forced him to miss some time at the start of the year. Once he returned, he was slotted into the starting lineup before another injury against the New York Jets knocked him out again.
He missed the team's TNF loss to the Chicago Bears in Week 7, but returned to play in the next two games.
It's been a trying time for this offensive line. The Patriots have already lost Mike Onwenu, Alijah Vera-Tucker and Greg Van Roten to IR, forcing Bown, Rouse and Matt Pryor to have larger roles in the offense. Despite that, the Patriots are sitting at 5-4 (still currently in the AFC playoff picture) and could end up making things interesting as winter rolls around.
"We're five and four. I think there's going to be a lot of contending teams that are five and four," Vrabel said. "I think that's the nature of the National Football League. We got to draw a line here. Now we got to think that we're zero and zero, and we got to start putting ourselves in position to play meaningful games in January or in the middle of January."
With Brown unlikely to go against the Detroit Lions in Week 10, that could be a sign that the veteran Van Roten, who's 21-day window to be activated off of IR began last week, could make a return to the roster. It also might end up being a sign that the Patriots need some more interior depth ahead of Tuesday's NFL trade deadline .
"That's something that we'll look at," Vrabel said. "He's eligible and has been working hard to get back, so we'll take a look at that and see where he is tomorrow or Wednesday when we practice."

title: Patriots Running Game Needs to Step Up After Several Players Go Down
full_text:
FOXBORO — Nothing went well for the New England Patriots in their 45-27 loss to the Green Bay Packers Sunday. The running game, down TreVeyon Henderson, didn't amount to much either.
Despite having their running back trio run for 91 yards, the group of Rhamondre Stevenson, Corey Kiner and Lan Larison didn't impact the game in the way they might have been able to. Yes, Stevenson had some nice runs and found the end zone as a receiver, but this group continues to struggle.
Most of Kiner's rushing yards came deep into garbage time, well after the score had been out of hand and after Stevenson was ruled out with a knee injury. He'd score his first-career touchdown to make the score look a bit more respectable, but for all intents and purposes, it didn't work.
"He wasn't able to return," Mike Vrabel said postgame on Stevenson, who also fumbled the ball in the loss. "I'm not sure the extent of what it is. He just came off, so we'll take a look at it, and we'll see. I don't want to speculate right now."
The Patriots are going to have to get that part of their offense going at some point, and right now, there are question marks surrounding that group.
How will Stevenson respond this week after walking to the locker room injured? Will Henderson, who put out a statement about neurological issues he's dealing with, even return this year ? Will a player on the trade block a la Derrick Henry or Jonathan Taylor find their way to New England in 48 hours?
There's a lot to figure out about this team right now as a whole, but the running game — one that's struggled a bunch all season — needs to find even footing.
Playoff teams, at least good playoff teams, rely on running the ball when the weather gets cold. It can't just be up to Drake Maye and his group of oft-injured, ragtag receivers every single game. Sooner or later, with or without Stevenson in the game, the Patriots are going to need and carry the rock 25-30 times a game with efficiency.
For most of Sunday, they couldn't do that against Green Bay.
"We lost, and we got our asses kicked. There's no two ways around it," Vrabel said. "We have to find ways to be balanced offensively."
Through nine games, the Patriots are averaging 4.1 yards per carry. Far from great.
Maybe the Patriots feel like they have to make a move for someone, especially if Stevenson isn't able to suit up in Germany next weekend. For now, considering the struggles that Maye displayed against the Packers , this running attack will become super important in these must-win games down the stretch.

title: 3 Winners, 3 Losers in Patriots Smackdown Loss Against Packers
full_text:
On Sunday, the New England Patriots were outplayed in countless facets in their 45-27 loss against the Green Bay Packers.
Throughout the season, New England has dealt with numerous injuries to its squad, with those absences being highlighted against Green Bay.
With many of the Patriots' issues on Sunday stemming from the top of their roster, here are the three biggest winners and losers from their blowout loss to the Packers.
On Sunday, Gonzalez had the worst game of his NFL career by a mile. In fact, he had one of the worst games out of any cornerback this season.
Gonzalez allowed 187 yards in coverage, the third-most by any player this season, after he had allowed 196 yards in his first six games combined.
In coverage against Packers wide receivers Matthew Golden and Christian Watson, Gonzalez forced just one incompletion and allowed a whopping 10 receptions. To add more fuel to the fire, both Golden and Watson set career-highs in receiving yards on Sunday.
"When your best players don't play good, you don't have much of a chance in this league," New England head coach Mike Vrabel said. "So, we expect a lot more. He expects a lot more. We need more from him and everybody else."
Early in the season, Maye struggled with poor decision-making, forcing passes downfield in unacceptable situations. Although he had largely cleaned up his act since then, he reverted back to his old ways on Sunday.
The third-year gunslinger finished the day with three interceptions, all of which came in the first half. Those turnovers quickly put the Patriots in a hole they could not dig themselves out of.
"I'm disappointed in myself for, you can't put the team in the hole straight off the bat, first possession, first half," Maye said. "I feel like in the times we had chances to get back into the game, I messed them up, and we had chances to put us back within three points multiple times, and just frustrating...I wasn't good today."
While the Patriots wide receiver room struggled as a whole, Douglas was the lone bright spot. The 25-year-old finished the afternoon with five receptions for 102 yards, providing the lackluster New England offense with some big-play ability. Plus, he has now tallied at least 65 yards in four of his past five games.
"We got to keep going," Douglas said after the loss. "We're still in it. I feel like we just got to work. A lot of people are going to have a lot of opportunities and it's time for people to step up. When they roll call, it's time to go."
Yes, Maye made plenty of poor decisions against the Packers. However, his offensive line was not doing him any favors.
On 43 dropbacks, New England allowed 27 pressures, 13 of which were unblocked. Plus, it let up 17 hurries, four quarterback hits and four sacks. Maye was playing under durress all evening due to the poor performance up front.
Heading into the week, it was questioned whether or not Barmore would even play on Sunday. The 27-year-old did not participate in Wednesday's practice due to an illness and was the topic of trade talks from national reports.
Despite this, Barmore took the field and was one of New England's lone bright spots. His takedown of Packers quarterback Jordan Love helped extend his streak to four-consecutive games with at least half a sack. Plus, he also tallied a pair of run stops.
It may not be the best day in the office when your punter is one of your best players on the field. But, naturally, that was the case for the Patriots against the Packers.
Wishnowsky had an impressive performance Sunday, with four of his five punts pinning Green Bay inside its own 20-yard line. One of the 34-year-old's punts also landed perfectly inside the 5-yard line.

title: Drake Maye 'Disappointed' In His Play: Patriots QB Throws 3 Interceptions ... Again
full_text:
Remember that awful season opener in Seattle ? It felt like a replay of that loss at Gillette Stadium.
The New England Patriots got outclassed, outworked, outmanned, out-whatevered in a 45-27 drubbing to the Green Bay Packers . The biggest headline was Drake Maye and how he tossed three interceptions in the first half, eerily similar to his performance in Week 1.
Nothing seemed to click for him, despite chucking the ball to the tune of 21 completions, 299 passing yards and three touchdowns. Ignoring the picks, it looked like a pretty normal day. But it wasn't normal for Maye .
"I'm disappointed in myself for, you can't put the team in the hole straight off the bat, first possession, first half," he said postgame. "I feel like in the times we had chances to get back into the game, I messed them up."
In the first quarter, on his first throw, he airmailed a throw across his body intended for Mack Hollins into the arms of Packers safety Xavier McKinney.
Three drives later, he forced a pass to Kyle Williams down the left sideline. Tipped up. Grabbed by Evan Williams. Interception No. 2.
Then Maye threw a touchdown to Rhamondre Stevenson the following drive and it looked like the Patriots could claw their way back into it.
Nope. Next series, Maye telegraphed a pass to Eli Raridon over the middle that McKinney jumped perfectly.
It was Maye's second-career three interception game, and both of them have come this season. Both also came in just one half of play. The turnovers continue to haunt this team.
"We haven't had a clean, a turnover-free game yet," Maye said. "It's one of the biggest differences between winning and losing football games."
What's leading to these errant throws? For the last few games, Maye looked good. He dominated against the Raiders, pulled out a win over the Jets, was lights out in Chicago and led a comeback in Miami . What changed?
"Yeah, just throwing the football in spots that I don't think I should've thrown it," he said. "The first one, I think I just got to see, see the guys deep, see the safety positions. The second one happens, maybe throw it a little farther. And the third one, like I said, they're jumping cross routes, so I got to see in front."
"The turnovers are disappointing because, first of all, that's what (the Packers have) done all year, so that's not a surprise," head coach Mike Vrabel said. "Guys made plays."
There was still the talented plays that we've come to appreciate from Maye. The escaping of the pocket. The arm talent. It just couldn't pull the Patriots out of this one.
The defense also didn't help. 45 points allowed is the most since the 2021 postseason and the most ever given up on Gillette Stadium turf . This was a historic loss that didn't just fall on the shoulders of the 24-year-old quarterback. There are still, and have always been, those glimmers of what makes him one of the best in the league.
It just wasn't on display on Sunday. His teammates know that this showing wasn't who he is.
"I'm just proud of him," tight end Hunter Henry said. "He just continues to compete, continues to sling it and I got so much faith in that guy. And I know that he's going to continue to compete, continue to fight and we all got to be better too to help him out."
And Maye knows that too. They got a long week of travel coming up with a flight to Germany on deck. Then a bye week to reset. That's the best possible thing this team needs. They have all the talent in the world, but the Patriots just have to have their best players lead the way.
"I wasn't good. I wasn't good today," Maye said. "And we got to bounce back, and we're on a far flight, but we got to bounce back and know that there's still some games left and we're battling. We've got to battle."

title: The Good, Bad, and Ugly from Patriots' Week 9 Loss to Packers
full_text:
The New England Patriots' early-game deficit proved too much to overcome. After jumping out to a 17-0 advantage in the second quarter, the Green Bay Packers controlled the pace of play and never surrendered their lead . They finished with a final score of 45-27, dropping New England to 5-4 on the season. Let's go over the (few) ups and (several) downs from the Patriots' Week 9 matchup.
New England's franchise cornerstones, Drake Maye and Christian Gonzalez, both struggled heavily against Green Bay, making an already difficult loss even harder to swallow. Maye, the reigning AFC Offensive Player of the Month, looked more like his early-season self. After throwing just one interception over his previous four games, Maye threw three in the first half alone, including one on his opening pass attempt. It felt like that play foretold the outcome of this one. The Patriots never really got back in it. Maye's production helped New England hang around for a time. He finished 21 of 38 for 299 yards with three touchdown passes to Rhamondre Stevenson, Efton Chism III, and Mack Hollins. However, the Packers capitalized on his turnovers, scoring 14 points directly off those interceptions. That's simply not a winning formula.
Gonzalez, who became the NFL's highest-paid cornerback after signing a four-year, $135 million contract extension in September, had an uncharacteristically poor outing. Jordan Love and the Packers tested him throughout the game, and the results were costly. Gonzalez allowed 10 of 11 targets for 187 yards and a score. It's easily the worst outing of his career. "Obviously it's frustrating," Gonzalez said after the game. "They got the best of me today."
The Patriots knew they would have to limit Green Bay's downfield attack. They simply couldn't. Love had a stellar outing against a Patriots secondary that struggled to execute across the board. He finished the afternoon completing 23 of 29 passes for 373 yards and three touchdowns, adding another rushing score and a two-point conversion on the ground. Green Bay's talented wide receiver duo of Christian Watson (7 catches, 171 yards, one TD) and Matthew Golden (10 catches, 164 yards, one TD) combined for 335 receiving yards, nearly matching New England's offensive total (387 yards). They seemed borderline unstoppable against New England's secondary. The Patriots' defense also failed to force a turnover, continuing one of its biggest weaknesses this season. Entering Sunday's matchup, New England had forced just eight takeaways through its first eight games. They will leave Week 9 with that same number.
Any hope of a comeback, with New England trailing 34-14 and 4:27 remaining in the third quarter, disappeared when Rhamondre Stevenson had the ball stripped from him on a catch near the sideline. The Patriots' fourth turnover of the afternoon was immediately followed by a 39-yard Watson touchdown on the Packers' very next play. Green Bay then converted the two-point attempt, extending their lead to 42-14 at the time.
4th TURNOVER OF THE DAY 📺: FOX pic.twitter.com/QZPzUebkem
Stevenson had been one of New England's bright spots , hauling in a 30-yard touchdown pass from Maye in the second quarter. However, a costly issue that has followed him throughout his career reared its ugly head. His fumble was yet another mistake in an afternoon filled with them for the Patriots.
Pop has been Maye's most reliable WR this season, and that didn't change despite the loss. He led New England with five catches for 102 yards. It's a contract year for Douglas, who is set to become a free agent at the end of the season. His 31 catches, 434 yards, and four TDs are all team-high marks for the Patriots' receiving group.
Ben Brown (knee), Will Campbell (knee), Carlton Davis (knee), Brenden Schooler (hamstring), and Rhamondre Stevenson (knee) all exited Sunday's game with injuries. Losing five players in a single afternoon is far from ideal, particularly with the Patriots already dealing with significant injuries across their roster. The status of each player will be worth monitoring as New England looks to get back on track in their next matchup against the Detroit Lions in Munich, Germany.

title: 6 Immediate Takeaways from Ugly, Ugly, Ugly Patriots Loss to Packers
full_text:
FOXBORO — With a chance to gain some ground in the AFC standings, the New England Patriots really had the opportunity to test their mettle against a similarly-built team.
They didn't look good at all, as the Green Bay Packers scored on seven different drives and forced four turnovers in an ugly 45-27 loss for the Patriots. Led by Jordan Love's 372 passing yards, the visiting Packers were in full control from the first whistle to the last.
After weeks of great play, Drake Maye had a game to forget. He looked shaky from the first drop back he had and really couldn't get settled against a fierce Packers front seven. The Patriots offense would trail by 10 at one point, but it didn't matter — Green Bay had too tight a stranglehold on the scoreboard.
Here's what happened, and what it means moving forward:
After weeks of great football, i t didn't take long for the Patriots quarterback to make a mistake . After a one-yard rush by Rhamondre Stevenson, Maye's first pass attempt of the game was an easy interception for Packers safety Xavier McKinney.
Maye was trying to hit Mack Hollins in his return to the lineup, but hurried a pass across his body. Maye had moved up into the pocket on the right side and jumped when he threw it. Not a good start by any means.
The Packers would instantly capitalize, as Love scampered his way to a 13-yard rushing touchdown on what was just their second play of the game. The good field position helped give them the early 7-0 lead.
In the second quarter, trailing 17-0, Maye tried to make something happen. Targeting Kyle Williams deep down the left sideline, Maye's pass was tipped up into the air and nabbed by Evan Williams. It was Maye's 10th thrown pick of the year and it was part of the reason why the Patriots offense couldn't get going.
Maye looked like he'd settle in after hitting Rhamondre Stevenson on a 30-yard wheel route for a touchdown, but one drive later, telegraphed a crosser to Eli Raridon and was picked once again by McKinney. He ended the day going 21-for-38 with 299 passing yards, three passing touchdowns and those three interceptions — the first time since Week 1 he's thrown that many in one game.
On New England's second drive, a sack from Isaiah McDuffie forced the Patriots to punt it away. Mitch Wishnowsky had a great punt and forced the Packers to start on their own 14-yard line, but that would flip in an instant.
Love connected with Matthew Golden on a pair of gorgeous throws, one of them picking up 49 yards and flipping the field. That pair would hook up once more on a five-yard touchdown to double the lead, just a few moments after Christian Gonzalez's interception was overturned due to a defensive pass interference.
It never really got better for the Patriots as the night progressed . Even when Josh Jacobs got banged up with a hand injury, the Packers were able to run the ball to the tune of 129 yards and add a touchdown of their own on the ground (Kaleb Johnson's two-yard run in the second).
One would think that the Patriots' best cornerback would be someone Green Bay should avoid. In fact, Love continued to go at him ... and continued to win. Golden was lined up on him for most of the game and it started to get ugly.
At the end of the first quarter, Golden had six catches for 126 yards and that aforementioned touchdown. On a 43-yard pickup late in the first, Gonzalez looked like he slipped in coverage — allowing Golden to break free untouched.
Golden's day would end with 10/164/1. Gonzalez would also allow a 33-yard catch to Christian Watson in the third quarter, who'd eclipse 100 yards on the day as well (171). In the third, Watson would beat Gonzalez on a 39-yard touchdown that would balloon the score up to 42-14.
Rhamondre Stevenson had some of the game's best plays for the Patriots, picking up a long run to set up a touchdown and also has a 30-yard touchdown snag on a perfectly-executed wheel route.
But in the second half and the Patriots needing something to go their way, Stevenson coughed the ball up. Trying to make something happen after the catch, Stevenson had the ball ripped out of his hands by McDuffie. The linebacker would recover the fumble himself and that would help set up Watson's touchdown one play later.
The running back's day would end with six carries, 32 rushing yards, 46 receiving yards and that touchdown — which tied him with Curtis Martin (226) for the most points scored in franchise history. He would exit the game in the fourth quarter with a knee injury.
Already down running back TreVeyon Henderson (illness), wide receiver A.J. Brown (ankle/knee) and cornerback Charles Woods (hamstring), the last thing the Patriots needed was more injuries to their key contributors . But that's exactly what happened late in the first half.
Carlton Davis, who's missed several games this year with a neck injury, went down on a failed fourth down attempt from Green Bay. He came up gimpy in coverage and stayed on a knee for quite a bit, before slowly making his way to the Patriots sideline. On the ensuing Patriots drive, left guard Ben Brown would go down holding his knee and appeared to be in a lot of pain.
Davis would be replaced by rookie Karon Prunty and Brown would be replaced by Walter Rouse. Both Davis and Brown would be announced as questionable to return.
Special teams ace Brenden Schooler would also be listed as questionable with a hamstring injury. He'd stay on the sideline chatting with special teams coordinator Jeremy Springer, but wouldn't come back into the game. Stevenson, Jaylen Reed, Cameron Latu and Will Campbell would also get checked out.
It's never a good thing when the punter is one of the best players on the field .
The Patriots were forced to punt the ball five times, and Wishnowsky was lights out on every single one. He tallied 227 total yards and had pinned the Packers inside their 20-yard line four times.
His best one was in the first quarter, where the ball was stopped (quite impressively by Prunty, mind you) at the two-yard line.

title: Patriots Week 9 Inactives vs. Packers: Here's How Banged-Up Offense Will Look
full_text:
FOXBORO — Kevin Byard called this game a measuring stick for the New England Patriots this week, and he's right. Sitting at 5-3, the Patriots are right in the thick of things when it comes to the NFL playoff push here in November. So are the 5-3 Green Bay Packers , who are in the discussion despite being in last place in the NFC North.
They'll do battle today from Gillette Stadium, but they both won't be at full strength .
Here are all the inactives from both the Patriots and Packers for this game. For the Patriots, they'll be down a pair of key offensive stars for the second-straight week.
QB Behren Morton (emergency third QB)
RB TreVeyon Henderson (illness)
TE Josh Whyle (concussion)
WR A.J. Brown (knee/ankle)
CB Charles Woods (hamstring)
The Patriots had already ruled running back TreVeyon Henderson and wide receiver A.J. Brown out on Friday after they had missed all three practices this week. So the Patriots will have to rely on Rhamondre Stevenson, Corey Kiner and Lan Larison when it comes to carrying the rock.
Charles Woods, who was downgraded to questionable with a hamstring injury pregame, was running with members of the medical staff on the field. He didn't look great and was sporting a sleeve on his leg during the warmup, and after a meeting with Mike Vrabel, it's clear he won't be able to go. Rookies Karon Prunty and Channing Canada will both suit up.
Per usual, Behren Morton will only be allowed to play if both Drake Maye and Tommy DeVito get injured during the game.
One big note for Green Bay: Despite returning to the practice fields this week, star edge rusher Micah Parsons won't play as he continues to work his way back from a torn ACL suffered last season.
So why is Henderson not playing? It's because of what the team listed as an illness the last few weeks. On Friday, the second-year back released a statement sharing that he had undergone "an unexpected and unusual medical emergency involving a series of unexplained neurological symptoms that required hospitalization for several days."
This will be Henderson's third missed game of the season, and second in a row. He's also dealt with ankle issues this year and hasn't looked the same compared to his rookie season. Henderson remains on the active roster for this game, but could potentially end up being transferred to the non-football injury list.
"We'll just work through whatever," Mike Vrabel said. "I can't even put a timeline on it. I don't think that that's fair to anybody. So, we'll just have to focus on the guys that are available, how we prepare for the Packers and then also continue to care for TreVeyon, his wife and his family."
Two of the team's most important offensive vets — tight end Hunter Henry and offensive tackle Morgan Moses — were listed as questionable on the team's final injury report this week. On Sunday morning, the team got some good news when it came to the pair of them.
According to NFL Network's Ian Rapoport, both Henry (foot) and Moses (injury) would suit up to play against Green Bay. Henry got hurt last week in Miami and wouldn't return .
The Patriots had elevated offensive tackle Marcus Bryant off of injured reserve this week, and he will make his season debut in a reserve role.
Also activated off of IR was Mack Hollins , who'll return for the first time since injuring his calf in Week 4. Having Hollins back will help ease the pain left by A.J. Brown's absence. He's missed the last two weeks with both ankle and knee injuries that have kept him out of practice.
Before Hollins had gotten hurt, he was one of the team's most reliable targets — recording 15 receptions for 209 yards. Adding his size back into the lineup can help push the ball downfield for Drake Maye, who's shining in that department in recent weeks.
The Patriots didn't elevate any wideouts off of the practice squad this week, so they'll be rolling with Hollins, DeMario Douglas, Kyle Williams and Efton Chism III against the Packers.

title: Hurwitz: Tom Brady's Appearance at Rob Gronkowski's Patriots HOF Induction Was Perfect
full_text:
FOXBORO — Tom Brady would never miss Rob Gronkowski's New England Patriots Hall of Fame induction. Not in a million years.
But it was still great to see the legendary quarterback, back in town to broadcast the Patriots/Packers game one day later , take part in his first HOF ceremony as an inducted member.
Since being enshrined in a over-the-top ceremony in 2024, he had only been back in town once for his statue unveiling. Having Brady take part in the festivities, along with several other Hall of Famers, was special for Gronk.
“It meant everything and it worked out perfect,” Gronkowski told reporters after. “We're both with FOX doing the broadcasting. ... It just worked out perfectly to be able to have the game that we're calling here tomorrow, and just have him here up on stage, he wanted to be here."
Sure, Brady's name has been mentioned as someone who's now against his former team — partially because of the "no dog in the fight" comments before last year's Super Bowl. But to see the greatest player in franchise history support his longtime teammate was the perfect cherry on top for the event.
Does Brady truly have a soft spot for the Patriots despite the online chatter? Does he feel some type of way against his former team after years away? On Saturday, that didn't matter.
"We really wanted Tom to be here to celebrate with Rob," Patriots president Jonathan Kraft said. "But more importantly, Tom wanted to be here to celebrate with Rob."
The day was for Gronkowski, who became the 38th inductee into the Patriots Hall of Fame , and second tight end. His 79 career touchdowns (the most in franchise history) were part of the reason why he was so beloved. But it was also his personality on the field and most importantly off of it that made New England so in love with him.
It's also why Brady stopped by. Sitting down on the stage in his red jacket, beaming as he watched Gronkowski highlights on the TV , he was just as much a part of Gronk's journey to the Hall of Fame like the tight end was to his. Gronkowski knew how special it was seeing him, and the fans certainly did too.
"Tom could be anywhere else," Gronkowski said. "He's the greatest player of all time. It just meant a lot to myself, to my family, and to the fans, I'm sure."
For one day, all was right in New England. Gronkowski and Brady together, like it should be.

title: 3 Important Keys to Success for Patriots to Beat Packers
full_text:
The New England Patriots will square off against the Green Bay Packers , for what should be an exhilariting bout between two 5-3 teams.
The Packers have been on the precipice of great NFC teams, while New England just rejoined the party atop the AFC.
Standings update after Week 8️⃣ pic.twitter.com/LSsrfmwx9X
While Green Bay's record and statistics build a resume for legitimacy as one of the best teams in the NFL, they've yet to have a win that's impressed other teams. They've only beaten one team that currently has a winning record, and that was the Chicago Bears without Caleb Williams.
That make's Sunday's game against the Patriots just as meaningful for the cheeseheads, who compete in the most competitive division in football.
Here's how the Patriots avoid their fourth loss of the season, and get a much needed win against the Packers:
The Packers win games by extending drives with big-chunk plays. Utilizing Matthew Golden and Christian Watson , who are both top-10 receivers in yards on the year, Green Bay moves the ball through the air better than almost anyone else.
Quarterback Jordan Love ranks second in pass yards (1,402), third in touchdowns (10), and third in PFF grade (90.1) since Week 4. He's attempted the most passes of 20-plus yards this season, and 17 more than the next highest attempts from a passer.
Fortunately for the New England defense, which finds itself rarely healthy this week, Love also tends to turn the ball over. He's tied for seventh in interceptions (six) and has 15 turnover worthy plays on the season, the third highest of all quarterbacks.
Carlton Davis's return last week made New England's secondary fully healthy, which brings back one of the best pass defenses across the league. Additionally, Green Bay's offensive line is the worst pass blocking unit, according to PFF, and let up the second-most pressures. The Patriots interior pass rush is one of the best in the NFL.
If New England can apply quick pressure on Love and secure downfield threats, then the seventh-year quarterback for Green Bay will be forced to throw for short-yardage gains — a tactic that hasn't led to success for the Packers.
Green Bay has the worst run game by all accounts in the NFL. Their running backs combined rank last in rush yards, yards per carry, and yards after contact. The offensive line is also PFF's lowest rated run-blocking group.
In Week 7, star running back Josh Jacobs returned from the NFL's commissioner exempt list for a domestic assualt accusation. In his two games back, Jacobs is averaging just 37.5 rush yards per game, and is last in the NFL in yards per carry, running for just 2.3 yards for every attempt he has.
After a slow return to game-action, Jacobs is itching for a breakout performance. With New England's secondary having the capabaility to limit Green Bay's pass game, New England can expect the Packers to rely on their struggling rushing attack to power through the Patriot defense.
"Just the pure talent that he's got in the backfield," Mike Vrabel said this week about Jacobs' abilities. "He's got a great skill set. He's a tough tackle. He runs hard. They've started, I would say, just from the film, trying to implement him in the red zone. He's a guy that's got good hands, good matchup, good in space. He's dynamic, and he's a three-down back."
Green Bay has been an underrated defense this season. In the last five games, the Packer defense has allowed an average of 14.6 points per game. They've only let up more than three touchdowns once this season, and that came in a Week 3 loss where Atlanta put up 35 points.
A big contributor to Green Bay's defensive efficiency is their ability to pressure opposing quarterbacks. Three of Green Bay's edge rushers have 20-plus pressures on the season, tying New England for most amount of defensive ends with that many pressures.
Green Bay's defense also has 52 tackles for loss or no gain, the second most of all NFL defenses. They bring pressure with safeties and cornerbacks, as defensive back Evan Williams has the second most quarterback pressures this season among all players at his position.
New England's offensive line continues to deal with injurie s. After Morgan Moses was listed as questionable all week, he is expected to play through his foot injury on Sunday on the right side of the line. Additionally, New England gets much-needed reinforcements from tackle Marcus Bryant, who was activated off the injured reserve.
A few Patriots notes: - Mack Hollins activated off IR - G Greg Van Roten not activated yet -- 21-day window started Wednesday - T Marcus Bryant activated earlier this week - No elevations - WR A.J. Brown and RB TreVeyon Henderson ruled out - Henderson remains on the roster. Not… https://t.co/rr9smyvZ2X
If the Patriots offensive line unit can keep Drake Maye clean, which they've excelled out despite harsh injuries to the interior line, the MVp-caliber quarterback can control the game with his limited weaponry.

title: The Good, Bad and Ugly From Saints' Wild Overtime Win Over Browns
full_text:
The New Orleans Saints finally gave their home crowd something to celebrate Sunday, securing a thrilling 23-22 overtime victory over the Cleveland Browns at Caesars Superdome.
But while the Saints improved to 3-5 and snapped their home winless streak, the victory was far from pretty.
For Kellen Moore , the victory provided some much-needed relief, but it also exposed several problems that continue to plague his team and will keep him on the hot seat.
With a difficult stretch of the schedule ahead, the Saints have plenty to clean up if they want to build momentum.
Here’s a look at the good, the bad and the ugly from New Orleans' dramatic overtime victory over Cleveland.
Tyler Shough continues to show his clutch gene, even if the organization he plays for is in shambles.
Shough completed 21 of 35 passes for 265 yards and a touchdown while adding 51 rushing yards on 10 carries. While he didn’t do much for most of the game, it’s when his team needed him the most he stepped up. His composure in critical situations stood out.
Trailing 13-9 late in the fourth quarter, Shough orchestrated a 55-yard touchdown drive in just 50 seconds, highlighted by a 33-yard completion to Chris Olave that set up Audric Estimé 's 2-yard touchdown run.
After Cleveland forced overtime, Shough responded again, leading an 11-play, 74-yard touchdown drive capped by a perfectly placed 15-yard pass to ever-reliable tight end Juwan Johnson . That drive was his fifth game-winning drive of the season.
The performance was particularly encouraging, given that Shough was sacked five times and played late in the game without starting center Erik McCoy .
Estimé also provided an unexpected spark, rushing for 72 yards and a touchdown on 15 carries just days after being claimed off waivers.
Despite scoring 23 points, the New Orleans Saints ' offense struggled again.
The Saints didn't score a touchdown until Estimé’s run with 58 seconds remaining, settling for field goals despite moving the ball effectively at times. The Saints also only converted on two of their five red zone opportunities.
Their struggles were particularly evident in the first half, when New Orleans outgained Cleveland 176-80 but entered halftime tied 3-3.
The offensive line also had its share of problems, surrendering five sacks and repeatedly forcing Shough to escape pressure.
Even with left tackle Kelvin Banks Jr. back, the Saints struggled to protect their quarterback consistently.
Sure, several individuals had encouraging performances, but New Orleans still lacks inspiration on offense and the ability to put opponents away.
Without starting quarterback Deshaun Watson , the Saints had multiple chances to take control against Cleveland but instead needed late-game heroics.
The Saints won't always be fortunate enough to overcome those shortcomings. The Carolina Panthers are up next, but the following three games: two road games back-to-back against the Chicago Bears and the Cincinnati Bengals and a home matchup against the Green Bay Packers .
If there's one area that should frustrate Kellen Moore more than anything else, it's the Saints' inability to protect the football.
New Orleans committed two costly second-quarter turnovers, both involving rookies, that completely changed the complexion of the game.
First-round pick Jordyn Tyson , making his NFL debut after missing the first seven games with a hamstring injury, fumbled near Cleveland's goal line moments after making his first career reception on the same play.
The turnover wasted a promising scoring opportunity after Shough connected with Barion Brown for a 52-yard gain.
Things somehow got worse moments later.
After the defense forced a punt, Brown fumbled the return, giving Cleveland possession at the Saints' 19-yard line.
Fortunately for New Orleans, the defense bailed out the offense and special teams, stopping Quinshon Judkins on fourth-and-goal from the 1-yard line.
But the mistakes weren't limited to turnovers.
The Saints' defense also surrendered a 64-yard touchdown pass from Shedeur Sanders to KC Concepcion Jr. immediately after taking a 9-6 lead in the fourth quarter.
Then, after Estimé put New Orleans ahead with 58 seconds remaining, the defense allowed Cleveland to move into position for a game-tying 51-yard field goal.
And even after Shough delivered an overtime touchdown, the Saints surrendered a 39-yard touchdown reception to Harold Fannin Jr. , forcing the defense to make one final stand.
New Orleans escaped with a victory, but the combination of turnovers, blown coverage and late defensive breakdowns nearly turned a much-needed win into another devastating loss.

title: Saints Turn Snoozefest Into Thriller, Escape With Overtime Win Over Browns
full_text:
The New Orleans Saints secured their first home victory of the season in thrilling fashion on Sunday at Caesars Superdome, defeating the Cleveland Browns 23-22 in overtime.
Quarterback Tyler Shough connected with tight end Juwan Johnson for a 15-yard touchdown pass with 4:17 remaining in the extra period, giving New Orleans a seven-point lead. Cleveland quickly countered with a touchdown drive of its own, but the Saints’ defense shut down the Browns’ potential game-winning two-point conversion attempt to seal the dramatic win.
With the victory, the Saints improved to 3-5 while snapping a frustrating home winless streak. The loss dropped the Browns to 5-4. What began as a sluggish defensive battle turned into one of the wildest finishes of the NFL season, featuring 20 fourth-quarter points and an overtime showdown after three quarters dominated by field goals.
Shough delivered an impressive performance, completing 21 of 35 passes for 265 yards while adding 51 rushing yards on 10 carries.
On the other side, Browns quarterback Shedeur Sanders was equally stellar, throwing for 297 yards and two touchdowns on 19-of-31 passing.
However, running back Audric Estime proved to be New Orleans’ secret weapon. Re-joining the team just days before kickoff after being cut following training camp, Estime provided a massive spark with 15 carries for 72 yards and a touchdown to open up the offense.
The game reached peak chaos late in the fourth quarter. Up 9-6, New Orleans watched Cleveland reclaim the lead on a dramatic 4-yard touchdown connection from Sanders to receiver Concepcion with 5:21 left. Sanders hit Concepcion on a deep route before the receiver cut left and sprinted into the corner of the end zone, stunning the home crowd.
Unfazed, the Saints executed a swift scoring drive that took just 50 seconds. Shough found wideout Chris Olave for a 33-yard completion to Cleveland’s 10-yard line, setting up Estime’s 2-yard touchdown run with 58 seconds remaining to put New Orleans ahead 16-13.
Cleveland answered immediately as Sanders orchestrated a quick drive into field goal range. Browns kicker Andre Szmyt drilled a 51-yard field goal as regulation expired to tie the game at 16-16 and send it into overtime.
In overtime, Shough led the Saints downfield and found Johnson for a touchdown to take a 23-16 lead. Sanders responded once more, connecting with tight end Harold Fannin Jr. for a 39-yard touchdown pass to make it 23-22.
Rather than kicking the extra point to force double overtime, Cleveland aggressively went for two. However, a crucial holding penalty pushed the Browns back, and Sanders’ forced pass attempt fell incomplete to preserve the Saints’ victory.
The frantic second half stood in stark contrast to the opening two quarters, which ended in a 3-3 deadlock. Despite outgaining Cleveland 176-80 in total yards during the first half, the Saints struggled to finish drives due to costly mistakes.
Saints kicker Charlie Smyth opened the scoring with a 30-yard field goal midway through the first quarter after missing a 52-yard attempt earlier in the game. Szmyt answered for Cleveland with a 41-yard field goal with 10:30 remaining in the second quarter.
New Orleans had multiple opportunities to take control early. Following Szmyt’s field goal, Shough hit receiver Barion Brown for a 52-yard completion to Cleveland’s 11-yard line. However, rookie wide receiver Jordyn Tyson fumbled at the Browns’ 2-yard line, turning the ball over and squandering a prime scoring chance.
The Saints’ defense provided key plays to keep Cleveland contained. Linebacker Kaden Elliss executed a goal-line stand late in the second quarter, stopping Browns running back Judkins for no gain on fourth-and-goal from the 1-yard line to preserve the tie entering halftime. Defensive end Cameron Jordan and edge rusher Carl Granderson also recorded key sacks on Sanders during the game.

full_text:

Saints win a wild one at home 😮‍💨 pic.twitter.com/eZ52EBujMt
After three field-goal-dominated quarters, the game erupted with 20 fourth-quarter points. Cleveland took a 13-9 lead on a 4-yard touchdown pass from Shedeur Sanders to Concepcion with 5:21 left. New Orleans answered 50 seconds later with a 2-yard touchdown run by Audric Estime —set up by a 33-yard pass from Tyler Shough to Chris Olave . Cleveland’s Andre Szmyt hit a 51-yard field goal as regulation expired to force overtime tied at 16-16.
In overtime, Shough threw a 15-yard touchdown pass to Juwan Johnson with 4:17 remaining. Cleveland responded with a 39-yard touchdown pass from Sanders to Harold Fannin Jr. , but after a holding penalty on their two-point conversion attempt, Sanders’ pass fell incomplete to secure the Saints’ victory.
Shough finished with 265 passing yards, a touchdown, and 51 rushing yards. Sanders threw for 297 yards and two touchdowns. Estime, re-signed days before kickoff after being cut in training camp, added 72 rushing yards and a touchdown on 15 carries.
Moore: "We spent all week just talking about, hey, we're coming off a bye week. It's all going to be about response, eyes forward, moving forward, what's in front of us. And that's all you've got to focus on.
"Proud of our guys, the way they battled. Obviously, we lost the turnover battle, and that was a huge indication of where this game went, but our guys battled, and really proud of them."

"I thought Audric ran really hard. I thought Alvin had some really good runs in there as well. Timely runs, especially late in the game. I thought he did an excellent job of getting some dirty runs there.
"I thought our guys played a physical brand of football. We've got to sustain that, and I thought that was a good thing for our football team."
Moore: "I think there were some positives in there. Again, every week's going to be its own challenge, so we've got to continue to evolve and get better.
"But I thought the physicality in which we ran the football, downhill runs, particularly against the structure in which those guys play, I thought there were some positives there."
Moore: "Once he went to practice on Wednesday and basically recalled everything, we really had no expectation of potentially — we didn't even say he was going to be up for the game necessarily when we claimed him.
"We just brought him in, and I thought he had a couple really physical runs at Wednesday's practice. Kind of set the tone. Seemed like he knew every single assignment. He was dialed in.
"It became a no-brainer to me that, all right, let's roll. Let's get him ready to go. I thought his juice and physicality were real."
Moore: "I think he'll be a great one to ask those questions. He did break the team down about being back home.
"There's a business side of this thing that's always a challenge, and when you lose guys like Audric, you're kind of sitting there, 'Oh man, our whole team loves that guy.'
"We had an opportunity to bring him back. It was a no-brainer. I thought the way he broke that team down, it's a special locker room for him."
Moore: "It's incredible, to be honest. I don't know how many guys can do that, especially for the amount of plays that he played.
"He's a special person, special player. I think our whole locker room's fired up that he's back in there."
Moore: "Two really big drives there. Obviously, we were scoring points. We unfortunately did not handle the plus range and red zone and those sorts of things. We missed our opportunities there.
"But the two-minute drive right before the end of regulation, big plays. C.O. [Chris Olave] on the catch. Incredible throw and catch there.
"I thought Alvin had a really good route out of the backfield, and we were able to finish it in the end zone.
"Then a team comes back, they get a field goal, game's in overtime, and again, you've got to respond. You've got to reset.
"I thought our guys did a good job of just playing really clean football there. Tyler getting completions, the run game, I thought it was really good tied in together."
Moore: "I think there's an emotional stability and ability to take away all the things that happened in the past and be present in the moment.
"I think Tyler does a phenomenal job of that. I thought our team did a phenomenal job of that as the game went on.
"There's opportunities we're going to learn from. There's going to be red-zone things that obviously we want to do better and score down there because it's going to be a different game if that's the case.
"But to clean-slate it and say, 'Hey, we've got the ball with a chance to go take the lead late in the game,' that's all you can ask for.
Moore: "I think that's a potential anytime you play a team with man. They're defending players. They're not eyes on the quarterback.
"If you can get out of the pocket, you're going to have opportunities to run, and I thought Tyler did a good job of that."
Moore: "The NFL, it's tough. All these teams are talented. There's good players on every team, and you've got to compete every single opportunity you have.
"Just proud of our guys to stay with this and be resilient.
"I think that's the type of stuff you need because, again, moving forward, these games are going to continue to get challenging, and we've got to keep responding the right way.
"Just proud of the way our guys fought all the way to the end."
Moore: "Again, eyes forward. This was all our focus was. Hey, we're where we are coming out of the bye week. Let's respond the right way.
"Found a way to get this one in, and we've got more opportunities ahead of ourselves.
"We've just got to focus on the task at hand, one step at a time, and this will be a fun journey."
Moore: "Obviously, this place is special. Having a chance to play in the Caesars Superdome is always a special opportunity for our guys.
"They know that responsibility. It was awesome to feel the energy, especially late in that game.
"We're going to have another opportunity here next Sunday, and we'll just keep this thing going."
Moore: "I thought relentless effort. Make them earn it all.
"I thought the run game was a very important part of that thing.
"They were able to make some plays downfield, obviously, but I thought our pass rush was just relentless.
"I thought it was awesome by those guys. Showed up all the way to the last play of the game."
"Kaden, it's just awesome to have him back. He's a general. He leads this whole thing. His versatility is incredible.

"He's just playing a really awesome brand of football."

"That was huge by our defense because obviously we were getting the ball back, and now we had to play another hard down."

full_text:
The New Orleans Saints will take on the Cleveland Browns at noon Sunday.
The Saints are coming off a much-needed bye week after a 2-5 start to the year. Meanwhile, the Browns are off to an unexpected 5-3 start but will be without starter Deshaun Watson .
Here are our staff predictions.
This is a game I would have picked the Saints to lose, but things change.
Cleveland quarterback Deshaun Watson is questionable for Sunday’s game, so the organization will start Shedeur Sanders . Because of this revelation, it 100% benefits the Saints.
Watson has been one of the league's better quarterbacks all season. However, with him out for this game, the Browns’ offense is less of a threat, even with solid receiving options in wide receiver Denzel Boston and tight end Harold Fannin .
Then, add to the fact that left tackle Kelvin Banks is back after missing significant time due to an ankle injury and rookie wide receiver and first-round pick Jordyn Tyson will finally make his debut after suffering a hamstring injury during fall camp, the Saints’ odds of winning only increase.
This is a great opportunity for the Saints to get a win, especially with a three-game slate coming up.
However, if the Saints don’t get a win, there will be a lot more questions than answers in New Orleans, especially for head coach Kellen Moore and the man who hired him, general manager Mickey Loomis .
The Saints made some moves after the bye week, firing their run game coordinator and bringing in a familiar face at kicker. I asked earlier this week in my column if it was a step in the right direction or window dressing.
This week also carries with it the return of Kelvin Banks Jr. from injured reserve after limited practice opportunities Wednesday, Thursday and Friday.
Add to that first-round pick Jordyn Tyson makes his debut in a Saints regular-season uniform this weekend.
The surprise move for me was the timing of cutting 4th year running back Kendre Miller . Though I have been on the "get rid of Miller ASAP" train for a while, I did not expect it to happen the day before a game.
These moves force me to look back at the first half of the season and wonder if this Saints team has gotten better as the year has worn on. The answer is no.
The kicking game move to Charlie Smyth is a lateral move, maybe a little better. The return of Banks will be an improvement, but the Saints weren't doing all that well running the ball with him in the lineup before the injury. Replacing a run coordinator cuts down the amount of feedback you're getting as a coach about your rushing attack. That could be good and bad. The defense cannot stop the run, while the offense can't get it going.
This is not a good team. Some want to blame Mickey Loomis, some Kellen Moore, some want to put the onus on the athletes that have been brought into the fold (or kept).
I say all that to say this: Even with Shedeur Sanders starting at quarterback Sunday for the Browns, a definite step back from the usual starter Watson, this Saints team has quite a lot to prove before I can say with confidence that they can scratch out a win.
I would love for this to be the game where the Caesars Superdome regains its reputation as a hell-hole for visiting teams. I would love to see Audric Estimé be the back who makes the difference (the way Saints fans would love him to be) instead of a guy who has bounced around from practice squad to practice squad his entire career. I would like to have Chase Young continue to hunt down opposing quarterbacks, and while he's at it to stop the run, too.
And I'd love to see the Saints win Sunday. I just don't see it.
