title: Saints-Browns Final Injury Report: Banks, Tyson Questionable; Donaldson Out
full_text:
Sign up for the daily Saints Newsletter by clicking here .
With just two days remaining before the New Orleans Saints ’ first game in two weeks, there are several notable developments involving both the Black and Gold and the Cleveland Browns .
For the Saints, offensive tackle Kelvin Banks (ankle) and wide receiver Jordyn Tyson (hamstring) remain questionable for Sunday’s game, though there is still a good chance that one or both could suit up. Safety Justin Reid , who initially did not practice Thursday because of concussion-like symptoms, is expected to play Sunday.
Running back CJ Donaldson will not be available because of ongoing issues related to a concussion and his shoulder. The Saints claimed running back Autric Estime off waivers Wednesday, which suggests the team’s brass was already preparing for the possibility that Donaldson would not be able to suit up against the Browns.
For the Browns, the biggest storyline continues to center on the quarterback position. Their regular starter, Deshaun Watson (concussion), is questionable to play Sunday.
If he can't go, the Browns will turn to Shedeur Sanders , and that appears to be the preferred plan rather than a fallback, as Sanders has been named the starter for Sunday’s game .
The only other player ruled out for the Browns is defensive tackle Maliek Collins (elbow).
The two teams will kick off at noon at Caesars Superdome. It will be the first meeting between Cleveland and New Orleans since Nov. 17, 2024, when the Saints won 35-14.

title: Saints vs. Browns: 3 Things to Know About Cleveland's Defense
full_text:
The New Orleans Saints will look to get their offense back on track Sunday when they face a Cleveland Browns defense that has experienced its share of ups and downs this season.
Despite losing superstar defensive end Myles Garrett , Cleveland has remained a formidable defensive opponent, especially at generating pressure and creating turnovers.
However, the Browns have also struggled to stop the run, giving the New Orleans offense an opportunity to exploit that weakness.
For quarterback Tyler Shough and the Saints, exploiting Cleveland's weaknesses while limiting costly mistakes could be the difference between another frustrating offensive performance and a much-needed bounce-back win.
With New Orleans preparing for its first game following the bye week, here are three things to know about the Browns' defense heading into Sunday's matchup.
Cleveland made significant offseason changes, but none were bigger than trading superstar defensive end Myles Garrett to the Los Angeles Rams.
Garrett was coming off a historic 2025 season in which he established an NFL record with 23 sacks and recorded 33 tackles for loss.
His departure, combined with defensive coordinator Jim Schwartz's resignation, raised questions about whether Cleveland could maintain its defensive identity.
However, the Browns have remained competitive defensively under first-year coach Todd Monken .
Cleveland has recorded 21 sacks through eight games, ranking ninth in the NFL, while collecting six interceptions.
Several young defensive players have also contributed, including defensive end Jared Vers e, who arrived from Los Angeles as part of the Garrett trade.
The Browns are allowing 126.9 rushing yards per game and 4.7 yards per carry, ranking among the league's bottom 10 in both categories.
Those struggles were especially apparent against Pittsburgh, which rushed for 200 yards in Sunday's victory.
That's an encouraging matchup for New Orleans, which has struggled to establish a consistent rushing attack throughout the season.
The Saints managed just 18 rushing yards in their 16-10 loss to Pittsburgh before entering their bye week.
If New Orleans can exploit Cleveland's defensive weaknesses on the ground, it could take considerable pressure off quarterback Tyler Shough and create more opportunities through the passing game.
Although Cleveland has struggled against the run, its secondary remains one of the defense's more dependable units.
The Browns are allowing 214.6 passing yards per game and have surrendered 11 passing touchdowns through eight games.
However, they have also intercepted six passes and held opposing quarterbacks to a relatively modest 6.6 yards per pass attempt.
Much of Cleveland's success in coverage begins with veteran cornerback Denzel Ward .
Ward has continued to establish himself as one of the NFL's premier coverage defenders, earning a 91.6 coverage grade from Pro Football Focus, the highest among qualified cornerbacks entering Week 9.

title: Saints-Browns Injury Report: Key Offensive Players Progressing Ahead of Week 10
full_text:
The New Orleans Saints received encouraging news on several key offensive players Thursday, while the Cleveland Browns still face quarterback uncertainty ahead of Sunday's matchup at the Caesars Superdome.
Rookie left tackle Kelvin Banks Jr. (ankle) and wide receiver Jordyn Tyson (hamstring) remained limited participants for the second consecutive day , keeping both players in contention to return against Cleveland.
Banks' potential return would provide a significant boost to an offensive line that has battled injuries throughout the season. Tyson, meanwhile, continues working toward his NFL debut.
However, rookie running back CJ Donaldson was downgraded from limited participation to a nonparticipant because of shoulder and concussion issues.
Guard Cesar Ruiz (knee) practiced fully for the second straight day, while safety Justin Reid and defensive lineman Nathan Shepherd were removed from the injury report.
For Cleveland, quarterback Deshaun Watson remained sidelined Thursday as he continues dealing with concussion symptoms.
Watson's absence increases the possibility that second-year quarterback Shedeur Sanders could start Sunday against New Orleans.
The Browns also remained without defensive tackle Maliek Collins (elbow), while tight end Harold Fannin Jr. (groin) and safety Emmanuel McNeil-Warren (hip) were added to Thursday's report.
Both teams will release their final injury reports Friday, providing additional clarity on player availability ahead of Sunday's noon kickoff.

title: Saints Get Major Injury Boost as Browns Face Quarterback Uncertainty
full_text:
The New Orleans Saints received encouraging injury updates Wednesday as left tackle Kelvin Banks Jr. and rookie wide receiver Jordyn Tyson returned to practice ahead of Sunday's matchup against the Cleveland Browns .
Meanwhile, Cleveland could be without starting quarterback Deshaun Watson , who entered the NFL's concussion protocol Wednesday after reporting symptoms following Sunday's loss to the Pittsburgh Steelers .
Watson initially passed concussion evaluations and finished the game but reported symptoms Monday night, putting his availability against New Orleans in question.
If Watson cannot play, second-year quarterback Shedeur Sanders is expected to make his first start of the season.
Sanders started seven games as a rookie in 2025, throwing for 1,400 yards, seven touchdowns and 10 interceptions. However, he has seen limited action this season, completing just three passes for 2 yards.
Watson has started all eight games for Cleveland this season, completing 65.5% of his passes for 1,806 yards, seven touchdowns and three interceptions.
Despite his efficiency, the Browns have struggled offensively, ranking 29th in the NFL with just 17.4 points per game.
For New Orleans, Wednesday's biggest development was the return of Banks, who practiced for the first time since undergoing ankle surgery in September .
The second-year left tackle has progressed considerably faster than initially expected, returning more than a month ahead of schedule.
The Saints now have a two-week window to activate Banks from injured reserve, potentially providing a significant boost to an offensive line that has struggled in his absence.
Backup left tackle Asim Richards has experienced difficulties adjusting to coach Kellen Moore's offensive scheme while filling in for Banks.
Initially expected to return in mid-December, Banks could reclaim his starting role once medically cleared, giving the Saints additional protection up front.
New Orleans also welcomed back Tyson, the No. 8 overall pick in the 2026 NFL Draft out of Arizona State.
The rookie wide receiver participated on a limited basis Wednesday after missing the entire season to this point with a hamstring injury suffered during training camp .
Although his availability for Sunday's matchup remains uncertain, Tyson's return represents another encouraging development for a Saints offense looking to improve its passing attack.
With Banks and Tyson progressing toward their respective returns and Cleveland potentially facing a quarterback change, Sunday's matchup could feature a considerably different outlook for both teams than initially anticipated.

title: Giants Defensive Player Grades: Arvell Reese Is Unblockable as Pass Rush Overwhelms Eagles
full_text:
The New York Giants defense faced the Philadelphia Eagles on Sunday and delivered one of their season's finest performances.
New York delivered seven sacks, 10 tackles for loss, 11 quarterback hits, four pass breakups, one forced fumble, and one fumble recovery.
They held old friend Saquon Barkley to just 22 yards on 13 carries, a 1.7 yards-per-carry average. Other than a 24-yard run by newly minted starting quarterback Joe Milton III, the run defense was spectacular overall.
This week, there were many heroes, both up front and behind the scenes. Arvell Reese was a monster — anyone else sitting there wondering why five teams passed on this play-making young man like we are?
Kayvon Thibodeaux, while not delivering the numbers in the pass rush, made a bunch of little plays that helped others shine. Shelby Harris and D.J. Reader were clutch. And inside linebacker Micah McFadden once again was “super sub,” as he didn’t come off the field.
All in all, it was a stellar performance by the defense —perhaps their best of the season—and we don’t care if you want to argue it came against backups, because those guys still get paid.
Special teams? Without Dominic Zvada and Jordan Stout, this unit would be our pick for the goat horns this week. The unit was sloppy with penalties and communication, but thankfully it didn’t hurt the team.
Let’s get into this week’s individual player grades for the defense and special teams — there’s a lot to like for sure.
Continuing to give this team one of the biggest bangs for their free-agent bucks, Reader recorded his first sack of the year with a resounding clean-up of an outside rush to the spot where he was crashing.
He added another quarterback hit while providing the only inside pass rush that this team can create. We’re not here to talk about Reader’s pass rush, since his run defense shows up on every down.
He seems to relish sticking his nose into the middle and is avoided on running downs like the plague.
By the way, his other tackle this week (besides the sack) also came in the backfield. Reader is not just absorbing double-teams; he’s beating them.
One of the more interesting developments on this young team is the play of its until-now unknown rookies.
Jamison-Travis (like offensive lineman J.C. Davis, also a sixth-rounder) has taken over the rotation at nose tackle, and he’s playing the position well.
He recorded three tackles today on running downs while absorbing doubles and beating singles. He’s not only absorbing, but he’s also flashing out there.
This kid has life in his legs that gets him to places a nose tackle doesn’t normally go, but it’s his play at the point of attack that is drawing notice.
Continuing to give the defense its best defensive end play this year, Harris’ veteran eyes help him anticipate and crash spots and gaps; he’s just lacking the goods to finish off these quick attacks.
When left to play it straight up, he’s not exactly lighting things up, but he was in the backfield on a couple of passing-down snaps that contributed to the general chaos around today’s Eagles pocket and helped the defense accrue its season-high seven sacks this week.
Getting the last of today’s sacks on the game’s final play, Alexander smartly closed down on the front of the pocket and cleaned up the mess the outside pressure had created.
It was a smart veteran move by this second-year player who played one of his better games today. He knocked down a fourth-quarter pass, recorded two tackles, and showed good upfield movement on several passing downs.
We’re still waiting for the physicality to show up, but he’s got the goods to blow things up inside if he wants to. The question is, does he want it?
Playing through an illness that kept him on the injury report all week, Carter was not himself out there and finished the game with just one measly assist, this on a day where the defense recorded seven sacks.
Carter was drawing double teams whenever he lined up on the edge, which opened things up for the rest of his teammates to attack.
What a testament to Carter’s impact that when his play is quiet, the defense plays one of its best games of the year. It’s certainly a good sign that this defense has a lot of good players.
Continuing to play a solid, assignment-clean style, Thibodeaux probably played his best game of the year this week. Though he was shut out on the sack sheet, Thibodeaux’s pass rush got home, and the blitzing created chaos that freed him up to attack the pocket.
He had two quarterback hits and four total tackles on his sheet, and his edge run defense really showed its teeth again.
We’ve stopped waiting for flash plays from this player and accepted that he’s contributing to a good defense that seems to be improving by the week.
Of note, both of Thibodeaux’s quarterback hits came off inside rushes from the edge, as he continues to lack the bend and speed to get around the corner.
Continuing to provide solid outside linebacker rotation snaps, Ford got in on one tackle when he ran the quarterback out of bounds.
He’s been playing a lot of coverage during these snaps, but not so much this week.
Elevated from the practice squad for today’s game, Smoot got plenty of playing time in the edge rotation and recorded two tackles, including credit for a sack when he dove at the quarterback’s legs in pursuit of a 1-yard fourth-quarter sack.
Smoot is a jumbo-sized outside linebacker whose pass-rush game was ho-hum, but he was consistently physical.
The Giants’ star rookie had one of those halves that almost defy belief. We’re talking about his first half, where he recorded nine of his team-high 12 tackles, and two of his three sacks.
Some will like Reese’s blind-side sack, as thunderous a hit as you will ever see on a football field, while also forcing a fumble the Giants recovered.
Reese’s other first-half sack came off of a middle blitz on which he played contain. His third sack of the day came in the second half when Reese lined up over the guard standing up, beat him with a quick swim move, and then finished him.
Our favorite Reese play? A second-quarter outside run by Saquon Barkley that had opened up for the back.
Suddenly, out of nowhere, Reese flashes into the play and absolutely rag-dolls Barkley to the turf for no gain; it was one of the more breathtakingly violent takedowns and finishes that we’ve ever seen.
Reese made tackles this week in every imaginable fashion—in coverage, edge blitzes, inside pass rushes—you name it.
Playing him at off-ball inside linebacker was one of the smartest things this braintrust ever did. You can’t run and hide from a great off-ball inside linebacker. The field isn’t big enough.
The Giants lost veteran inside linebacker Tremaine Edmunds several weeks ago, and this defense hasn’t skipped a beat. In fact, it almost feels like it’s getting stronger.
McFadden had a top-shelf game of his own today, recording nine total tackles, one sack, and a fumble recovery off an Arvell Reese sack.
On another day, we’d be raving about McFadden’s game and impressed by how perfectly this defense fits what he does best.
McFadden not only has a great nose for the football, but he’s also an excellent blitzer. He times things up very well, and he has a plan of attack on every single blitz, always attacking with aggressiveness and some surprising power.
He hasn’t been the great liability in coverage we expected him to be. The coaches just aren’t using him much in coverage; they are blitzing him instead.
It’s one of the things that he does best. Credit to the coaches for putting McFadden in positive positions, and to McFadden for capitalizing on these opportunities.
Coming off the three-year extension that the Giants gave him this past week, Newsome played a top-notch, all-around corner game, excelling in both press and zone coverages.

title: Giants Expect J.J. McCarthy and Cam Skattebo Back for Thursday Night vs. Commanders
full_text:
The New York Giants don’t have much time before they host the Washington Commanders in a critical Thursday night divisional game.
But Big Blue can at least take some solace knowing that two key injured starters, quarterback J.J. McCarthy and running back Cam Skattebo, both should be good to go for that game.
McCarthy was injured in the third quarter when Eagles linebacker Zack Baun hit him on the side. McCarthy went to the medical tent for evaluation before walking to the locker room with members of the team’s medical staff, presumably to have X-rays done.
McCarthy, who was replaced by Jameis Winston for a series in which Winston led the Giants to the go-ahead touchdown, later returned to the team’s sideline with renewed energy. He then went back in to finish the game.
“He’s doing well,” head coach John Harbaugh said of McCarthy. “We’ll find out more during the course of the day and in a couple of days, but it does look like he’s gonna play. We feel fairly good about that but don’t want to get out over my skis with it, but it seems good so far.”
Skattebo is also trending in the right direction, according to Harbaugh. The second-year running back has been nursing a hamstring strain suffered on his final run in the Giants’ Week 7 win over the Houston Texans.
He was close to playing against the Eagles despite not practicing in the week leading up to the game and being listed as doubtful.
Ultimately, the team decided that with the quick turnaround and Skattebo likely to be slightly limited, it made more sense to hold him out of the game against the Eagles and instead aim for him to be ready for the Washington game.
“We just decided not to take the risk that would go with it,” Harbaugh said. “There were some things he was gonna be limited just a little bit; maybe that we decided not to go down that road because of the short week this week.”
The Giants running game struggled against the Eagles, finishing with a dismal 2.6 yards per carry. While that was largely a result of the poo run blocking effort by the offensive line, not having Skattebo in the lineup certainly didn't help matters.
The Giants head coach added that Skattebo “should be full-go Thursday night.”

title: Giants-Jaguars Week 11 Game Flexed to National TV Spot
full_text:
Ah, the joys of playing winning football.
The New York Giants' Week 11 home game against the Jacksonville Jaguars, originally slated for a 1 p.m. kickoff, has been moved to a 4:25 p.m. start and will now be nationally televised, replacing the Eagles-Steelers game that was originally scheduled for the 4:25 p.m. slot and was to be nationally broadcast.
The Giants, who just beat the Eagles 19-11 in Philly to snap a 13-year losing streak at Philly’s home stadium, stand at 5-2-1 and are comfortably in control of the NFC East.  Meanwhile, the Jaguars hold a 6-2 record and first control of the AFC South.
The Giants and Jaguars have played each other eight times in regular-season history, with the series deadlocked at 4-4. The two teams last met at MetLife Stadium on September 9, 2018, when the Giants lost 20-15 in what was their first home loss to Jacksonville in series history.
More recently, the two teams last met on October 13, 2022, when the Giants won 23-17 in what was their first road win against the Jaguars.
Jacksonville has outscored the Giants 190-161 in the eight games played between the two teams.

title: Four Key Factors in Giants' 19-11 Win Over Eagles
full_text:
For the first time in 13 long years, the New York Giants breathed a sigh of relief as they walked off the turf at Lincoln Financial Field after a 19-11 road win against the Philadelphia Eagles.
Taking down their rivals in the Eagles’ fiery home environment was once again no easy task for John Harbaugh’s Giants. Still, the outcome carried far more significance than simply casting away the nightmarish matchups with their most hated opponents from before he arrived as head coach.
With a rare win on their return from a bye week, the Giants got nearly the perfect scenario they asked for in the lead-up to Week 9: they beat the Birds to add another important win to their division tally and saw two other NFC East members fall on Sunday.
The Giants will definitely celebrate their overdue occasion. Still, they know they have a lot to improve, with a short week ahead and a second duel with the Washington Commanders on Thursday night at MetLife Stadium.
In the spirit of recognizing what got them to 5-2-1 this week, here are the four things that defined a special yet gritty win for New York over the Eagles.
The Giants had their ups and downs on offense, but the defense had to have left defensive coordinator Dennard Wilson grinning ear to ear as his group put on a clinic against the Eagles’ offensive line.
In a game where points were at a premium and both teams’ offenses struggled to play complementary football, the Giants’ defense kept New York within striking distance of the lead with a total onslaught of pressure toward Philadelphia quarterback Joe Milton.
New York held the Eagles to 220 total yards on Sunday, the lowest total in a single game this season. Against the pass, Milton and company managed just 128 yards and were held out of the end zone, thanks to eight drives stalled in fewer than three plays.
Even on possessions where Philadelphia tried to make something happen, Milton barely had room to breathe as the Giants’ pass rush got home for a season-high eight sacks, plus five more hits and another season high of 25 total pressures .
The biggest hero of the day? None other than rookie inside linebacker Arvell Reese, who put forth arguably the best day of his debut year with three pressures, all of them sacks, and pressured Milton on a team-high 23.1% of his pass-rushing snaps.
Milton certainly won’t be forgetting the one blow he took from Reese on 3rd-and-5 from the Giants’ 42-yard line in the early second quarter, which jarred the football loose for Micah McFadden to recover and kept New York’s deficit at 8-6.
The Giants also did a solid job against the run, holding Saquon Barkley and the Eagles to under 100 yards, a modest average of 3.7 yards per carry and one touchdown in the first quarter.
Still, the pass-rushing department deserved all the praise for never giving Philadelphia a chance to really hurt the Giants through the air. Reese has been a true draft win for Big Blue, and the sky is the limit if he keeps performing at a high level.
There was real concern when J.J. McCarthy had to leave the game with what was reported as a right-side rib injury that affected his ability to throw clean passes on the sidelines.
The injury happened on the second play of the Giants’ first possession in the third quarter, when McCarthy pulled the football and took off downfield for a three-yard gain on a left-side quarterback keeper.
Eagles inside linebacker Zack Baun came up to make the big hit on McCarthy and stop a potential big conversion by No. 18. Still, the impact left the Giants’ gunslinger grimacing in pain as he tried to shake off the blow, forcing Harbaugh to turn to Jameis Winston.
It’s been a back-and-forth year for Winston, who was benched for McCarthy in Week 7 ahead of the game in Houston. Once again, the veteran reminded Giants fans why a demotion didn’t mean he wasn’t still valuable to the franchise.
Just the opposite: Winston led the huddle back out on the next possession and authored an impressive 14-play, 76-yard drive, connecting with five different receivers and even flashing his legs with a 10-yard scamper for a first-down conversion.
Despite fears the Eagles’ relentless pass rush would get home to a less mobile quarterback with ease, Winston’s poise under center paid off with a five-yard connection to a wide-open Isaiah Likely in the back of the end zone on 2nd-and-goal from the Philadelphia 5-yard line that put the Giants back up 13-8.
On the next drive, McCarthy was cleared to return to the game, and the Giants never gave up the lead the rest of the way. Winston salvaged what could have been a bad turning point for Big Blue, going 6-of-8 for 71 yards with the Giants’ lone touchdown pass to Likely, and was arguably the biggest difference maker in the win.
It could have easily gone the other way, but the Giants wanted to keep Winston as the initial backup signal-caller for a reason. That experience showed again as the Giants didn’t let a sudden injury derail their chances of winning a football game.
After watching their rookie struggle to cash in on opportunities during a three-week skid, Dominic Zvada was back to being rock solid in the Giants’ kicking department.
In his first four games, the undrafted kicker looked like he’d been doing it forever, converting all nine field goal attempts, including a perfect 3-of-3 from 40 yards or more.
The Michigan product’s first taste of adversity came against Washington, where he missed three from that range. It opened a rough stretch of five total botched kicks in two of the team’s next three contests, against the Saints and Texans.
Perhaps the bye week was just what the doctor ordered for Zvada, who stepped into an unfriendly environment in Philadelphia and was lights out.
He made all four of his field goal attempts, including two from 49 yards and one from a game-high 53 yards on the Giants’ first two possessions.
New York has had to witness some unfortunate kicking miscues inside Lincoln Financial Field during its 13 years of losing in that stadium. Still, Zvada wasn’t going to add his name to the list of misfortunes that cost his franchise.
Without his improved long-range performance, the Giants wouldn’t have walked away with the win, and their NFC East chase would look very different, with the Cowboys playing catch-up at 4-5 after their win over the Colts.
The big question is whether Zvada can keep his efficiency in Thursday night’s game against Washington. If he is called upon to help put up points, he can’t let what happened in Week 5 haunt his confidence in the rematch.
The lead-up to the NFL trade deadline has focused on whether Harbaugh and the Giants will target a big-name running back to strengthen their rotation for a deep season run.
The group’s limited effort against the Eagles didn’t quiet the noise. The running back room was pretty much down to Devin Singletary and Greg Desrosiers Jr., who was just picked up from the Chargers’ practice squad, backing up the veteran in the absence of Cam Skattebo and Tyrone Tracy Jr.
Still, the pair of backs, joined by six combined keepers from McCarthy and Winston, couldn’t get the job done for New York. The Giants finished with 80 yards on 31 total carries for an average of 2.6 yards per attempt, the second-lowest in a game this season.
Many of the rushing woes could also be attributed to the utter dominance that Philadelphia’s defensive front displayed in clogging the interior lanes and pushing the offensive linemen back into the plays.
Beyond that, the Giants surely realized how much they missed Skattebo, whose aggressive running style is huge for shaking up early tackles and gaining extra yards that take pressure off the passing game to convert longer second or third downs and keep drives alive.
Skattebo was likely disappointed he couldn’t return to the same stadium where his rookie season was cut short by an ankle injury in Week 8 of 2025. Still, one could wonder how effective he would have been, given the run-stop success the Eagles produced at…

title: Giants Winners and Losers: Arvell Reese Dominates as Giants End Long Drought in Philly
full_text:
The Big Blue football world was a very different place the last time the New York Giants beat the Philadelphia Eagles at Lincoln Financial Field on October 27, 2013.
Eli Manning was still the starting quarterback and Tom Coughlin the head coach. The Giants were two seasons removed from a Super Bowl championship. Offensive lineman Justin Pugh was a rookie. Victor Cruz was salsa-ing his way into the hearts of Giants fans. And fans were getting down with JPP (Jason Pierre-Paul).
Yes, it’s been a long time, but the winless drought in Philadelphia is finally over for the Giants. Relying on old-school physicality and timely completions, Big Blue earned a 19-11 road win over their longstanding foe.
It wasn’t perfect, but it was the desired result. So let’s look back at those who really stood out and those who didn’t.
The No. 5 overall pick has emerged as the Defensive Rookie of the Year favorite before the Giants battled the Eagles. Still, he solidified himself as one of the league’s top linebackers this season after a dominant showing in Philly.
Arvell Reese was instantly labeled a draft-day steal not only because of his run-stopping ability, which he displayed again, but also because of his pass-rushing prowess. That was also on display Sunday afternoon.
Reese registered three sacks, 10 solo tackles and a forced fumble, posting the best game of a young yet highly promising NFL career. He continues to move with force and speed, a brutal combination that terrorized Joe Milton III and the Eagles’ offensive line.
Dennard Wilson’s defense was excellent overall, but No. 52 claimed most of the spotlight. When a 21-year-old with limited NFL experience can carry a unit to a divisional victory, the future should be bright. Heck, the present is already looking quite sunny, and Reese is a big reason why.
The 32-year-old defensive tackle who signed with the organization almost two months after free agency began has become one of the team’s most important players .
Reader has been a pillar of consistency for the Giants, and Week 9 was no different. He recorded his first sack of the year in the first quarter and had four total pressures , per Pro Football Focus.
Reader is helping New York’s run defense gradually leave the NFL’s bottom tier and inch toward adequate territory.
The veteran wide receiver’s stock has fallen since he joined the franchise, but he can still produce in spurts. Darnell Mooney was arguably the Giants’ most dependable and clutch pass-catcher against the Eagles.
The 29-year-old deep threat linked up with Jameis Winston for a critical 27-yard reception in the third quarter on what became the go-ahead drive. He finished with a team-high 54 receiving yards, averaging 18.0 yards per catch.
New York already feels good about Malik Nabers and Isaiah Likely, and there is plenty to like about rookie Malachi Fields. If Mooney can occasionally do damage downfield, then a previously listless pass-catching group may actually be quite stout.
Fresh off signing a three-year, $46 million contract extension , Greg Newsome II made his presence known in coverage and against the run. He allowed two receptions on four targets for a measly 13 yards and posted three stops, according to PFF.
Newsome is showing great awareness on the field, staying close to WRs and adjusting as a tackler when necessary. No longer a question mark, the sixth-year cornerback is a stabilizing force in the secondary.
The unpredictable signal-caller was under center for only one complete series, but he maximized his playing time and delivered the difference-making drive.
While J.J. McCarthy nursed a hip injury , Winston gashed the Eagles’ defense. He made stellar throws to Mooney and Fields, did not get rattled, and found Likely for a five-yard touchdown.
His 71-yard outing gifted the G-Men a 13-8 lead, which is all a dialed-in defense needed to secure the W. There are obvious drawbacks to employing Winston as a regular starter, but at his best , he can make momentum-swinging plays. He might get the chance to do so again if McCarthy is forced to miss time.
We cannot overlook the undrafted rookie kicker. Dominic Zvada has been in the “Losers” lounge lately, but he showed incredible mental fortitude by bouncing back and converting all four of his field goal attempts.
Given the offense’s scuffles, New York would not have won without Zvada. He drilled a 53-yarder less than five minutes into the game and added two 49-yarders, the second of which put the Giants up two possessions with 4:24 left.
Few kickers can save themselves from free fall and enjoy a midseason turnaround. Zvada is back on an upward trajectory.
Jon Runyan Jr. is one of two guards in this category, but I need to make something clear. Almost the entire offensive line could be here. Even Andrew Thomas struggled to contain Philly’s front seven. The interior, however, had an especially tough time.
Runyan surrendered four pressures , three of which were hurries. His showing in fact continues to raise questions as to why the Giants inked him to a two-year, $22 million extension in September that included new money.
Backup quarterbacks and injury-ravaged backfields require more support from the O-line. Runyan was undoubtedly the biggest part of the interior offensive line that didn’t bring its A-game to the party this week.
After enjoying arguably the best game of his rookie campaign in Week 7, Francis Mauigoa struggled against the Eagles' more physically dominating defensive front.
He was overpowered at various points during this divisional clash. The 21-year-old right guard allowed one sack and one other pressure , but he still looked outmatched far too often. His run blocking, like that of his fellow interior offensive linemen, was atrocious, MAuigoa earning a season-low 39.9 mark from PFF.
Better days will come, just as one did in Week 7, but until then, Mauigoa will continue to experience growing pains.
The Giants hoped for the best with putting Jones out there despite the hand injury that kept him on the injury report all week.
The decision nearly hurt them. Jones failed to track a ball early in the second quarter, but he tried to catch it anyway. His bold attempt to salvage the play resulted in a muffed punt that gave the Eagles possession on the Giants’ 47-yard line.
Fortunately, a ford fumble by Arvell Reese spared Jones further embarrassment and kept New York within two points.
Jones is hurting, and the Giants are short on viable returners, so there may not be a quick fix. At the very least, they must keep the ball off the ground.

title: Giants Offense Grades: Winston Provides the Spark, O-Line Struggles in Win Over Eagles
full_text:
If we’re being blunt, the New York Giants won their Week 9 game against the Philadelphia Eagles more by riding the coattails of their defense than anything else.
We’ll review the defense in a separate piece, but in terms of the offense, which admittedly did enough (including winning the time of possession battle 34:45 to 25:15), there were some concerns.
The running game, sans Cam Skattebo, struggled, averaging just 2.6 yards per carry. Devin Singletary, this week’s RB1, rushed 21 times for 31 yards, averaging 1.5 yards per carry.
Granted, the running backs didn’t exactly get help from the offensive line, but it was alarming to see eight of the Giants’ 31 rushing attempts (25.8%) register as tackles for loss. That number, by the way, was the most by any team in Week 9 according to TruMedia ( via the Locked On Giants podcast ).
Interestingly, there’s still chatter about the Giants trading for Jonathan Taylor of the Colts. While Taylor would be a solid addition, unless the run blocking up front gets better and in a hurry, we’re not sure how much it would matter.
Let’s get into this week’s offense grades.
The more we watched McCarthy this week, the more he showed the limitations of a pocket-passing offense in today’s pressure-happy league. If all your offense does is drop back the quarterback, the defense knows exactly where to find him; the pressure to make big plays on those dropbacks is huge.
Take away that quarterback’s first read, as the Eagles did, and you need your quarterback to find that second read in the blink of an eye. McCarthy was not doing that.
If you can’t keep opposing defenses off-balance – à la the Jaxson Dart offense that makes so many plays off of Dart’s legs – scoring points will continue to be a challenge, as it was this week.
That said, McCarthy’s overall game was spotty. He threw some dimes downfield to his wideouts, but those deep throws are tough to execute.
He overthrew Jalin Hyatt on a deep ball for the second week in a row, and some of his short throws lacked touch. His first half was a struggle.
He showed more in the second half by shrugging off a helmet to the midsection. McCarthy may have pretty good straight-line speed, but his running instincts need work.
He took a read-option not only into the teeth of the defense, but he lowered his head when it was obviously time for a slide, ergo the big hit.
His first-half passing numbers (9-of-13 for 101 yards) and just six points scored (on two long field goals) included five sacks. He’s got to do a better job of getting the ball out of his hands.
On the plus side, he didn’t force anything; his ball security was immaculate despite the pressure and the big hits.
McCarthy’s toughness is not to be taken for granted; when you’re big, strong, and tough like he is, it tends to keep you on the field and helps you hold onto the ball.
We’re not sure he’s enough of a quick-twitch thinker or thrower (his windup is a bit long), but relying on that deep drop to make your plays is a tough way to make a living in this league.
He’s also not a read-option, roll-out kind of guy; he makes very few plays on the move. In today’s NFL, it’s great to make plays from the deep pocket, but clean pockets are tough to come by; you need some variety in your game to help slow down the rush.
A running game would help (a mere 16 first-half yards), but this team doesn’t seem to have the backs to scare defenses from crashing the line of scrimmage. When McCarthy’s behind center, it’s all downfield throwing or nothing.
McCarthy wasn’t sacked in the second half, missed two series after that big hit on the zone-read, and finished with a mediocre 12-of-19 for 127 yards overall. That’s not good enough on most days.
Stepping in for the injured McCarthy early in the third quarter, Winston finished off that possession with a punt, and then engineered a 14-play, touchdown-scoring drive that not only gave the Giants a 13-8 lead, but took the starch out of the entire Eagles team.
In fact, Winston’s performance inspired his own sideline, especially with some very clutch throws. A 3rd-and-15 connection with Malachi Fields on a deep out was probably Winston’s best throw of the day.
An improbable 10-yard scramble, then a 27-yard teardrop to a deep-crossing Darnell Mooney, and another 14-yard dart to Fields down to the 2-yard line set up Winston’s too-easy throw to Isaiah Likely in the end zone for the second half’s only touchdown.
McCarthy re-entered the game on the team’s next possession, leaving the fan base with the knowledge that Winston may not be the long-term answer, but he can play top-level NFL quarterback in a pinch and is, in fact, one of the best backup quarterbacks in the league.
It wasn’t expected to be pretty for Singletary today, starting and managing most of the running back load against an inspired Eagles defense. That it turned out so ugly was hardly Singletary’s fault, as he had room to run on perhaps two of his 21 handoffs.
The rest of his touches? We’ll let his numbers speak for themselves: 21 carries for 31 yards (1.5 avg.). That’s as ugly as it gets.
And yet, with all that lack of production, the Giants still managed a time-of-possession advantage of 34:45 to 25:15. Go figure.
One of the secrets to this ugly win was the big fat zero in the offense’s turnover column. Give Singletary credit for the ball security.
On the negative side, Singletary was involved in several of the sacks allowed with some poor blitz pickup attempts.
Known for his reliability in that part of the game, we were surprised to see this veteran come up so small today.
Picked up recently off the Los Angeles Chargers’practice squad, this 25-year-old, 200-pound scatback type did his best Dave Meggett impression, gaining 20 yards on his 3 touches and bringing a level of quickness to the offense that was sorely lacking.
This kid looks like an ideal change-of-pace back to call on in the coming weeks. We’re also interested to see him returning kickoffs.
Desrosiers did enough, not only with his quick feet but also with his vision, toughness, and ball security, to warrant more touches.
Nabers had his four-game 100-yard receiving stretch interrupted, with just 53 yards on five catches. His final target should have added 20 yards and a touchdown to his line, but he dropped a perfectly thrown pass he earned with a sharp route to get behind the defense.
After throwing little hissy fits throughout the game at his lack of attention despite leading the team in targets, it was embarrassing to see him fail to complete a basic play.
Nabers had another drop and seemed to struggle to get off the ground after several catches.
Continuing his solid play, Fields caught two of his three receptions from Jameis Winston, both coming on the crucial second-half scoring drive and both clutch, big-time connections.
Fields’ route-running seems to be getting sharper, as he squared off both routes, giving his quarterback plenty of space to attack.
He also drew one pass interference call and should have drawn another that wasn’t called, both on throws from J.J. McCarthy.
Fields was part of today’s poor run-blocking effort; in space, he whiffed more often than he made contact, and he seemed more effective inside the tackle box, where he relished the contact.
It was a good sign to these eyes that Mooney was spotlighted a bit more by the game plan, as we like matching up Mooney’s game against the opposition’s third cornerback.
Mooney went 3-54-18.0 on the day, leading the team in yards. Mooney’s big play was the 27-yard deep crosser that Jameis Winston hit for the big, clutch gain.
It put the Eagles’ defensive backs on their heels; soon enough, the Giants were scoring their lone touchdown of the game.
These coaches need to keep incorporating Mooney’s speed and hands into the game plan, as he’s a professional wideout who knows how to play the position.
Getting about a dozen snaps and his weekly fly pattern to run, Hyatt made the effort to dive for the overthrown ball at…

title: Giants Grades: Defense Earns an A in Win Over Eagles
full_text:
The grades are in on the New York Giants ’ 19-11 win over the Philadelphia Eagles.
The Giants outscored the Eagles, but honestly, that was because the defense played so well. The offensive line was repeatedly beaten in the trenches, allowing six sacks. The run blocking wasn’t much better, lacking any push, and the Giants averaged an abysmal 2.6 yards per carry.
The good news? Jameis Winston came in and did what he’s being paid to do: carry the team through when the starter goes down, for however long it takes.
Winston stepped in after J.J. McCarthy suffered a hip injury that knocked him out for the rest of the third quarter before he could return. In the meantime, Winston threw the go-ahead touchdown pass, a 5-yarder to tight end Isaiah Likely.
Malik Nabers had a quiet afternoon, recording just 43 yards on five catches. He also had a big drop in the end zone, though thankfully that didn’t hurt his team. His streak of 100-yard receiving games ends at four.
Let’s call it what it is: the Giants defense carried the team in this game with solid play across the board.
After giving up 121 net yards to the Eagles in the first half, the defense buckled down and limited Philadelphia to just 99 yards in the second half. Philly’s first four drives of the half were four plays or fewer, three of them three-and-outs, and totaled 21 yards.
Rookie linebacker Arvell Reese, who should be this week’s NFC Defensive Player of the Week, was all over the place, but in a very good way. We’re talking about a team-leading 12 tackles (10 solo), three sacks for -18 yards, three tackles for loss, three quarterback hits, and a forced fumble.
In all, the Giants had seven sacks, 10 tackles for loss and 11 quarterback hits. Kudos, too, to the run defense, which allowed Philly just 92 yards on 25 carries, a 3.7-yard average, with only 64 of those yards coming from old friend Saquon Barkley.
Simply put, the Big Blue defense dominated, forcing seven three-and-outs on the Eagles’ 13 possessions.
Come on, guys, how hard is it to have the right number of personnel on the field on any given play? At least twice this season, only 10 were lined up.
This time, 12 lined up, which gave the Eagles a redo on a PAT that they turned into a two-point conversion. The Giants’ special teams units also picked up four penalties in all, which shouldn't be happening this far into the season.
Thankfully, the unit’s grade gets bailed out by kicker Dominic Zvada, who bounced back from his pre-bye struggles with solid field goals of 53, 49, 28, and 49 yards, and by punter Jordan Stout, whose highlight was his final punt of the day, which pinned the Eagles at their own 5-yard line.
One day, a Giants win will come a lot easier instead of boiling down to the final two minutes, but hey, a win’s a win, right?
Kudos to head coach John Harbaugh, who kept the team on track by picking up where it left off before the bye and coaxing the players to forget about the 13-year winless stretch in Philly.
Extra kudos to defensive coordinator Dennard Wilson, who sent a blitz on 16 of the Eagles’ dropbacks. Philly quarterback Joe Milton III completed just seven of 10 attempts against it, and the other six dropbacks were sacks.
We initially questioned whether the offensive game plan was a touch too conservative. Few designed runs were called, which let the Eagles’ pass rush harass McCarthy all day. Running the ball better would have definitely made a difference.
Special teams coordinator Chris Horton has got to get this unit right on communication about who should be on the field at any given time.

title: Giants WR Malik Nabers Responds to Broadcasters’ Criticism
full_text:
At times during the New York Giants’ 19-11 win over the Philadelphia Eagles, receiver Malik Nabers didn’t seem very happy.
At least that’s how Fox Sports play-by-play man Joe Davis and color analyst and former NFL tight end Greg Olsen saw things based on Nabers’ body language.
Davis said Nabers’ body language “has been terrible today,” and Olsen agreed.
When Nabers learned of the criticism, he took to his Instagram account to fire back at the duo.
“(Y’all) be trying (to) create a narrative on me so bad, it’s actually crazy,” Nabers wrote in an IG story.
“If you (don’t) like the way I play the game, keep the camera off me!! SIMPLE! But (Olsen) calling me a bad teammate when every team I’ve been on, there’s NOBODY I’ve played with (that) has said (that about) me is crazy!
“My face is the same way if I’m having a good game, bad, winning or losing. If it’s a problem: 1. Keep the camera off of me. 2. Pray (about) it! Simple.”
Davis and Olsen may have been onto something regarding Nabers' frustration level, who finished with five receptions for 43 yards and dropped a 20-yard touchdown pass from J.J. McCarthy.
After the game, Nabers was asked about the offense’s ebb and flow and admitted to having some frustration.
“I felt like we were just lackadaisical out there, just playing, letting the game come,” he said.
“I feel like in a division game you have to go attack people, you have to go attack the game. I felt like we were lollygagging our way through the game.
“I had frustration about that, trying to wake everybody up just to make sure we’re playing a game right now. We need this win. So I was just frustrated about how we were handling the offense.”
Nabers said that at halftime the coaches challenged the players to come out with more fire, which they did in taking the 13-8 lead in the third quarter.
Nabers has also not been shy about his growth as a leader or his voice, saying that he's no afraid to speak up if he sees or senses something isn't right.
Earlier this season, he spoke up about not getting the ball enough, a problem that was corrected.

title: J.J. McCarthy Showed Guts After Injury Scare in Giants' Win Over Eagles
full_text:
The New York Giants got a chilling sense of déjà vu during the second half of their eventual 19-11 Week 9 win over the Philadelphia Eagles at Lincoln Financial Field.
With 12:16 remaining in the third quarter, quarterback J.J. McCarthy completed a three-yard run to the 27-yard line. In the process, Eagles defender Zack Baun hit him hard. McCarthy quickly jogged off the field in visible pain due to the hip injury, while backup Jameis Winston took over.
For the second time this season, New York feared losing yet another starting QB1.
Unlike Jaxson Dart’s season-ending knee injury in Week 2, however, McCarthy returned to the sideline and re-entered the game with time expiring in the third quarter, seemingly averting a potential crisis at the position.
In addition to his toughness and strong resolve, the 23-year-old credited the Giants’ trainers for helping him get back on the field so quickly.
“It’s feeling good,” McCarthy said postgame of his hip injury. “Football is a physical game, and I can’t thank the training staff enough for helping me get back on the field as fast as possible. But yeah, it’s feeling pretty good.”
McCarthy finished the game 12-of-19 for 127 yards, while absorbing five sacks on a day when the Giants struggled to establish the run.
Starting running back Cam Skattebo was sidelined due to a hamstring injury, and veteran Devin Singletary managed only 31 yards on 21 carries in the lead role against Philadelphia.
Though New York’s rushers struggled, they got little help from their interior offensive line, which had one of its worst first-half run-blocking performances of the season.
To spark New York’s offense, coach John Harbaugh and coordinator Matt Nagy adjusted their strategy at halftime to give McCarthy more designed runs. Less than five minutes into the second half, McCarthy incurred his injury on a zone read.
Still, the former Michigan Wolverine accepted responsibility for the hit at his postgame podium, vowing to improve his reading skills.
“Yeah, obviously the play was a quarterback-driven run, and I pulled it based on my read, and the goal is to get to the numbers, get out of bounds,” McCarthy explained.
“I pulled it back inside, and saw a bomb late and tried to get my shoulder down, but didn’t get it down enough and made a great hit. At the end of the day, I’ve just got to protect myself and do a better job of doing that.”
Meanwhile, Winston went 6-of-8 for 71 yards and threw the Giants’ only touchdown pass in relief of McCarthy.
The 12-year veteran also relieved Dart during the team’s Week 2 loss to the Los Angeles Rams. After the game, several Giants players, including McCarthy, praised Winston for his leadership and field savvy in the face of adversity.
“It’s just a testament to him [Winston],” McCarthy said. “He’s a true pro. To be able to step in there and be that spark and lead the team down the field, it was absolutely awesome to watch, and just so proud of him and the way he carried himself throughout the entire week and throughout this whole process. I was really happy to see him do that, and a great catch by [Giants WR] Isaiah [Likely].
“So many guys were making plays,” he added. “It was really awesome. It was great for our team to go down there and get some points.”

title: Giants Won’t Overpay for a ‘Short-Term Fix,’ Harbaugh Says Amid Taylor Buzz
full_text:
With the NFL trade deadline rapidly approaching, New York Giants head coach John Harbaugh did not shoot down a report of the team’s interest in Indianapolis Colts running back Jonathan Taylor. Asked about it, he said he’s “not saying that report’s not true,” and he left the door open for a deal if circumstances change.
“I’d say we’re open to any situation, but I will say this: things do change. Things change day-to-day,” he said. “So it’s not like one day you may do something and the next day something happens, and it changes your position. I’m not saying that report’s not true.
“Those conversations are taking place, and if something happens for any player, I can’t talk about any player because they’re with other teams right now, but we’re not ruling anything out, but I don’t see anything particularly imminent right now either.”
The Giants struggled to run the ball in their 19-11 win over the Philadelphia Eagles. New York finished with 80 yards on 31 carries without Cam Skattebo, who was inactive with a hamstring injury, and Tyrone Tracy Jr., who is on injured reserve with a hamstring strain.
But it wasn’t just the running backs. The offensive line struggled in run blocking, and the Giants lost yardage on nine plays.
Those struggles have fueled speculation that the Giants might look to make a deal for a running back. According to Fox Sports insider Jay Glazer, New York had offered second- and fifth-round picks for Taylor, but the Colts wanted more, and the Giants pulled the offer. Another insider, Jordan Schultz, suggested the Colts might even hang onto Taylor and look to move him next offseason.
Harbaugh, who also said there is no one on the Giants’ roster they want to trade away, stressed that any acquisition must make sense in the short and long term.
“It’s got to make sense short term and long term. We’re not just going to go for a short-term fix at an exorbitant cost. We’re not going to do that. That’s not where we’re at. And usually when you do that sort of thing, it doesn’t work out for you. You end up paying a hefty price, and you don’t get the return,” he said.
“I never think that you’re one step away, one player away,” he continued, noting that the front office has “been making a lot of calls” around the league to see what might be available and make sense for the franchise.
“To me, it’s always just a total momentum kind of thing anyway. But if the right opportunity comes and there’s a deal that makes sense for us, we’ll do it.”

title: Why I Fully Trust Jets GM Darren Mougey Ahead of the Trade Deadline
full_text:
The Jets have been a rough watch in 2026. The team is 2-7 through nine weeks and appears headed for an 11th straight losing season. Despite that, the New York team still has hope: draft capital. The Jets currently hold nine picks in the 2027 draft , three of them first-rounders.
That is general manager Darren Mougey's doing.
Jets fans should continue to have faith in the second-year GM. Gang Green will likely sell at the deadline— as proven by Monday's Andre Cisco trade with the Lions —and Mougey has shown he can make a deal with the best of them.
The Jets are in good hands in the roster-building department, despite it not carrying over in the win-loss column just yet.
Darren Mougey has sent three former first-round picks out the door in his time as the Jets' GM. Early on, it seems as though Mougey got every one of those decisions right. The Jets parted with Quinnen Williams, Sauce Gardner, and Jermaine Johnson II in the past year; all three left the Jets on the better side of those trades.
Pro Football Focus has Williams (23rd), Gardner (48th), and Johnson (59th) all ranked outside the top 20 at their positions, marks they had met when they were in New York. Mougey seems to have gotten rid of talent that wasn't producing at just the right time.
Williams and Gardner were seen as franchise cornerstones before their respective trades. Now the Cowboys and Colts may have buyer's remorse. Gardner is having one of the worst seasons of his career. Williams isn't doing much better . Mougey seems to have shed bloated contracts at the perfect time.
Mougey got rid of two players who are being paid top-five numbers at their positions and one who was toward the end of a rookie contract. None of those players are currently performing like top players at their respective positions. The Jets GM has had to sell, and he's done it at the perfect times. With the deadline looming, expect him to sell again at the right time.
Fleece. That is one word people have used to describe the Jets' trades over the past year. Thanks to Mougey, the Jets currently hold three of the first 13 picks in the 2027 Draft. Mougey has made the most of his blockbuster trades so far, and should be itching to see what he can accomplish during this year's deadline.
The Jets used the first-round returns from the Gardner and Williams trades to land Kenyon Sadiq and Omar Cooper Jr., who have shown flashes of stardom in their rookie seasons. Mougey has not parted with players cheaply. Rather, he has gotten the best possible return for the team. Even the Johnson trade netted the Jets T'Vondre Sweat , who is grading higher than his predecessor , Williams.
If Mougey has shown one thing during his tenure at the helm, it's that he can win trades. The Jets are currently watching the Colts' and Cowboys' seasons slip away with a smile on their face knowing that every loss means better draft capital for the team. Jets fans can trust that their GM is dedicated to being on the winning side, even though a blockbuster trade this season seems unlikely
Mougey has been the most productive member of the Jets' organization during his tenure as the GM. The man has gotten rid of players who were not worth their contracts and gotten the best return possible for them. The Jets should trust the man who has been able to produce six first-round draft picks in two years' time.
The Jets look better than last year despite an ever-present uphill climb in the win-loss department. Mougey is a huge reason for that improvement. As the trade deadline looms, fans and the organization should be happy that the 41-year-old GM is at the helm.

title: Faria's Focus: 5 Jets Thoughts Following 4th Straight Loss (Trade Deadline, Long-Term Plans & More)
full_text:
The numbers speak for themselves. The outcomes speak for themselves.
Aaron Glenn's Jets are a bad football team . They showed it throughout their 35-12 loss at the hands of the Chiefs on Sunday . Whether it was their nine penalties, turnovers, or inability to play complementary football to an almost comical level, what can go wrong will go wrong for this team.
As always, it's time to give some thoughts following their fourth straight loss, and seventh in their last eight games. From Glenn's future employment problems to lone bright spots, there's a lot to discuss about what this team is and will be going forward.
There are a lot of problems with New York's coaching staff. Glenn is at the top of the list . Even when the team makes the right call—like challenging the Chiefs' third-down fumble—there's little done afterward to build on it.
The problem there is the fact that the Jets are selectively aggressive. On the opening drive, they reached a goal-to-go situation and felt like taking the field goal was acceptable. They were so focused on just dinking and dunking down the field that the team refused to take shots against Kansas City's defense until it was too late.
If Glenn and his staff want to be successful, they need to actually choose what kind of staff they want to be. At this rate, though, it really doesn't matter. Glenn's job is all but gone after an abysmal 5-21 start to his run with Gang Green. His inability to stay aggressive, or even get aggressive in the first place, will be one of many reasons why it failed.
As the Chiefs were running down the Jets' throats in the second half, I was left with one major thought.
David Bailey is an awesome draft pick, one that the Jets actually got right at such a high selection. But if the team is going to watch him reach T.J. Watt or Myles Garrett-level effectiveness, they need to put him in a better defense for his skill set.
Bailey recorded two sacks and two fumbles forced in Sunday's loss. He's now up to 7.5 sacks and five fumbles forced in eight games played—second-most in that span, behind Julius Peppers with the Panthers.
"No surprise, that is who he is," Glenn said of Bailey after the game. "Each game, he is learning and getting better. It’s good to see that. We expect him to make plays like that. We expect him to be on the field as much as he can and to do that."
At the time of the 2026 draft, the Jets were choosing between Bailey and Arvell Reese. Reese is on his way to another excellent rookie season and will get plenty of flowers after his three-sack effort against Philadelphia.
But Bailey has been as productive, if not more, in his first year. The Jets just need to put him in the kind of wide-nine alignment that will get the most out of his skill set as a pass rusher and someone who sets the edge nicely in run fronts.
When the team inevitably makes a coaching change at the end of the year, they should find a coordinator who will fit Bailey into the right scheme.
During the Jets' loss to Kansas City, it was clear that frustration was boiling over on the sideline. Quarterback Geno Smith and right tackle Armand Membou were both seen throwing their helmets to the ground in frustration (h/t Glenn Naughton).
Now it's Armand Membou's turn.  Allows a sack on 3rd down.  It's the fifth sack the @nyjets have allowed today. pic.twitter.com/CDWrJRzkIq
After the game, Smith clarified that his frustration came from trying to be better for his team.
“I was just frustrated with not getting it done. I am always the type of guy that is going to look inward," Smith said. "I am really just looking at myself and figuring out how I can be better for the guys and the team so we can get it done.”
Then came the aftermath. Not even 24 hours after the Jets' loss, edge rusher Will McDonald requested a trade to a better situation —one where he will play over 50% of the snaps compared to his time with the Jets.
McDonald is a good edge rusher, but it's obvious at this point he's not a fit for the defense Glenn wants to run. Should the head coach boast that his coaching plan would set the former first-round pick back dating to last year? Absolutely. But it's no use crying over spilled milk.
At this rate, the milk is spoiled; players in need of new contracts are going to start wanting out.
Smith and Membou aren't on that list. But it's evident the Jets have reached a tipping point under Glenn. With eight games left in the regular season, this may get a whole lot worse before it gets better.
We've already mentioned McDonald's trade request, but it highlights the Jets' bigger problems as a front office. They don't have much top talent to ship off, and any deadline fire sale will only muster a couple of late-round draft selections.
That doesn't mean the Jets should stand pact with where they are.
New York is going nowhere this season. All the players brought in to fit Glenn's mold of what a team should look like have failed. The Jets and general manager Darren Mougey should look to sell off some of their talent and try to get as much capital as they can for the next coaching staff when they come in during January.
Among the names are McDonald, Harrison Phillips, Nahshon Wright and Jarvis Brownlee. Breece Hall will be another name that is talked about in trades, but I get the sense the team wants to keep their 1-2 combination with Braelon Allen intact.
It's hard to tell if the Jets will actually make a move at the deadline this year, but if the last few weeks are any indication, they absolutely should.
We're at the point in the season where the Jets' outlook will not be based on wins, but on the quality of play from their young performers and on how high a draft pick they will be able to obtain.
New York should not be making any legitimate coaching changes either. If the Jets lose to the Bills on Sunday (expected considering their current four-game losing streak), they will drop to 2-8 for the year. It wouldn't make sense to make a coaching change then—it would be best for the team to ride out the final months of the Glenn era and then make a move once the season ends.
At 5-21, there's little hope that Glenn can turn around the program. He's been given two years to show improvement and hasn't. But if the Jets can get a top pick, then this era will not be a complete loss. It will, at the very least, set the next coaching staff up for success down the road.
But that also means Glenn needs to stay on to complete the team's troubled run. Any change, and the Jets risk missing out on a top pick.

title: Aaron Glenn Address Jets' Deadline Uncertainty Following Will McDonald IV's Trade Request
full_text:
Jets edge rusher Will McDonald made some breaking news Monday morning with a reported trade request following the team's loss to the Chiefs.
The former first-round edge rusher out of Iowa State has just three sacks on the season and has played under 50% of the snaps for the defense. Once a 10-sack defender, McDonald has been relegated to a situational role at best.
And now he wants to go to a place better suited for his talents.
But with a year of team control, the Jets don't appear so willing to get rid of a player they still have high hopes for.
Speaking to reporters on Monday morning, Jets head coach Aaron Glenn was clear about the team's outlook with McDonald: they weren't going to give him away just because the edge rusher is frustrated.
"I just know we're in the business of keeping good players, so Will's going to be here," Glenn said.
Glenn also added that he and McDonald had a "productive" conversation following Sunday's loss to Kansas City as well.
Glenn's productive conversations with McDonald can go all the way back to when the coach was first hired last season. During training camp, Glenn was asked why the Iowa State product had not broken out in a major way as a first-round pick.
A year and a half in, it seems Glenn and his current staff simply aren't cutting it when it comes to getting the most out of the team's players. With the trade deadline drawing nearer, the team's coaching struggles have highlighted several players who may be on the move.
But like McDonald, the Jets seem comfortable keeping everything as the status quo.
All the talk will be centered on McDonald after his trade request, but the Jets also have players on expiring deals who could use a change of scenery. Veterans like Harrison Phillips, Jarvis Brownlee, Nahshon Wright and even quarterback Geno Smith have been names that have been floated around.
On Monday, though, Glenn cleared the air on the team's plan going forward.
Of course, it's fair to point out that the Jets are in the same situation they were in last year and ended up trading Sauce Gardner and Quinnen Williams. Will the same thing happen in 2026? New York was able to get top draft capital for their best players last year, but that same talent isn't available this year.
Unless a team is willing to overpay for any of New York's starters, the team may not be willing to part with players for the return of a day three pick. McDonald may end up being the only one worthy of an overpay.
Even then, there's no guarantee the Jets will budge.

title: 5 Jets Awards to Give Out in Blowout Loss to Chiefs: Stars to David Bailey and the Colts
full_text:
Tell me if you heard this before: the New York Jets were outcoached and outplayed when it mattered most in another loss.
Gang Green dropped their seventh game in their last eight tries, the latest coming in a 35-12 shellacking by the Kansas City Chiefs at Arrowhead Stadium. New York was shut out in the second half and did not score a touchdown in their fourth straight loss.
We have five awards to give out, so let's get to it now.
Every time the Jets coaching staff makes a good decision, it's followed up by mind-boggling calls that clearly hold the team back. Whether it was kicking field goals in goal-to-go situations when the team needed a touchdown, or trying hard not to turn the ball over against the blitz and taking bad sacks when they could least afford, the Jets made calls throughout the game that kept them from winning.
If anything, Glenn and his staff coached not to lose Sunday's game compared to being aggressive enough to go and win it.
Even more alarming is the fact that there were several Jets players who seemingly let their emotions get the best of them. Whether it was Geno Smith screaming on the sideline, or Armand Membou committing a personal foul penalty for slamming his helmet down on the field of play, New York is unprepared and undisciplined when it matters most.
It's the clearest indictment against Glenn at this point.
"It's all about our process, to be honest with you," Glenn said. "It gets tough, I know it does, but it's the belief. We've shown spurts that we can play at a high level."
One of the lone bright spots from the Jets on Sunday was rookie David Bailey. The second overall pick in the 2026 draft recorded two sacks and two forced fumbles on the day. While his run defense remained inconsistent, the Jets got him in situations to succeed.
Through his first eight games in the NFL, Bailey has recorded 7.5 sacks and five forced fumbles. He has the most sacks through his first eight games as a first-round pick since Julius Peppers. Considering Peppers is a Hall of Famer, Bailey's start has been nothing short of special.
"It's always a blessing just getting out there and just playing football, playing the game I love," Bailey said.
He is heating this defensive rookie of the year award list up.
In the first half, the Jets offense had gone up and down the field against the Chiefs' mighty defense. While they didn't score a touchdown, there was hope the talent level on the unit would be good enough to keep things competitive.
Things only got worse, though.
New York lost the second half 21-0, and recorded just 46 yards of offense in the second half. To put that into perspective, the Jets recorded 64 yards in their first drive of the game - and failed to get close to that point in the second half. After seeing three straight 100-yard rushing games from Braelon Allen, the Jets gave him just seven carries on the day, while giving more carries to Breece Hall.
Those adjustments didn't work. It only capped the offense further.
"It’s disappointing, the only thing we can do is go back to work and try to figure out how can I, as the head coach, get us to play two halves at a high level and not have a lull at any part of the game," Glenn said. "That’s something I’ll think long and hard about to make sure I get that done. A lot of thinking to do. A lot of thinking to do. Just look forward to getting back to work."
New York was abysmal on Sunday, but its uncompetitive offensive performance in the second half was the worst of the worst.
The good? New York forced two turnovers today courtesy of fumbles forced by David Bailey & a muffed quarterback sneak.
The bad? They should've had at least three more fumble recoveries and have gone five straight games without an interception.
New York's inability to fall on the football has been well documented. Some of it is just poor football luck as a collective franchise. In other cases, especially with their lack of interceptions, it's a coaching problem as well. The Jets don't do enough to force mistakes by the opposition. When they do, they are unable to take advantage of those opportunities.
At the end of the day, it's just a further reason why the current staff is not up to par.
As the Jets continued to struggle against the Chiefs during the second half, they did get good news throughout. The Indianapolis Colts ended up losing to the Dallas Cowboys at home, dropping their record to 2-7 on the year.
By virtue of the Colts' loss, the Jets continue to own three of the top 13 picks including two inside the top six overall selections. As New York and the Colts continue to lose, especially with games against the Dolphins and Chargers ahead on their schedule, it's clear the Jets are going to have plenty of chances to get top players in the 2027 draft.
Things aren't going well for the team right now. But the draft offers a bit of hope.

title: 3 Potential Will McDonald  IV Trade Destinations for Jets After Monday's Demand
full_text:
When the season began, Jets edge rusher Will McDonald seemed to be at a crossroads in his career. The former first-round pick had a 10-plus-sack season early in his career but has struggled to find consistency.
ESPN and NFL Network 's Ian Rapoport reported Monday morning that McDonald has been "extremely frustrated" with his role on the team and has requested a trade out of Florham Park. The Jets have not commented on the request at this time.
#Jets pass-rusher Will McDonald IV has informed the team that he wants to be traded, sources say. McDonald has played sparingly this season and is extremely frustrated with his usage. The former first-rounder wants more opportunities and the team is aware. pic.twitter.com/QCxFC0Ciwn
McDonald openly asking for a trade leaves the Jets with two opportunities :
If the Jets do decide to trade McDonald, here are three teams who could come calling.
When Aaron Glenn first took the team's head coaching job, he made it clear the reason why McDonald hadn't broken out to that point was simple - "coaching."
Turns out, his defensive alignment was even worse for the former first-round pick than before.
Now, with over a year of control left on his rookie contract, it seems like the best fit for McDonald is a return back to the wide-nine scheme and a reunion with Robert Saleh out in Tennessee. The Titans have an affinity for bringing in former Jets players, and McDonald would fit their pass-rushing need nicely at this point.
Detroit is certainly on its way to a playoff spot this year, and that means they will be buyers over the next 48 hours. If the Lions are smart, the first thing they'll target is their pass rush. Detroit gets plenty of pressure, and their defense has played well throughout the 2026 season, but you could never have enough edge rushers.
With McDonald, the Lions could have a situational player in a division where they'll need to put pressure on some quality young quarterbacks like Jordan Love and Caleb Williams. Glenn's relationship with head coach Dan Campbell could help facilitate a trade as well.
The Cowboys are 4-5, three games out of the division lead, and have seen their defense struggle for most of the year. So why exactly would they be buyers?
After a less-than-thrilling victory over the two-win Colts, the outcome could be enough to entice owner Jerry Jones into making a trade at the deadline for more pass rush help - something the organization desperately needs.
If the Cowboys are going to try going all-in again with Dak Prescott at quarterback, McDonald seems like an honest move up for the team without mortgaging even more of their future going forward.
