title: Every Jets Quote That Mattered After Humiliating Loss to Chiefs
full_text:
Another loss, another week of searching for answers for the New York Jets.
Their 35-12 defeat at the hands of the Kansas City Chiefs was the fourth straight, and seventh in their last eight games. The talent on the team is undeniable, but it's also clear that they aren't coached or playing well enough to win.
In Sunday's loss, it seemed like the Jets kept finding new ways to make mistakes. And it's left the Jets reaching for new ways to answer questions about their future.
It feels like we've seen that kind of Jets loss before. New York competed hard in the first half, only to be outcoached in the second half to go along with execution mistakes that sunk their chances. At the end of the day, though, the Jets are 2-7 on the season, and 5-21 under Glenn as head coach.
"We just go back to work and try to figure out, how can I, as the head coach, get us to play two halves at a high level, and not have a lull at any part of the game," Glenn said. "That's something I will think long and hard about, to make sure that we can get that done."
Players refuse to give up on Glenn, though. New York's locker room focused more heavily on its own struggles than what the coaching staff was doing.
“It is always going to come down to execution," Geno Smith said.
While Glenn is not the sole reason for the team's losing record this year, there is no way the Jets can excuse his record. As the losses pile up, it seems like a foregone conclusion he is coaching in the final months with the Jets.
New York's offense recorded just 46 yards of offense in the second half. The defense gave up 21 points and was gashed on the ground. Kenneth Walker scored three touchdowns in a rebound performance.
To the Jets, the struggles from the whole team in the second half weren't just about one play or performer. It was about everyone.
"We didn't play up to par," Glenn said. "I know that offensively we didn't have as many possessions as we needed to, against a team like this. Defensively, we didn't hold up well against the run in the second half."
As to what led to the offensive struggles, Breece Hall noted that having just seven team rushing yards in the second half as a clear design that failed right away. In fact, both Braelon Allen and Hall had a combined three carries in the second half. That's not going to cut it for a struggling offense.
"I think we went away from our bread and butter, which is running the ball," Hall said. "I think they sped us up a little bit because they got out to a little bit of a lead."
Part of the team's abandonment of the run game is based on their defense giving up touchdowns on drives to start the second half. New York had to start throwing the ball. But had the team been more successful in the first half, or managed to record touchdowns, the Jets may have been able to stick with their run game.
Instead, everything became discombobulated.
The losses are piling up. So too are the frustrations from their players. After turning the ball over on downs in the fourth quarter, Smith was seen slamming his helmet on the sidelines and screaming at his team.
After the game, Smith explained his freakout.
“I was just frustrated with not getting it done," Smith said. "I am always the type of guy that is going to look inward. I am really just looking at myself and figuring out how I can be better for the guys and the team so we can get it done.”
To their credit, the rest of the Jets agreed with Smith's reaction.
"We're frustrated with him," Hall said. "He's been doing very well distributing the ball and leading this offense. He definitely deserves for us to play better for him."
For what it's worth, right tackle Armand Membou was called for a personal foul penalty after also slamming his helmet on the ground before he walked off the field. Frustration has clearly boiled over for the organization.
And it looks like the coaching staff will need to address is further beyond Sunday.
Braelon Allen's streak of 100-yard games is over. That wasn't much of a surprise, though, with Breece Hall returning from a quad injury. What was disappointing was the way the Jets shared the snap totals for each running back.
Hall received 15 carries for 61 yards. Allen got just eight carries for 33 yards. New York had 99 yards in the first half, but just seven in the second as they went away from the run. But the fact Hall received nearly twice as many touches as Allen shows the Jets believe the former second-round pick remains better.
And it forces Allen to be nothing more than a role player again.
"We don't have any other choice," Allen said. "What are we going to do, pack it up and go home? You got to get back in the building tomorrow, learn from it, and get back on the field on Wednesday."
Should the Jets swap their running back totals? Time remains to be seen. But it's clear that Allen's time as the lead back is over, for now.
One of the few positives that came from the team on Sunday was the play of David Bailey. The second overall pick recorded two sacks and two forced fumbles, becoming the first player since Julius Peppers with over seven sacks in his first eight NFL games.
For the Jets, though, it's nothing they haven't seen before.
"No surprise, that is who he is," Glenn said. "Each game he is learning and getting better. It’s good to see that. The more he is on the field, the more that gives us an opportunity to make plays."
Bailey's professionalism and ability to make big plays with forced fumbles and sacks will make him a Pro Bowl player for years to come. As the team looks to get better, it's his humbleness that makes him extremely important going forward.
"It's always a blessing just getting out there and just playing football, playing the game I love," Bailey said.

title: Jets Week 9 Report Card: Grading Every Position After Latest Blunder vs. Chiefs
full_text:
The losing streak now stands at four games after the Jets only mustered four field goals and struggled to finish out drives in a 35-12 loss to the Chiefs on Sunday at Arrowhead Stadium.
Granted, it is not like the Jets were expected to pull off the upset against a Chiefs team coming off back-to-back losses and hungry to get back in the win column on home soil. That said, to come away with zero touchdowns and seemingly have no answers for Kansas City defensively was just another reminder of the various issues that continue to plague Gang Green.
Even though WR1 Garrett Wilson was sidelined with a concussion, it was a much more encouraging injury report coming in as RB1 Breece Hall and rookie David Bailey made their returns. Still, that was not enough to overshadow the poor coaching and execution issues that reared their heads once again in another frustrating loss.
Before the Jets return home to MetLife Stadium for another divisional game against the explosive Bills, let's hand out some grades for each unit following another poorly executed game against the Chiefs.
After throwing for multiple TDs each of the last two weeks, Geno Smith took a step in the wrong direction on Sunday. He was 18-of-32 for 165 yards with zero TDs and zero interceptions, in addition to getting sacked five times and failing to establish any rhythm from the opening kick.
It was not for a lack of ball movement, either. The Jets had a pair of drives in the game that went for at least 12 plays and took at least six minutes off the clock, only to settle for a field goal both times. In fact, the opening drive of the game got all the way down inside the five-yard line, but the Jets could not punch it in as Smith averaged a total of just 5.2 yards per throw and could not convert any explosive plays.
The Jets were already at a huge disadvantage against the Chiefs, but their problems were only compounded without Wilson on the field. However, instead of distributing the ball to their other capable wideouts and making the most of the situation, rookie Omar Cooper Jr. was the only WR with any impact on the game with eight catches (on 11 targets) for 58 yards, a huge step forward from his zero-catch performance in Week 8.
Fresh off a breakout outing with seven catches for 142 yards and a TD against the Raiders, Adonai Mitchell was nonexistent with zero receptions on seven targets the entire game. This unit simply failed to generate any chunk plays and fill the void left behind by Wilson , even though the Chiefs have struggled creating pressure defensively all season.
While the TEs were not much better against the Chiefs compared to the wideouts, there were at least some positives to take from the game. Largely invisible with just five combined catches in the last five games, rookie Kenyon Sadiq showed some glimpses of that seven catch, 105-yard, one-TD performance against the Lions back in Week 3 with four catches (on four targets) for 49 yards.
The same was not true for second-year TE Mason Taylor, however, as he only recorded one reception (on two targets) for 11 yards, just two weeks removed from his first two-TD game. While that level of play should not be expected every week from the TE group, there is still some room for improvement after making a minimal impact overall as receivers and failing to contain Kansas City's pass rush throughout the game.
Many wondered what the Jets would do as Hall made his return from a five-game absence due to a quad injury, especially after the success that Braelon Allen has experienced during that time. It was a solid return overall for the RB1 with 15 carries for 61 yards and a better yards per carry average (4.1) than his season-long average in four games (3.2).
Taking the RB1 role away from Allen seemed like it would be a mistake entering the game considering how well he has performed, but Hall was efficient on the ground and in the pass game (three catches, 26 yards). Allen, meanwhile, had eight carries for 33 yards, but he also committed this fumble (h/t The Jets Wall) that led to a go-ahead TD from the Chiefs just two plays later.
The bad: Allen fumbled The good: absolute HIT STICK by Geno pic.twitter.com/5LlIzgbseT
Had it not been for the solid first half when the OL paved the way for the run game to average more than five yards and 99 combined yards, this grade would have been even lower for the unit up front. From the five sacks allowed to the constant pressure that Smith faced in the pocket, there was not much to be pleased with after showing some positive signs in the loss to the Raiders.
The inability to finish drives down in the red zone and convert on third down (2-of-12) reached a breaking point when Armand Membou threw his helmet coming off the field and was given a personal foul penalty as a result. It was all part of the bigger picture for a Jets team that was penalized nine times for 57 yards, but it was just insult to injury for an OL that did not have much success holding its own up front as the game progressed.
Before we get to the bad, let's highlight the most obvious success story of the game for the defensive front. Of course, that would be none other than Bailey, who returned from a one-game absence due to a groin injury with nine tackles (five solo), two sacks, three tackles for loss and three QB hits. He also forced this fumble on Chiefs QB Patrick Mahomes (h/t SNY Jets) that resulted in a Jets recovery, although they missed a field goal and got nothing out of it.
David Bailey forces the fumble and the Jets recover! Patrick Mahomes walked off the field in pain after the hit pic.twitter.com/NQaGRnyR2N
Aside from Bailey, it was a disaster for the rest of the DL. In addition to Mahomes going for 242 yards and two TDs, the Jets could not take advantage of the key matchup against RB Kenneth Walker III by allowing him to amass 102 yards and one TD on 18 carries. The Chiefs were 5-0 coming into the game when he rushes for at least 70 yards, and the Jets did not seem to catch onto that with an inability to contain Kansas City for the duration of the game.
Veteran Demario Davis had nine tackles (five solo) and recovered a fumble on the first drive of the game for the Chiefs to help New York maintain control in the early going. While that type of play and some key plays against the run highlighted some of the good that came from this unit, it still had no answer for Walker on the ground and failed to provide a spark when the Chiefs started to gain the upper hand.
Jamien Sherwood also had nine tackles (five solo), but it was nowhere near enough to account for the situational football from the Chiefs. Furthermore, the fact that Kansas City was nearly able to double-up the Jets in first downs (27-15) only speaks to how this unit consistently failed to make the stops when it needed to in order to swing the momentum.
It was much of the same for a secondary that continues to be unable to create takeaways each week. Veteran Minkah Fitzpatrick led all players on the unit with five solo tackles, while Dane Belton added three and Brandon Stephens came away with a tackle for loss. Still, there were numerous breakdowns in key coverage situations and 391 yards of offense allowed.
Combine that with the three TDs given up in the second half, including the 10-play, 60-yard drive out of the half, and it was just not a good recipe for success. title: Biggest Jets Studs & Duds in Week 9 Loss to Chiefs: David Bailey Shines, Coaching Struggles Again
full_text:
It wasn't as if the final score was shocking.
The New York Jets competed hard early against the Kansas City Chiefs on the road. But poor coaching and execution mishaps held them back in an eventual 35-12 blowout defeat, bringing them to 2-7 for the year.
That said, plenty of people deserved blame for the team's fourth straight loss. So let's go through some of the biggest studs and duds from another Jets defeat.
By the time the offense got anything consistent in the second half, the Jets weren't going to be able to run the football. In the first half, though, the Jets showed exactly the blueprint they would want to show for the Braelon Allen/Breece Hall duo.
Much was made about what the Jets would do with Hall back from a quad injury in Week 3. In their first game together since Allen's breakout, the group seemed fine to start.
Hall recorded 15 touches for 61 yards and 4.1 yards per carry, while Allen saw just eight touches for 33 yards. At the half, the Jets averaged over five yards per carry and 99 yards total. They recorded just five in the second half.
With how poorly the rest of the team played, they get to be studs in this game...by default.
There's not much else to say. The Jets are being held back each and every week by the coaching staff - even when they make a single correct call to start the game.
Glenn correctly challenged what became the first Jets' turnover forced on the day. He proceeded to coach a passive contest by not going for it when they reached goal-to-go situations. Add in an extra nine penalties committed by the team during the game, which gave Kansas City plenty of chances, and the team was unable to do much, especially in the second half.
They were passive offensively when they needed to be aggressive, and overly zealous when a more conservative mindset was needed. All in all, the Jets are a bad team due to their coaching mishaps.
No clearer was that made than in the second half.
New York trailed Kansas City 14-12 at the half. At the start of the third quarter, Andy Reid and the Chiefs adjusted to Glenn's defensive plans, and it worked. New York simply didn't have a response in the second half. Reid vs. Glenn was always going to be a coaching advantage for the Chiefs, but Sunday's loss highlighted even more how poorly the Jets are led across the board.
If it wasn't for Sanders, the Jets would have been shut out, so he absolutely belongs in the stud column, even if he missed a 53-yard field goal.
Sanders was 4-for-5 on field goals made during the day and is 21-for-24 this year. He remains one of the few positives on the Jets' special teams unit, which has taken a clear step back as a collective group.
We already talked about the team's lack of discipline. It was so bad that it really needs its own blurb.
The nine penalties almost always came in a back-breaking situation. Whether it was a holding penalty that ended any chance for the team to go for a touchdown on a scoring drive, or a penalty allowing a Chiefs drive to continue, it's clear the team is not composed enough to make plays when it matters most.
We're beginning to reach uncharted territory with the second overall pick. Bailey was the first rookie in over a decade to record two sacks and two forced fumbles in a single game. His two sacks late in the first half gave the Jets a chance to take the lead going into the break. The offense couldn't do anything with it, but Bailey remains a top player.
This season, the Texas Tech product has 7.5 sacks and five forced fumbles. He's well on his way to a 10-sack season in his first year in the NFL. He remains a special player and a fundamental piece to the Jets going forward.
Things have reached a boiling point for the Jets. After the Jets failed to score in the red zone for a fourth time, quarterback Geno Smith was seen screaming on the sideline. Two series later, Armand Membou threw his helmet down coming off the field and took a personal foul penalty.
The Jets, as a collective organization, are not going anywhere this season. They have gotten worse with each passing game. Now, it's clear the locker room's frustration is coming out.
It will be up to Glenn and the staff to keep the team engaged. But with how poorly the coaching staff has held them back, it may not be enough for anyone going forward.

title: What Jets Are Saying About Week 9 Injury Report Ahead of Sunday
full_text:
There is good news and bad news when it comes to the New York Jets injury report heading into Week 9 against the Kansas City Chiefs.
The good news is that edge rusher David Bailey and running back Breece Hall are both expected to play. Bailey missed Week 8 with a groin injury while a quad injury kept Hall out for the last five. Even better, the team could have their full collection of edge rushers with Joseph Ossai potentially back as well.
But with every piece of good news there is also bad. Wide receiver Garrett Wilson has been ruled out for Sunday's contest with a concussion. He reported the injury on Monday and has been in protocol ever since.
His absence, coupled with the return of some key veterans, have Jets players and coaches talking about their chances in Week 9 against Kansas City.
Here's the full injury report from the Jets' practice on Friday with three clear distinctions on who is out for Sunday:
Friday’s injury report for #NYJvsKC pic.twitter.com/S8vga27YX3
Of note, the three players that are out extend beyond Wilson. Special teamer Trevin Wallace is also out while Ossai, rookie safety VJ Payne, defensive tackle Harrison Phillips, and corner Nahshon Wright are all listed as questionable.
The good news is Mason Taylor, Hall, and Bailey are all starters and will need to be on the field for the Jets to have any chance against the Chiefs.
Speaking to reporters before practice on Friday, Glenn was clear: the team was prepared to play without Wilson, but that doesn't mean his absence will be anything less than a major blow to the entire unit.
"I think it speaks for itself," Glenn said. "Any time you lose a player of that magnitude, it's always tough, right, but we do have other players, and those guys will look forward to the challenge."
Glenn did acknowledge the benefit that came from having Hall back in the lineup . He made it clear that the former second-round running back was going to have a role in the offense on Sunday, and it will be to work with rising star Braelon Allen.
"I know we're trying to get in this who's going to be the starter and try to spin sort of a negative situation, but nothing's changed from how I see this," Glenn said. "Both of those guys will play and that's just what it is."
The same can be said for the second-overall pick in Bailey. His return gives the team more flexibility to rush the passer—even one as elite as Patrick Mahomes.
"He (Bailey) just has to understand that with Mahomes is going to fake throw," Glenn said. "He's going to move around, and we just got to make sure we squeeze the pocket and make sure we don't let him out of the pocket in situations like that."
It's hard to envision a Jets victory on Sunday without Wilson. But getting several starters back healthy will certainly help.

title: 3 Eagles Might Be Due for Bigger Roles After the Trade Deadline
full_text:
Trades are being announced across the NFL. It's only a matter of time before Philadelphia gets involved before Tuesday's deadline. The Eagles have lost seven straight games and sit at the bottom of the NFC East. They are lined up to be sellers, with several players available at the right price.
There's an obvious focus on who will no longer be wearing midnight green after Philly's bye week. It's important to put focus on who will be, too. Making a trade usually opens a spot for someone lower on the depth chart to take over. It's an intriguing development during a retooling campaign.
Here's a look at three Eagles who might be due for bigger roles following the NFL trade deadline.
General manager Howie Roseman shifted from the norm when he selected Eli Stowers in the second round of the 2026 NFL Draft. The John Mackey Award winner was expected to make an immediate impact on Philadelphia's offense, but has been limited by injuries and blocked by Dallas Goedert.
Goedert could be moved at the deadline , considering he is 31 years old and playing on an expiring contract. That would give Stowers a chance to handle a steady role in an offense in need of change. It would also give the Eagles a window to evaluate whether the rookie can be trusted as a starter.
Second week in a row we are seeing Eli Stowers (No. 87) give this kind of effort blocking a CB Baby steps! pic.twitter.com/l5FhR3fGRI
Stowers logged 53 yards on three receptions in Week 8 (13 offensive snaps) and flashed solid blocking skills in Week 9 (seven offensive snaps). There's no time like the present to expand his route tree and depend on him to secure running lanes along the edge. Stowers is healthy and ready to roll .
There's no questioning defensive tackle Ty Robinson's potential. He has the strong frame (6'5", 288 lbs) needed to push back offensive linemen and an explosive first step that catches opponents off guard. The Eagles will never know whether that potential can turn into reality if he isn't on the field, though.
Robinson has served as the fifth option in the defensive tackle rotation since being drafted in 2025. That could change after Tuesday. The defensive tackle position is in high demand. The Eagles can capitalize by dealing Moro Ojomo or Byron Young, both of whom will be free agents next offseason .
Robinson was praised as a "wrecking ball" in college. The former Nebraska standout is violent at the line of scrimmage and always plays through the whistle. Robinson could be the spark Philly is missing in its disappointing run defense. The Eagles rank 24th in rushing yards allowed per game (126.1).
This selection is a bit more intricate than the other two. Outside linebacker Jalyx Hunt is already a reliable player on Philly's defense. However, his role has been reduced behind Jonathan Greenard and Nolan Smith lately. Hunt has played in fewer than 45% of the defensive snaps in each of his last four games.
Roseman could swing big by trading Smith at the deadline . He has posted five sacks in eight games and remains under contract in 2027. It'd be a move that brings back valuable draft capital for the Eagles. In that case, Hunt would become Greenard's counterpart, wreaking havoc in the backfield.
Hunt has tallied eight sacks, 12 tackles for a loss and 33 quarterback hits in 41 career games. The 25-year-old has shown versatility with six pass breakups and four forced fumbles. The final eight games of 2026 could go a long way toward determining whether Hunt is eventually signed to an extension.

title: McMullen: Joe Milton Isn’t to Blame After Eagles Set Him Up to Fail in Week 9
full_text:
PHILADELPHIA, P.A. — In the thick fog that settles over an organization after a seventh consecutive loss, the usual postgame noise quickly transformed into apathy in the shadow of the Eagles' 19-11 setback to the Giants on Sunday .
At 2-7, the Eagles are past the stage of searching for a spark and into the quieter territory of just trying to get through the remaining weeks of the 2026 season before rebooting in the offseason.
Into that haze walked Joe Milton, three weeks on the roster and making his first NFL start. He inadvertently said the quiet part out loud. ⁠
During a desperate final drive with seconds waning and no timeouts, Milton noted he trusted the embattled offensive line and loved the communication he was privy to despite the year-long issue with unaccounted-for pass rushers.
It was the kind of honesty only extemporaneous speech provides.
“I will learn y’all verbiage. I will,” Milton told his bodyguards. “That’s something that I put on myself to do for sure.”
Three weeks to absorb an offensive line’s language—the calls, the slides, the checks, the ‘who’s got the free runner’ signals—and the promise he would catch up.
That is not a quarterback complaining. That is a quarterback admitting the assignment was heavier than the preparation time allowed. ⁠
The play that made it obvious came from athletic rookie Arvell Reese, who came free on the right side, breezing by fellow freshman Markel Bell before nearly splitting Milton in two.
Milton never saw Reese, who separated the QB1 from his senses for a moment and the football.
Afterward, head coach Nick Sirianni did what he usually does when the film is going to be ugly . He said he was not going to assign fault.
Then he walked through the accountability coaching checklist: anytime a guy is free, look at the coaches first; ask whether everything possible was done to help the players; both coaching and execution matter; it starts with him; every product on the field is his responsibility. Yadda, yadda, yadda.
Sirianni’s monologue and Milton’s admission are not necessarily in conflict. They describe the same problem from different viewpoints.
Milton was signed off the Cowboys’ practice squad on Oct. 16. By the time he took the first snap against a Giants team that blitzes often and had the quickly ascending Reese, who finished with three sacks overall, Milton had a limited number of practices in the scheme under his belt.
The offensive line has been a problem all year for the Eagles. Protections have been a problem all year. Putting a new quarterback behind that line and asking him to diagnose, communicate, and correct in real time did not give Milton a chance.
It was testing whether the young signal caller could survive while still learning the language the line already speaks.
Sirianni is right that he owns the product. That ownership includes the decision to start Milton when the verbiage was still unfinished business. It includes the protection packages that left Reese with a free run. It includes the cumulative reality that seven sacks and a lost fumble on an unblocked blitz happened on the first start of a player who had just promised the line he would get their calls down.
Milton put the learning curve on himself, as professional quarterbacks do. The organization put him in the game before the curve was flat enough.
The Eagles did not hand Milton a functional offense and ask him to elevate it. They handed him a protection problem that has gone unsolved for weeks and told him the answer was on the field Sunday. He did what he could with what he had.
The result was what the setup predicted.

title: Riq Woolen Makes Trade Deadline Hopes Clear as His Eagles Future Remains Uncertain
full_text:
PHILADELPHIA, P.A. — Riq Woolen doesn’t want to leave. The cornerback wants to see the season through with the Eagles, but that's out of his control.
Woolen has struggled in his first nine games with the Eagles, but he is still an attractive trade candidate for teams that believe they can challenge for the Super Bowl. Like, say, the Bears.
It’s up to general manager Howie Roseman to find a dance partner as the trade deadline arrives at 4 p.m. ET on Tuesday.
“It sucks as a human when you don't know the unknown, but you wanna know the unknown, you know what I'm saying?” Woolen said after the Eagles lost for a seventh straight time, falling to the Giants on Sunday afternoon .
There are other players who could be ex-Eagles by the time the trade deadline comes, including Moro Ojomo, Dallas Goedert, and maybe Landon Dickerson.
Could there even be a blockbuster for Jalen Carter?
It’s hard to do one deal, let alone two. Soon enough, we will find out how many times Roseman hits the dance floor.
For his part, Woolen is trying to stay focused on playing football, leaving the heavy lifting to Roseman and his agent on what his immediate future could hold.
“I'm gonna just leave it to them, and whatever I have to do, I still gotta suit up and play football, and I still gotta be able to provide for my family,” he said.
Even if it means he could be traded to a contending team?
“I mean, if you woke up every day with your friends, some of your close friends, and y'all worked hard as hell every day, and you just up and disappear when stuff got hard or when you just up and disappear, then it'd seem kind of weird, especially when it's on you, you know?” Woolen said. “If it's up to Howie and the GM and my agent, then I'm gonna leave it to them. But me as a person, I've worked hard with these guys, and I'd love to be here and stay here with them.”

title: Eagles Stock Market: New QB, Same Old Story With Milton After Giants Loss
full_text:
PHILADELPHIA—Another Sunday produced another loss that feels heavier than the final score.
The Eagles fell 19-11 to the Giants at Lincoln Financial Field, their seventh consecutive setback, and now sit at 2-7 heading into their bye week. Three weeks into his Philadelphia tenure, Joe Milton got the first NFL start, Saquon Barkley punched in an early score against his old team, and for a few minutes it looked like the offense might finally find a pulse.
Instead the second half turned into the same familiar grind: short drives, pressure, and a crowd that started leaving to beat the Olivia Rodrigo concert traffic that was looming across the street.
Here's our weekly Eagles' stock market:
The Eagles generated pressure, finished with five sacks, and made J.J. McCarthy uncomfortable before knocking him out for a short period with a hip injury. It wasn’t consistent all afternoon, but it was the clearest sign that the defensive front can still disrupt when it gets a chance. On a day short on bright spots, that was one of the few that actually pushed the other side backward.
Milton’s mobility gave the offense a different look. He picked up 64 rushing yards and converted the two-point conversion himself, creating a brief 8-6 lead. It wasn’t enough to sustain anything, but the mobility created a couple of positive plays that Tanner McKee, a pure pocket passer, hasn't produced in recent weeks. It's a small sample, but it was the one offensive wrinkle that didn’t immediately get stuffed.
In the same game Eagles punter Braden Mann had an 86-yard effort, the longest by an NFL player since the Giants' Rodney Williams' 90-yarder on Sept. 10, 2001 vs. Denver, the veteran also had one for minus-2 after mishandling a high snap from Rocco Underwood, and another for only 17.
There were no declarative statements about job security as the Eagles enter their bye week. Head coach Nick Sirianni is likely safe for now but scapegoat season could be ready to start earlier than expected with offensive coordinator Sean Mannion, offensive line coach Chris Kuper and run game coordinator Ryan Mahaffey all in some kind of peril.
"We'll talk," Sirianni said when asked if staff changes are on the table. "Obviously, right now my job is to be there for our guys and to go watch the tape and go look through everything. I think we always think -- we'll do everything. I'll do anything I can to help this team win football games. Like I said, I'll look at myself internally first and then go from there.
"My job is to coach the players and to coach the coaches, and anything I can do to help this team win games, we'll do. Everything can always be on the table, but I don't think you change just to change because that's what your record says that -- you've got to look at what's really real and not react to anything else. Again, I just don't believe you just change just to change. If you have a strong reason to do things in anything, not just change, but in anything and you're convicted on it, that's how we'll go about our business."
Milton the passer faded quickly, finishing 18 of 34 for 169 yards, while being sacked seven times and losing a fumble. Once the Giants adjusted, the rocket arm never found a rhythm and the protection broke down. The early spark was extinguished and by the second half the stock was trading like every other recent Eagles quarterback outing.
"For my first game here, I feel like I did all right," Milton said. "There are a lot of things that I can clean up as far as protection, just helping those guys out with protection. That's something that we're going to get better [at] this week coming up for sure.”
The offense after the first quarter was the clearest underperformer. Three points the rest of the way, repeated three-and-outs, and no sustained drives once the Giants got a beat on the tortured offensive system.
"Obviously, none of us offensively have done a good enough job," Sirianni said when asked about the embattled Sean Mannion. "We're not going to sit here as coaches -- and it's not Sean, it's all of us and it starts with me. I think the correct question there to me is, 'Do you think you've done a good enough job?'
"Obviously, I haven't done a good enough job. We all have things that we've got to get better at and we've got to figure it out on offense. I mean, I think our defense is playing solid. I think they're doing really good things and it's hard to keep the game there. I think we've got some things that we're doing on special teams that have been really good, and then we can be more consistent in that particular case, but we have to figure it out on offense. That's coaches, that's players, that's everybody.
"So no, I haven't done a good enough job yet. The only way you grow in the midst of adversity is to get up, keep fighting, and work and stick together because you need everybody to do that. But adversity gives you opportunities for growth that steady times never would, but only if you do all those other things. We'll fight and we'll keep going."
Unaccounted for rushers remain a weekly staple and a drain on the Eagles' offense. Milton was under constant pressure, the pocket collapsed on multiple series, and the line never established a consistent ability to communicate.  The lack of protection turned what started as a manageable game into the same stalled effort that has defined the losing streak. Until the offensive line stabilizes, the rest of the offense will stay limited.

title: Kracz: Nick Sirianni Looks Out of Answers as Bye Week Brings Decision Point on Job Security
full_text:
PHILADELPHIA – It’s quite possible the Eagles end the season with a 15-game losing streak, a 2-15 record, and a top-five draft pick.
It’s quite possible Nick Sirianni won’t be around to see the Eagles threaten the NFL record for consecutive losses. The 2008 Lions and 2017 Browns both went 0-16, so 16 is the record.
It’s quite possible that Sirianni has coached his last game. With all eyes on Tuesday’s trade deadline, there will be some rubbernecking this week with all eyes on Sirianni as the Eagles take their bye.
Jeffrey Lurie fired Chip Kelly with one game left in the 2015 season, but he allowed Ray Rhodes to stay until the end of a 3-13 season in 1998, he allowed Andy Reid to complete a 4-12 year in 2012, and Doug Pederson to finish a 4-11-1 year in 2020 before dropping the guillotine.
It stands to reason that Sirianni will be allowed to finish this year, no matter how it ends. He has made the playoffs in all five of his seasons and has taken the Eagles to two Super Bowls, helping the franchise win its second Lombardi Trophy just two years ago.
For some reason, he doesn’t get much credit for all that because the assumption is that he was handed a championship roster, which is the wrong assumption. What coach does that without talent, and how many coaches fail to do it with all that talent?
You could make the case that Sirianni should be allowed to return for the 2027 season because, really, what team can survive 12 games without its starting quarterback? To run it back in 2027 is probably asking too much at this point, because the coach doesn’t seem to have any answers on how to end this losing streak.
Maybe the decision to relieve him of his duties has already been made. The coach was late to his press conference after Sunday’s 19-11 loss to the New York Giants—another game in which the offense was terrible.
It took about 75 minutes after the game ended for him to get to the podium. Asked about his tardiness, he said he had players stopping by his office to talk. There is speculation that maybe they stopped in to say good-bye, knowing he won’t be back when the team reconvenes after taking this week off.
Here’s what the coach said about keeping reporters waiting to fire questions at him: “Everyone puts everything they have into this, so I want to make sure I talk to every guy first of all after the game.
“Then a couple of the guys stopped in the office just to talk through it. That's not unusual. I appreciate the connection that we have there. But yeah, it was a little bit later because of that. So, I appreciate you guys waiting around and waiting on that because I'm always going to be there for my players first and foremost.”
The locker room isn’t a fun place these days, obviously. The mood is somber, almost funeral—no music, no smiles, just beaten-down players trying to find answers.
If one thing is clear at this stage, it’s that Sirianni has no ideas how to turn the team’s fortunes around.
He continues to talk about details and how everything is on the table, but that change for the sake of change isn't necessarily the answer. Of course, he said that last week too about Tanner McKee, anointing him “our guy” one day, then 24 hours later, changing his mind.
So, who knows what to believe from him anymore?
“We all have things that we've got to get better at and we've got to figure it out on offense,” he said. “I mean, I think our defense is playing solid. I think they're doing really good things and it's hard to keep the game there. I think we've got some things that we're doing on special teams that have been really good, and then we can be more consistent in that particular case, but we have to figure it out on offense. That's coaches, that's players, that's everybody.”
Eagles on SI followed up by asking why the offense has been so difficult to figure out halfway through the season.
His answer: “It's a little bit of everything and it starts with me, and I have to do my best and get everybody playing with the level of detail and coaching with the level of detail that has become our standard here for the Philadelphia Eagles. I'll fight like hell to do that.”
Nine games in it seems he has lost the fight.

title: 5 Losers & 5 Winners From Eagles' Week 9 Defeat to Giants
full_text:
PHILADELPHIA – Some players may have played their final game in an Eagles uniform . General manager Howie Roseman now knows where his team stands after losing to the New York Giants, 19-11, on Sunday afternoon at Lincoln Financial Field.
It was the Eagles' seventh straight loss, but more importantly, their third straight defeat inside a dreadful NFC East.
Turning to Joe Milton didn’t help much, though the quarterback showed his mobility and led the team in rushing with 64 yards on nine runs and was 18-for-34 with 169 passing yards.
New York coach John Harbaugh improved to 16-3 coming out of a bye, and he led the Giants to their first win in Philly since Oct. 27, 2013.
To get a sense of just how long that has been, Michael Vick was the starting quarterback, but a hamstring injury forced him to yield to Matt Barkley. Linebacker Najee Good scored the Eagles' only points on a two-yard fumble return for a touchdown.
This year’s version of the Eagles are now 2-7 as they head into their bye. They could look different when they take the field again at home on Nov. 22 against the Pittsburgh Steelers. The NFL trade deadline is Tuesday at 4 p.m.
Will players like Moro Ojomo, Dallas Goedert, Riq Woolen, and maybe some others still be here on the other side of the deadline?
They probably shouldn’t be. The win lifted the Giants to 5-2-1. That’s three games clear in the win column ahead of the Eagles. There's no sense pretending that they can, so it’s time to shift into evaluation mode and load up with some draft picks for the future.
Sean Mannion: There’s no reason that, halfway through the season, his offense is still struggling to find traction with its first-year offensive coordinator . The Eagles went three-and-out on their first three second-half possessions.
Is it any wonder the defense gets gashed late in games? They simply run out of gas.
The defense gave up 27 unanswered points in last week’s loss to the Commanders and didn’t score until 1:56 was left in the game on a 45-yard field goal from Jake Elliott to cut the deficit to 19-11.
Pass protection: Line coach Chris Kuper has to figure this out. Milton was sacked seven times. It was surprising he got back up after another unblocked pressure got home when Arvell Reese raced untouched off the edge and de-cleated the Eagles' QB. Reese should have wrapped up NFC Defensive Player of the Week honors with three sacks and 12 tackles.
Riq Woolen: This is a recording. It was another bad game in a string of them for the cornerback.
Second quarter decision: Faced with fourth-and-1 from the NY 40, the Eagles lined up in a shotgun formation and handed the ball to Barkley. The play went nowhere as the offensive line was overwhelmed at the point of attack. No problem with the decision, but you have a 6-5 quarterback who was already successful on a goal-line tush push. Why not try it again?
Third-down woes: The Eagles converted just 5-of-17 (29 percent). They were also 1-for-2 on fourth down.
Pass rush: The Eagles entered with 10 sacks and got five in the first half. They finished with six. Jonathan Greenard got the sack parade started with his first since arriving in the offseason. Zack Baun had two with Jalen Carter, Jordan Davis, and Nolan Smith adding one each on quarterback J.J. McCarthy. It was the fifth of the season for both Carter and Smith.
Makai Lemon: The rookie was active early and finished with six receptions for 61 yards. It was his third straight game with at least five catches and 50 yards. However, he did drop two passes.
Braden Mann: Sure, the punter had a 27-yard shank, and there was the -2 yard punt when he had a snap sail through his hands, but his boot saved the Eagles from possibly allowing points at the end of the half. He booted an 86-yard punt from his own end zone with 26 seconds left in the half; the Giants had designs on trying to grab points, but Mann ended those hopes, helping the Eagles take an 8-6 halftime lead. It was the longest punt since Rodney Williams had a 90-yard punt on Sept. 10, 2001.
Saquon Barkley: For the third straight game, the banged-up running back scored a rushing touchdown. All three of them came in the first quarter. His three-yard burst on Sunday gave the Eagles an 8-6 lead.
First quarter decision: It’s rarely advisable to take points off the scoreboard once they’ve been added, but Nick Sirianni did just that when the Giants were called for too many players on the field after Jake Elliott made a PAT. Sirianni accepted the penalty, and the ball was placed at the 1. Milton’s tush push was good for two points, so instead of leading 7-6, it was 8-6.

title: Eagles’ Backup Quarterback Carousel Has Been a Self-Inflicted Mess
full_text:
PHILADELPHIA - The Eagles have spent the better part of two years proving they never really trusted Tanner McKee, and the results have been predictably ugly.
It started in 2025. Multiple teams called on the former sixth-rounder who had shown some promise in limited action. One NFC South club even put a third-round pick on the table, according to an NFL source. The Eagles said no.
Per his reputation, GM Howie Roseman wanted a second-round pick. That would indicate the Eagles were high on McKee. That's what they said publicly and intimated behind the scenes as well.
Actions speak louder than words, however. Even if you want to ignore Sam Howell's acquisition in 2025 and trace it to McKee's thumb injury, which he suffered in training camp, in hindsight, it’s pretty obvious that McKee would have had a very short leash if he needed to play that season.
This offseason, the more accomplished Howell signed with Dallas and is now backing up Dak Prescott, ironically beating out Joe Milton for that role, who will start Sunday for the Eagles against the NFC East-leading New York Giants after McKee was benched despite what head coach Nick Sirianni called “solid play.”
Rewind to spring, when the Eagles traded a future seventh-round draft choice for veteran Andy Dalton.
That move told you everything about the organization’s belief, or lack thereof, in McKee. You don’t spend a draft pick on a 38-year-old veteran if you’re truly comfortable with the young guy already on the roster.
Through this spring and summer, the Eagles split the backup reps, but the lean was clear. Dalton got second-team work more often. He opened the regular season as the official QB2.
That lasted until Chicago. Jalen Hurts took a hit and went into the blue tent for a concussion check. Dalton came in and, on his only throw of the night, threw an interception. McKee was immediately elevated back to the primary backup even though the next game was on a short week.
The further context was a Philadelphia Inquirer report that rookie Makai Lemon ran the wrong route , essentially hanging Dalton out to dry on the pick in the end zone.
Then the roster crunch hit. The Eagles released Dalton to make room on the 53-man roster. When Hurts developed blood clots and it became clear he was done for the year, the organization wanted Dalton back. He chose Atlanta instead.
The veteran they’d traded for, favored in camp, and briefly installed as the starter’s understudy wanted no part of returning. Meanwhile, McKee's confidence waned while on the Yo-Yo, and his play suffered.
The Eagles signed Milton off the Dallas practice squad after Dalton's snub . Within a week, he was the QB2 over the Eagles' own 2026 draft pick, Cole Payton.
Three weeks after he arrived, with the team at 2-6 and McKee having gone 0-3 as the starter, Sirianni made the switch . Milton, who had never started an NFL game and had been with the Eagles for less than a month, was named the starter.
The entire McKee situation is an advanced class of mismanagement. Instead of selling high when they could have, the Eagles got greedy and passed on meaningful draft capital for McKee, then undercut him by bringing in Dalton and favoring the veteran.
From there, it was demoting Dalton after one interception that wasn’t his mistake and releasing him when it was convenient.
A strong relationship between Dalton’s wife and Sirianni’s was not enough to repair the work relationship, though, so the Eagles had to go outside the organization for a practice-squad arm, albeit a very impressive one, and use that card despite only being in the Jefferson Health Training Complex for three weeks.
Amazingly, the Eagles began the tortured 2026 season with four QBs on the initial 53-man roster (Hurts, Dalton, McKee, and Payton), yet believed in one (and there were plenty of questions inside the organization about Hurts as well).
None will start this Sunday in what will be the last opportunity to salvage the second half of the season.
Instead of selling when McKee’s stock was highest, the Eagles will now either move him for next to nothing at next Tuesday’s trade deadline or watch him sign a minimal deal elsewhere next spring.

title: Eagles vs. Giants: Who Wins and Why in NFC East's Week 9 Matchup
full_text:
PHILADELPHIA – The Eagles will reach their bye after hosting the New York Giants on Sunday (1 p.m.). Will they make it there with a seven-game losing streak and a 2-7 record, or will the slide end against their NFC East rival?
The Giants are the Eagles’ third straight opponent coming in rested. New York was on its bye last week. The Washington Commanders entered last week’s game off their bye, while the Dallas Cowboys entered Monday night’s matchup two weeks ago with11 days off.
Here are some matchups to watch:
Joe Milton will make his first career start against a Giants defense ranked 11th overall, and he will do so without the team’s top two receivers, DeVonta Smith and Tay Wicks. Smith has played just four games for the Eagles this season, yet still leads the team in receiving yards with 310. This will be Wicks’ third straight game missing from the lineup.
Milton gives the Eagles more mobility in the pocket than Tanner McKee did, but he has only been with the Eagles for three weeks.
“How much of the playbook do I think I know? Shoot, whatever’s in this week,” said Milton earlier in the week. … it’s a rough estimate for the percentage, but I feel like I know what I need to know for sure.”
New York has one of the best secondaries in the game and is ranked third in the league in pass defense, allowing184.9 yards per game. Milton could lean on the rookie in the pass game.
Lemon has had at least six catches for 50-plus yards in his last two games. His 31 catches are fourth-best among all rookie receivers, behind Carnell Tate (34), KC Concepcion (33), and Germie Berand (32).
Philly has been historically bad at stopping the run this year, surrendering more than 100 rushing yards in every game this year. It is the longest streak to start a season since 1968, when the Eagles went 2-12.
The Eagles may catch a break with Cam Skattebo listed as doubtful. Devin Singletary would likely get the bulk of the carries if Skattebo can’t play.
Left tackle Jordan Mailata is the only player on the Eagles’ offensive line who has played every snap and is the only OT in the league in the top five in run blocking (83.7) and pass blocking (82.2), per Pro Football Focus. Rookie right tackle Markel Bell struggled mightily in last week’s loss to the Commanders.
The Giants’ primary edge rushers are Abdul Carter and Keyvon Thibodeaux after losing Brian Burns to a season-ending injury. Carter has two sacks while Thibodeaux is still looking for his first of the season.
The Giants receiver was named the NFC player of the Month for October after a having 36 catches for a league-high 509 yards and two touchdowns.
The All-Pro Mitchell is quietly having a good season despite the team’s poor play overall. PFF has him ranked second in passer rating allowed at 65.5 just behind Jacob Parrish’s 65.3. Mitchell has given up 27 receptions on 50 targets for 293 yards, per Next Gen Stats.
Predicted season record: 8-0

title: Eagles' Bet on Joe Milton's Unique Trait Could Actually Pay Off
full_text:
PHILADELPHIA - The Eagles have spent the past six weeks watching their season slowly drain away one disappointing drive and stalled possession at a time. Now, with the record at 2-6 and the offense looking lifeless, they’ve decided the only remaining move is a fastball.
They’re handing the keys to Joe Milton and his souped-up right arm.
It’s a pure talent bet, the kind of Hail Mary organizations make when conventional options have already failed. Jalen Hurts is out indefinitely with blood clots. Tanner McKee went 0-3 as the starter despite “solid” play, according to head coach Nick Sirianni.
The offense has been outgained by nearly 900 yards during the Eagles’ six-game losing streak. So they reached for the 6-foot-5, 236-pound quarterback with the rocket launcher hanging from his right shoulder who was still on the Dallas practice squad three weeks ago.
That arm talent, coupled with impressive mobility, are the selling points with Milton.
“Obviously, he's talented, and he's been here for a couple weeks now,” Sirianni said. “Very talented arm, very talented athlete, can process and make decisions out there. Just a lot of good qualities that he has. I like his confidence and everything that he brings, and it's been fun getting to know him and working with him."
At the 2024 NFL Scouting Combine, Milton unleashed a 62 mph throw—the hardest recorded that year and a mark that sits near the top of combine history. Teammates have already started using the same language when discussing Milton’s juice when throwing the football.
“It is a f@#king cannon,” offensive tackle Jordan Mailata said after watching Milton throw. Both Eli Stowers and Makai Lemon marveled at the RPMs of his passes.
Milton doesn’t just have arm strength; he has the kind of velocity that changes the calculus for a defense. In theory at least, windows that close on other quarterbacks stay open longer when the ball arrives that fast.
On Thursday, speaking for the first time as the Eagles’ starter, Milton sounded like a man who had spent years waiting for exactly this moment.
Three weeks ago he was on the practice squad for Dallas behind Dak Prescott and former Eagles backup Sam Howell.
“I was just pretty much going through the plays, going through the week like I was a starter, or like I was playing, and just being ready,” Milton said. “And that’s what the NFL is about: just being ready when your name is called, and just preparing for those moments.”
The moment is here despite only a three-week crash course in Philadelphia’s offense. When asked how much of the Eagles’ playbook he’s mastered, Milton laughed.
“Shoot, whatever’s in this week.”
It’s the answer of a player who understands the assignment. This isn’t a long-term developmental plan. It’s a short-term attempt at creating a spark and keeping hope alive in one of the NFL’s worst divisions.
Milton has never started an NFL game. In five career appearances, he’s completed 37 of 53 passes for 424 yards with two touchdowns and two interceptions.
The most extended look came in the 2024 season finale with New England, when he went 22-of-29 for 241 yards and a touchdown while also scoring on the ground. The physical tools have always been obvious. The consistency has always been the question.
Milton’s approach on Thursday was about being present in the moment.
“Just be where my feet are. Smile,” he said. “I love seeing people around me smile, so just making sure everyone around me is smiling. Whatever the play call comes through my helmet, just call that play and execute.”
Milton has an ebullient personality. He often bounces around to the music during stretching and made sure to introduce himself to as many teammates as possible when he arrived in South Philadelphia.
It’s easy to be loose when you’re a backup, though. Now, the microscope is on Milton against the NFC East-leading New York Giants and QB J.J. McCarthy, like Milton, a former “Michigan Man” and a friend.
“I’m going to play my game and stay within the offense, and that’s the job,” said Milton. “It’s football and I’m looking forward to the opportunity to lead this team and play the game I love."
“This is a great opportunity.”
The Eagles are betting that the combination of arm talent and that mindset can create the explosive plays the offense has lacked.
Whether Milton can process quickly enough, throw with touch and accuracy when velocity isn’t the answer, and protect the ball while doing it remains the great unknown.
But the Eagles are out of better options. On Sunday against the Giants, they’ll find out whether the strongest arm in the game can do what the other options could not: make the season feel like it still has a pulse.

title: Nick Sirianni's Eagles QB Change Secrecy Shows His Desperate State
full_text:
Nick Sirianni wanted to keep the lid on his quarterback switch for as long as he could. The big secret lasted about an hour, when the information was given to a national media outlet instead of the 15-20 members of the local press who cover the team on a day-in, day-out basis.
Instead of telling the beat writers at his early afternoon press conference on Wednesday that Tanner McKee was being benched after three games and newcomer Joe Milton would be taking his place, the Eagles' head coach chose not to give up that information.
ESPN’s Adam Schefter broke the story. Sirianni defended his decision not to reveal the news an hour earlier when he talked to local beat reporters on Friday.
“I was going to hold onto that as long as I possibly could, every second, every minute,” he said on his final day of media availability before the first-place New York Giants visit on Sunday.
So, Sirianni clung to his secret for roughly 60 minutes , or 3,600 seconds. The coach clings to the idea of competitive advantage, but did it really matter that the Giants were in the dark for an extra hour?
“Again, I'm not real shy with you guys,” he said. “I'm going to tell you what I want to tell you guys. I respect the job that y'all have to do, but I'm going to tell you what I want to tell you guys because I'm always going to protect the team first and foremost.
“Every second that goes by in a situation like that, that you can hold onto information as long as you possibly can, is a little less time for the opponent to get ready for the game. I know there's a lot of interest in everything that you all want to hear, the fans want to hear. My job is to win football games, do everything we can do to help win football games, protect the guys here on this football team, and handle everything that I can inside.”
Sirianni’s secret left his players hung out to dry , to field questions about the QB switch. Jordan Mailata and Landon Dickerson tried to protect their coach’s competitive advantage by saying Milton and McKee split reps at Wednesday’s practice.
The coach said on Monday that McKee was “our guy,” which is what he told reporters during his Monday Zoom call. It was on Tuesday that he decided he was no longer the guy. What changed ?
“We had just gotten off of the game, and then you're starting to look through the game and the game plan,” he said. “As you start to put ideas down—and things are fluid, things are fluid. Like I said, the toughest part about this, in my mind, is that, again, I felt Tanner did solid. I thought he did a lot of good things. That's always tough, and you wear that as the coach. I know it's tough for Tanner, too.”
Sirianni said the decision to make the move was talked through in “great detail” with general manager Howie Roseman and a slew of offensive assistants, including offensive coordinator Sean Mannion and QB coach Parks Frazier.
“We just talk through it,” said the coach. “At the end of the day, my job as the head coach is to make these decisions that I think is best for the football team, but you discuss everything with everybody.”

title: Mike McCarthy Addresses Steelers Trade Deadline Urgency
full_text:
Pittsburgh Steelers head coach Mike McCarthy isn't wasting too much of his time or energy worrying about the impending NFL trade deadline, nor has he ever really done so.
During his press conference as the Steelers return from their Week 9 bye and get set to face the Cincinnati Bengals on Sunday Night Football in Week 10, McCarthy joked that he didn't even know when the trade deadline was for a large portion of his time as a head coach.
"I spent a decade in my life as a head coach, I didn't know when the hell the trade deadline was. I just knew it was somewhere around the middle of the season," McCarthy said.
McCarthy, who was originally asked if seeing other contending teams like the Jacksonville Jaguars be aggressive on the trade market could motivate Pittsburgh to make some moves, stated that his focus is on the players currently in the building and that he has confidence in the organization's brain trust to handle all of the deadline activity.
"I get it, everybody wants to improve their roster, and I have great confidence in [general manager] Omar [Khan] and [owner] Art [Rooney II] if there's something there, we'll do the right thing," McCarthy said. "But I think it's very important for me as the head coach to keep my eye on the target, and that's the 68-plus [players] that are in the building. So if we add someone that's gonna help us win, everybody would be for that... The most important thing is, I've always done this, I worry about the ones that are here. Coach the ones that are here and keep building what we got going. We have a lot of positive energy going right now, and we got a big-time game, Sunday Night Football in Cincinnati."
As has been the case for over a month at this point, all eyes are on the wide receiver market for the Steelers.
ESPN's Jeremy Fowler stated that Pittsburgh "doesn't want to give up a lot of draft capital" for a receiver during an appearance on "The Aftermath" and mentioned Tennessee Titans veteran Calvin Ridley as a player who might "make sense in that regard."
The likes of Josh Downs (Indianapolis Colts) and Brian Thomas Jr. (Jacksonville Jaguars) have been connected to the Steelers over recent weeks, though if the organization really isn't comfortable paying up for players in that sort of tier, they might have to settle for someone like Ridley or Jauan Jennings (Minnesota Vikings) in exchange for a late Day 3 pick.
Cornerback is another position to watch for Pittsburgh, though it's been a bit quiet on that front over recent days, and the team's priority at the moment appears to be adding a receiver rather than supplementing their secondary.

title: Steelers vs. Eagles Game Moved to New Time
full_text:
The Pittsburgh Steelers ' Week 11 game against the Philadelphia Eagles has been flexed.
Originally scheduled to kick off at 4:25 p.m. EST from Lincoln Financial Field, the NFL has now moved the start time of the contest up to 1:00 p.m. EST, per ESPN's Adam Schefter.
A matchup between the Jacksonville Jaguars and New York Giants at MetLife Stadium will move back to the 4:25 p.m. EST slot that the Steelers-Eagles contest has vacated.
Flex: A Week 11 schedule change with the Jaguars-Giants moving to 4:25 p.m. ET, and Steelers-Eagles to 1 p.m. ET.
What initially looked like one of the tougher games on Pittsburgh's schedule at the onset of the season has now lost a good amount of its luster, even if the Battle of Pennsylvania is still sure to draw some level of intrigue.
The Eagles are currently mired in a seven-game losing streak, which has seen their record plummet to 2-7, while starting quarterback Jalen Hurts is also out for the remainder of the year due to blood clots in his lungs and hasn't played since Week 5.
While the Steelers are always a draw in terms of ratings and fan interest, and the same could be said for Philadelphia, there just isn't as much stakes on the line for both sides as originally expected.
It's still a big game for Pittsburgh , though, who is currently 6-2 and riding a four-game win streak as it comes off of its Week 9 bye and gets ready to face the Cincinnati Bengals for a Sunday Night Football  showdown on the road this week before facing the Eagles in Week 11.
If the Steelers don't find a way to win in Philadelphia this season, it's probably just not meant to be as a whole.
While the two teams don't face one another often due to the fact that they play in separate conferences, Pittsburgh has still played a total of 41 road games against the Eagles.
Philadelphia has completely dominated those matchups, going 30-9-2 while outscoring the Steelers 820-528 over that span (per The Football Database ). The last time Pittsburgh won in Philadelphia was all the way back in 1965, and it is 0-4 at Lincoln Financial Field.
The Steelers have a fantastic opportunity to finally break that skid this time around, though. The Eagles' defense still has its moments, as evidenced by the fact that they recorded six sacks in a Week 9 loss to the Giants, though the offense has completely sputtered with both Tanner McKee and Joe Milton III at quarterback in place of Hurts.
In a tightly-contested race at the top of the AFC North with the Bengals, who are also 6-2, Pittsburgh really can't afford a loss to Philadelphia in what's shaping up as one of the easier games left on its schedule.

title: Josh Downs Performance Should End Steelers Trade Thoughts
full_text:
PITTSBURGH -- The Pittsburgh Steelers are in hot pursuit of a wide receiver to upgrade their offense. The 2026 NFL Trade Deadline is rapidly approaching, leaving general manager Omar Khan a brief window to bring a true offensive weapon to Pittsburgh.
The receiver most frequently tied to the Steelers is Indianapolis Colts pass-catcher Josh Downs. The 25-year-old has had two productive seasons in the NFL and is in the final year of his rookie contract, making him a low-cost option with upside.
Times are tough in Indianapolis. The Colts have sold off two key players already (Quenton Nelson and DeForest Buckner) and could make several more moves before the deadline passes. Downs makes a ton of sense for the Steelers,
Sadly, he demonstrated in the Colts' latest game that he has talent and potential, but he's not the answer for the Steelers.
The positives Downs brings are evident. He's incredibly quick and can create separation, two traits the Steelers desperately need more of in their wide receiver room.
But one play erased any of the upside that he might bring. The Colts took on the Dallas Cowboys in their Week 9 matchup. Downs has struggled over recent weeks, posting less than 50 receiving yards in five consecutive contests heading into the game.
Week 9 changed nothing for Downs or his trade stock. If anything, it plummeted it. On a third down play in the second quarter, the Colts needed eight yards to gain a first down.
Downs ran a simple hitch route that put him just short of the line to gain. The route was a perfect one for the defensive coverage the Cowboys played on third down, and quarterback Daniel Jones delivered a slightly off-target ball.
It wasn't a perfect throw, but it was a very catchable ball for Downs that could have easily gotten the Colts another set of downs.
Instead, Downs couldn't haul in the pass and the Colts' offense fled the field. NFL insider Ari Meirov shared a clip of the play via his X account.
#Colts WR Josh Downs dropped a pass, and his brother, #Cowboys S Caleb Downs, was right there to trash-talk him. 😂 pic.twitter.com/tWir58SXdo
A dropped pass isn't the end of the world, right?
Ordinarily, that is exactly the case. I would downplay concerns about dropped passes, but in this scenario, it was a flashing warning sign
The Steelers need a boost to their offense, but not just any addition. The offense needs a receiver who can come through in the toughest moments. Creating separation is one thing, but that receiver also has to earn the trust of one of the best quarterbacks in the history of the NFL.
The Steelers want to go on a long playoff run as Aaron Rodgers says his goodbyes to the NFL. Having another talented receiver helps, but it won't matter much if Rodgers doesn't trust him on third down.
That's who the Steelers need to acquire. Sadly, it's not Josh Downs.

title: Calvin Ridley Incident Could Complicate Steelers Trade Interest
full_text:
PITTSBURGH -- The Pittsburgh Steelers have just over 24 hours before the 2026 NFL trade deadline passes them by. The organization has multiple needs they will hopefully address before the deadline expires, but none feel more pressing than adding a wide receiver.
Because of that obvious need, the Steelers have been tied to nearly every possible trade candidate on the market. Whether it's the top name discussed, Indianapolis Colts receiver Josh Downs, or veteran Tennessee Titans pass-catcher Calvin Ridley, the Steelers have been connected to all of them.
Ridley has suddenly become a more coveted trade target in the final hours before the deadline, but a recent incident during his bye week might complicate things too much for Pittsburgh's liking.
According to a report from WKRN , a Nashville publication, Ridley was involved in an undisclosed incident at Nashville International Airport. The team released a statement confirming Ridley's involvement, but did not provide any further details.
"We are aware of the incident and are in communication with Metropolitan Nashville Airport Authority,” the team said. “We will not be able to comment any further at this time."
The team's interest in Ridley may not have him as their top target, but this news should end any thoughts about the possibility. No details are known about what transpired at Nashville International Airport, and that's perfectly fine. It's no one's business what happened.
Regardless, the Steelers should take any warning and sign of caution as encouragement to abandon any possible trade talks with the Titans.
The biggest reason for this is because the player is already a questionable target. Ridley is in his third season with the Titans, and each year has been another step backward for the veteran. His first season in Tennessee was a fantastic season, putting up 1,017 receiving yards and hauling in four touchdowns. Last season, injuries derailed his campaign, limiting him to just seven games with 303 yards.
So far in 2026, he's been an afterthought. He's played in seven games but has received only 13 targets. That's translated into six receptions for 91 yards and zero touchdowns.
That's a combined 49 receptions and 394 yards over his last 14 games played. The average yards per reception is exciting, sure, but it disguises the reality. Ridley is no longer the effective route runner and separator that made him a multiple-time 1,000-yard receiver.
Add in any sort of off-the-field issues, whatever they may be, and it's a bit of salt in the wound. Ridley was already a trade target who provided little excitement to the Steelers, and this latest incident only complicated the matter further.

title: Ladd McConkey for Roman Wilson? Steelers Trade Idea is Interesting
full_text:
PITTSBURGH -- The Pittsburgh Steelers are expected to be buyers at the NFL trade deadline and wide receiver is the position to watch.
As for who they are going to land, if anyone, it's still up in the air. Josh Downs of the Indianapolis Colts, Brian Thomas Jr. of the Jacksonville Jaguars and Calvin Ridley of the Tennessee Titans have all been floated as leading candidates. But there has also been some discourse about bigger names who may not be available, but teams may be trying to test the waters with.
Ladd McConkey has been one of those bigger names, being mentioned as a player teams like the Steelers may be interested in calling about. All reports claim the Los Angeles Chargers do not have interest in dealing their leading wide receiver, but that hasn't stopped conversations about opposing teams acquiring him.
CBS Sports' Bryan DeArdo was amongst those discussing the possibility, pitching a trade idea that lands McConkey and the Chargers' 2027 fifth-round pick in the NFL Draft in exchange for the Steelers' 2027 second-round pick and wide receiver Roman Wilson.
"It's possible that the Steelers wouldn't have to part with Wilson in this scenario, but if the Chargers want a replacement for McConkey, it would likely be Wilson, who had success at Michigan with Jim Harbaugh," DeArdo writes.
"The Chargers also probably don't want to part with McConkey, a former 1,000-yard receiver who is still playing on his rookie contract. However, getting another receiver — in addition to a second-round pick — could be enough for the Chargers to move McConkey."
It might. Wilson also has another year left on his rookie contract, so Los Angeles would be receiving a wideout who would stick around for longer than the season. Wilson is also in the midst of his first season as a real contributor to the Steelers' offense, catching 14 passes for 188 yards and two touchdowns in five games.
While Wilson is currently on Injured Reserve with a finger injury, he's eligible to return after Week 10 and has begun working with trainers on the sideline during practice, which is a good sign that he's getting ready to at least return to practice once eligible.
The Chargers would be more interested in the second-round pick over Wilson, but it might be the sweetener they'd need to actually consider trading McConkey.
As for the Steelers' side of things, there's no reason this trade wouldn't work. They should be willing to give up a second-round pick for a player who might take them to the next level offensively. Plus, McConkey comes with another year of play, meaning Pittsburgh could try to negotiate a long-term deal in the offseason without having to worry about losing him.
If it works out, he and Germie Bernard are an exciting duo to help welcome a younger quarterback next season and beyond.
Chances are, the Steelers have a much higher likelihood of landing Downs, Thomas, Ridley or a small name at the deadline . McConkey would be a game-changing move, though. And to give up Wilson and a second to land him and a fifth-round pick? It might be worth it.
